campaign.title: FlashSale mattress countdown
campaign.text: Own-brand webshop promotion for the CloudRest mattress. Every product page shows a red banner: 'HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41' with a live countdown, and 'Only 3 left in stock!'. The countdown resets to three hours whenever it reaches zero or the visitor returns, and stock is not actually limited (fulfilment is made-to-order with 2,000+ units weekly capacity). Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.

detected_practices: false scarcity claim ('Only 3 left in stock!')
false 'last chance / tonight only' recurring email claim
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is general adult EU consumers; no indication of specific minor targeting. GDPR flagged because email marketing to individual consumers necessarily involves processing personal data (email addresses, likely consent/opt-in and unsubscribe obligations).
triage.summary: Own-brand webshop and recurring email promotion for the CloudRest mattress using a resetting countdown timer and a 'Only 3 left in stock!' claim, despite unlimited made-to-order capacity, plus weekly 'tonight only / last chance' emails. The urgency and scarcity signals are objectively false, raising misleading-practice and dark-pattern concerns. Targeted at general adult EU consumers with no declared AI or personalisation.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The recurring weekly email to individual consumers is direct marketing that processes personal data (email addresses), which requires a valid lawful basis. For email marketing this is generally prior consent (per ePrivacy) or a narrowly qualified legitimate interest / soft opt-in. The campaign text provides no information on how recipients were enrolled or what basis is relied on, so compliance cannot be confirmed.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for the email list: confirm recipients gave GDPR-standard opt-in consent (or qualify for the existing-customer soft opt-in), and retain records demonstrating it for every recipient of the Thursday blast.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Every direct-marketing communication must respect the data subject's absolute right to object and must facilitate opt-out. A recurring weekly marketing email engages this obligation, but the campaign material does not describe an unsubscribe mechanism or suppression-list handling.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Ensure each email contains a clear, one-click unsubscribe link, that objections are honoured immediately and permanently via a suppression list, and that opting out is as easy as opting in.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Where an email marketing channel that processes personal data is used to convey objectively false urgency/scarcity signals (a countdown that silently resets and a false 'Only 3 left' claim), the fairness dimension of Art. 5(1)(a) is engaged in addition to the primary UCPD misleading-practice concerns. This is flagged for awareness; the deception itself is principally a UCPD matter.
findings.evidence_quote: HURRY — sale ends in 02:59:41
findings.recommendation: Align the marketing content with the fairness principle by removing the false urgency/scarcity claims; ensure any deadline or stock figure communicated through data-processing channels is truthful and verifiable.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's substantive violations (false urgency/scarcity, resetting countdown) fall under the UCPD, not GDPR. GDPR is engaged only because the recurring email blast is direct marketing that necessarily processes personal data (email addresses). The campaign text does not describe the lawful basis, consent capture, transparency notices, or unsubscribe/opt-out mechanics, so no GDPR breach can be affirmatively established from the material — but the relevant obligations (Art. 6(1) lawful basis, Art. 21 right to object, Art. 5(1)(a) fairness) are clearly engaged and should be verified. No profiling, personalisation, special-category data, or minor targeting is declared or evident.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: A resetting/perpetual countdown timer falsely states the offer is available only for a very limited time in order to elicit an immediate purchase decision. This is a per se prohibited practice under Annex I point 7 regardless of consumer impact — no averaging or materiality test applies. The reset mechanism is direct evidence the deadline is fictitious.

findings.recommendation: Remove the countdown timer, or only display a genuine, fixed, non-resetting deadline after which the promotional price actually and verifiably ends. Never reset the timer on return visits or when it reaches zero.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: A false low-stock claim ('only 2 left'/'Only 3 left') is expressly named in Annex I point 7 as blacklisted false scarcity. The trader admits stock is effectively unlimited via made-to-order production, so the statement is objectively false and prohibited in all circumstances.

findings.recommendation: Delete the 'Only 3 left in stock!' banner. Given made-to-order fulfilment there is no genuine scarcity; if real stock limits ever apply, display only accurate, real-time inventory figures.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The recurring 'last chance, tonight only' claim contains false information about the existence and duration of a specific price advantage, deceiving the average consumer about the terms and availability of the offer and likely causing a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. This is a misleading action under Art. 6, alongside the per se Annex I point 7 breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Stop describing a permanently recurring weekly promotion as 'last chance' or 'tonight only'. Only use finality/deadline language when the offer genuinely ends and will not be repeated.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The combination of persistent weekly high-pressure 'last chance' emails with on-site resetting countdowns and false scarcity applies sustained time pressure (undue influence) that can significantly impair the average consumer's freedom of choice, engaging the aggressive-practices prohibition through the factors of timing and persistence.
findings.evidence_quote: Email blast repeats 'last chance, tonight only' every Thursday.
findings.recommendation: Reduce artificial time pressure across channels: eliminate manufactured deadlines and repeated urgency messaging so purchase decisions are not coerced by false imminence.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses objectively false urgency and scarcity signals that are prohibited in all circumstances under UCPD Annex I. A resetting/perpetual countdown timer and an "Only 3 left in stock!" message, admitted to be untrue given 2,000+ units weekly made-to-order capacity, are textbook per se blacklisted practices (Annex I point 7). The same false statements also constitute misleading actions (Art. 6), and the relentless recurring "last chance/tonight only" pressure engages the aggressive-practices prohibition (Arts. 8-9). No good-faith interpretation makes these claims true; the fix is to remove or truthfully substantiate every urgency/scarcity signal.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes the CloudRest mattress on your webshop and via a weekly email blast, using a red countdown timer ("sale ends in 02:59:41"), an "Only 3 left in stock!" banner, and recurring "last chance, tonight only" emails. The core problem is that these urgency and scarcity signals are simply not true: the countdown resets every time it hits zero or a visitor returns, stock is effectively unlimited (made-to-order at 2,000+ units per week), and the "tonight only" sale actually runs every Thursday. Under EU consumer law (UCPD), false countdowns and fake low-stock claims are on the blacklist of practices banned in all circumstances — there is no "it depends" or leniency here, and no way to interpret them as truthful. The repeated high-pressure messaging also risks counting as an aggressive practice. Separately, the weekly marketing email raises GDPR housekeeping points (you must be able to show you have consent to email each recipient and provide a working unsubscribe), though these are lower-severity and can be verified. The overall verdict is critical: the campaign cannot run in its current form and needs the false urgency/scarcity elements removed before launch.
recommendations: Remove the resetting countdown timer immediately. Only show a deadline if the sale genuinely ends at a fixed date/time and the price actually rises afterwards — never reset it on return visits or when it hits zero.
Delete the 'Only 3 left in stock!' banner. With made-to-order fulfilment there is no real scarcity; show real-time accurate inventory only if a genuine limit ever applies.

Stop using 'last chance' / 'tonight only' language in the recurring Thursday emails. A promotion that runs every week is not a last chance; only use finality language when the offer truly ends and will not be repeated.
Reduce overall time pressure across web and email so purchase decisions are not driven by manufactured imminence (mitigates the aggressive-practices risk once the false claims are removed).
Verify and document the GDPR lawful basis for the email list — confirm each recipient gave opt-in consent or qualifies for the existing-customer soft opt-in, and retain the records.
Ensure every marketing email carries a clear one-click unsubscribe, and that opt-outs are honoured immediately and permanently via a suppression list.

Do not proceed with retargeting until this is in place.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Deliberately inferring and targeting individuals identified as being in 'financial difficulty' in order to push 312%-APR credit, combined with fabricated 'application expiring' messaging, is a paradigm of unfair processing: personal data (inferred economic vulnerability, browsing/retargeting signals) is used to exploit the data subject against their own interests. Covert or manipulative use of profiling data breaches the fairness principle regardless of lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Discontinue targeting based on inferred financial distress and remove fabricated urgency messaging. Ensure any profiling-based targeting serves rather than exploits the data subject and can be justified as fair; obtain independent DPO/legal sign-off given the vulnerable audience.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Financial-distress data is not itself a special category under Art. 9, so this is a conditional risk. However, distress-based targeting proxies can readily reveal Art. 9 data (e.g., health-related debt, gambling-related indebtedness). If the audience is built on signals that reveal or correlate with health, this engages Art. 9's prohibition, which requires explicit consent, and is separately banned for platform ad targeting under DSA Art. 26(3).
findings.evidence_quote: Targeting on inferred financial-distress signals may involve special-category or sensitive inferences
findings.recommendation: Audit the audience-building signals and lookalike sources. Exclude any inputs that reveal or infer Art. 9 categories (health, etc.). If such inferences are unavoidable, either obtain explicit consent or abandon the segment; confirm the platform is not targeting on special-category proxies.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing and to profiling related to it. A retargeting-driven direct-marketing campaign must provide and honour an easily accessible opt-out; the campaign material shows no mechanism for objecting to the profiling/retargeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy-to-use opt-out from direct marketing and retargeting in every ad touchpoint and landing page, and ensure objections stop the profiling immediately and permanently.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected (e.g., landing-page lead forms, loan applications) the controller must provide identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention, data-subject rights, and information about profiling at the point of collection. The ads drive users to conversion but the material provides no transparency information, mirroring the same opacity as the hidden-APR practice.
findings.evidence_quote: €1,000 in your account in 10 minutes ... Everyone qualifies
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered, accessible privacy notice at every data-collection point covering all Art. 13 items, including that behavioural profiling/retargeting takes place, before any data is submitted.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation/targeting and uses behavioural retargeting, which constitutes profiling under GDPR and requires a valid lawful basis, transparency, and respect for the right to object. The most significant GDPR concern is that targeting relies on inferring "financial difficulty" — a sensitive vulnerability inference — to steer distressed consumers toward high-cost credit, raising lawfulness/fairness issues under Art. 5(1)(a) and Art. 6(1). The campaign text alone does not evidence consent mechanisms, transparency notices, or opt-out handling, so several obligations appear engaged but unsubstantiated. Note that financial-distress data is not per se an Art. 9 special category, so that risk is flagged conditionally rather than as a confirmed breach.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: A false countdown/expiry message presented in an online-platform interface deceives and manipulates recipients and materially distorts their ability to make a free, informed decision — precisely the conduct prohibited by Art. 25. The urgency is fabricated because no application exists, so it is not a genuine deadline but a manufactured pressure device delivered through interface design.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated 'application expires in 15 minutes' countdown entirely. Only display time-limited or expiry messaging where an offer or application genuinely has that deadline, and reflect the true state of any application. Eliminate false-urgency creatives from all retargeting flows.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits presenting platform advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including where those categories are inferred via proxies. Behavioural retargeting of consumers segmented on 'financial difficulty' risks relying on sensitive inferences (e.g. health/disability, or proxies that map onto Art. 9 categories); if the targeting model draws on or infers any special-category attribute, the ad delivery is prohibited regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience is 'adults in financial difficulty'
findings.recommendation: Audit the targeting/retargeting parameters and audience-building signals to confirm no GDPR Art. 9 special-category data or proxies for it are used. If financial-distress segments are derived from or correlate with sensitive attributes, cease that targeting. Document that platform ad delivery does not rely on profiling using special categories.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Ads presented on online platforms (social, display) must let recipients identify in real time that the content is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is shown, who paid, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The submitted material shows none of these disclosures, and the personalised retargeting makes the targeting-parameter disclosure obligation directly relevant.
findings.evidence_quote: Search and social ads for a payday-style lender
findings.recommendation: Ensure every platform placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement with the advertiser's/payer's identity, and that the platform's ad-transparency panel exposes the main targeting parameters and how recipients can change them. Verify these are populated for all social and display creatives.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If any of these placements run on a Very Large Online Platform, the ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach will be published in a public ad repository under Art. 39. The misleading claims, buried 312% APR and targeting of vulnerable consumers would therefore be exposed to public and regulator scrutiny.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: search, social, display
findings.recommendation: Assume all creatives and targeting will be publicly archived on VLOPs. Ensure claims, pricing disclosures and targeting parameters can withstand public scrutiny before running the campaign on such platforms.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on online-platform channels (social, display, search) and engages the DSA on multiple fronts. The fabricated "application expires in 15 minutes" countdown — for an application that was never started — is a deceptive/manipulative interface practice caught by the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition. Behavioural retargeting of "adults in financial difficulty" raises an Art. 26(3) risk if targeting relies, directly or by proxy/inference, on GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. Platform ad transparency obligations under Art. 26(1) are also engaged and nothing in the material shows the required labelling, advertiser/payer identity or targeting-parameter disclosures.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: Annex I point 7 prohibits, in all circumstances, falsely stating that a product/terms are available for only a very limited time to elicit an immediate decision. A countdown telling the consumer their 'application expires in 15 minutes' when no application was ever started is a fabricated deadline — a per se blacklisted false urgency tactic requiring no case-by-case unfairness assessment.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove all countdown/expiry messaging that is not tied to a genuine, verifiable deadline. Never state that an application or offer is expiring where no application exists or the deadline is artificial.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits false information or deception about the main characteristics of the product. 'Guaranteed approval' and 'everyone qualifies' are almost certainly false for a regulated lender (responsible-lending/affordability checks apply), deceive consumers about the nature and conditions of the credit product, and cause transactional decisions they would not otherwise take. The fabricated 'expires in 15 minutes' claim is separately a false statement under Art. 6.
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks, no questions, no paperwork. Bad credit? Perfect credit? Everyone qualifies.
findings.recommendation: Remove unqualified 'guaranteed approval', 'no credit checks' and 'everyone qualifies' claims. Only state approval conditions that are true and reflect the actual affordability/eligibility assessment performed.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 makes it a misleading omission to hide material information or provide it in an unclear or untimely manner. For a credit product the representative APR and cost of credit are core material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision. Burying a 312% APR behind a separate 'rates' link, while headline messaging emphasises speed and 'guaranteed approval', hides material price information from the point of the invitation to purchase.
findings.evidence_quote: The representative APR (312%) appears only behind a 'rates' link
findings.recommendation: Display the representative APR and total cost of credit clearly and prominently alongside the headline offer in each ad creative, not behind a secondary link. Ensure the representative example meets consumer-credit disclosure standards.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive a practice that, through undue influence, significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice — with relevant factors including timing, persistence and exploitation of a specific misfortune. Emotionally pressuring people declared to be 'adults in financial difficulty' with family-guilt messaging, combined with escalating retargeting creatives and fake expiry countdowns, exploits their distress to push an impulsive high-cost borrowing decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Don't let your family go without this weekend.
findings.recommendation: Remove emotive family-pressure and urgency framing. Do not tailor escalating pressure messaging to consumers inferred to be in financial distress; give consumers time and neutral information to make an informed choice.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5, read with Art. 5(3), is the fairness safety-net and requires the practice to be assessed from the perspective of the average member of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group. The campaign explicitly targets financially distressed consumers — a group whose economic behaviour is more readily distorted — reinforcing that the misleading and aggressive elements above are contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their decisions.
findings.evidence_quote: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Reassess the whole campaign against the heightened Art. 5(3) standard for vulnerable consumers; apply professional-diligence safeguards appropriate to high-cost credit marketed to distressed audiences and avoid targeting on financial-distress signals.

verdicts.notes: This payday-lender campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including blacklisted (per se unfair) practices. The "expires in 15 minutes" countdown for an application that was never started is a false urgency claim blacklisted under Annex I point 7 and a misleading action under Art. 6. The 312% APR hidden behind a 'rates' link is a misleading omission of material price information (Art. 7). The "GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks... Everyone qualifies" claims are likely misleading actions (Art. 6), and the exploitation of financially distressed consumers through emotional pressure and escalating retargeting is likely an aggressive practice (Arts. 8-9), assessed against the vulnerable-group standard (Art. 5(3)). Overall high-to-critical risk.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises payday-style loans to people in financial difficulty using "guaranteed approval / no credit checks / everyone qualifies" messaging, a 312% APR hidden behind a separate link, emotional family-guilt framing, and a fake "your application expires in 15 minutes" countdown for an application that was never started. As drafted it is not fixable with minor edits — it breaks multiple EU consumer and platform rules at the most serious level. The fake countdown is a per se banned practice under the UCPD blacklist (illegal in all circumstances, no case-by-case assessment needed) and also a prohibited dark pattern under the DSA. The false "guaranteed approval" claims and the buried APR are misleading actions and omissions, and the pressure tactics aimed at distressed consumers are an aggressive practice. On top of this, targeting people you have inferred to be "in financial difficulty," combined with behavioural retargeting, raises serious GDPR fairness and lawful-basis problems and a DSA risk if that targeting touches any sensitive-data proxies. The AI Act does not apply. Verdict: do not run this campaign in its current form — it needs to be fundamentally reworked, not just tweaked.
recommendations: Remove the fake 'your application expires in 15 minutes' countdown immediately — this is a per se illegal practice under the UCPD blacklist (Annex I pt 7) and a prohibited DSA dark pattern; it cannot run under any circumstances. Only use expiry/urgency messaging tied to a genuine, verifiable deadline.

Delete the 'GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks — everyone qualifies' claims. These are almost certainly false for a regulated lender and are misleading actions; only state eligibility terms that reflect the actual affordability/credit assessment you perform.
Display the representative APR (312%) and total cost of credit clearly and prominently in the ad creative itself, alongside the headline offer — not hidden behind a 'rates' link.

Remove the emotive 'don't let your family go without this weekend' pressure and the escalating retargeting creatives; this exploitation of distressed consumers is an aggressive practice under the UCPD.

Stop targeting people based on inferred 'financial difficulty.' Using economic-vulnerability inferences to steer distressed consumers into 312% credit is very hard to justify as fair or lawful under GDPR, and if the audience relies on any sensitive-data proxies (e.g. health/gambling-related debt) it is outright banned for platform ad targeting under DSA Art. 26(3).

Establish and document a valid lawful basis for behavioural retargeting (consent aligned with ePrivacy, or a documented legitimate-interest balancing test that accounts for audience vulnerability) before any tracking-based ads run.

Provide a clear, easy opt-out from direct marketing/retargeting at every touchpoint, and a layered privacy notice at every data-collection point covering all GDPR Art. 13 information including profiling.

Ensure every social/display placement is labelled as an advertisement with advertiser/payer identity and populated targeting-parameter disclosures (DSA Art. 26(1)); assume all creatives and targeting will be publicly archived if run on very large platforms.
Given the vulnerable audience and high-cost credit, obtain DPO/legal sign-off and reassess the entire campaign against the heightened UCPD vulnerable-consumer standard before relaunch.

emotional exploitation of vulnerable consumers ('don't let your family go without')
targeting consumers in financial difficulty (vulnerable audience)
triage.audience_notes: Explicitly targets a vulnerable group — adults in financial difficulty — heightening UCPD scrutiny for aggressive/misleading practices. Personalisation and retargeting imply processing of personal data (GDPR) and profiling/advertising controls on platforms (DSA), including DSA rules on manipulative interfaces and ad transparency. Minors not the declared target, though social/display reach could incidentally include them; consumer credit sectoral rules (Consumer Credit Directive) also likely relevant beyond the four listed regimes.
triage.summary: A payday-style lender campaign across search, social and display targeting adults in financial difficulty, using misleading 'guaranteed approval / no credit checks' claims, a buried 312% APR, and false-urgency retargeting ('application expires in 15 minutes' though none was started). It aggressively pressures a vulnerable audience and relies on personalisation and behavioural retargeting. No generative AI declared, but multiple unfair commercial practices and data-driven targeting concerns are present.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: The declared personalisation and behavioural retargeting of an audience segmented as 'adults in financial difficulty' is automated processing evaluating/predicting the economic situation and behaviour of individuals — the exact examples Art. 4(4) gives as profiling. This classifies the campaign's targeting as profiling, triggering the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights).
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes ... Retargeting creatives escalate
findings.recommendation: Document the targeting as profiling in the campaign's record of processing activities and ensure the downstream obligations (Art. 6 basis, Art. 12/13 transparency, Art. 21 opt-out) are met before deploying the segments.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and behavioural retargeting require a valid lawful basis — in practice consent for tracking-based advertising, or a carefully documented legitimate-interest assessment. The campaign shows no consent mechanism and no LIA; a legitimate-interest balancing is highly unlikely to succeed for aggressive targeting of financially vulnerable people, whose interests and fundamental rights weigh heavily. Absent a demonstrable basis, the profiling is unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis before running the profiling/retargeting: obtain valid opt-in consent for advertising cookies/pixels, or complete a legitimate-interest assessment. Given the vulnerable audience, treat consent as the safe basis and do not proceed on legitimate interest alone.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires processing (including tracking-driven retargeting) to be fair and not misleading. Building retargeting messages on a fabricated premise (a non-existent 'application' that is 'expiring') deploys personal data in a manner that is deceptive to the data subject, breaching the fairness limb; the absence of any privacy information also implicates the transparency limb.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove retargeting messaging that misrepresents the individual's status. Ensure retargeting only reflects genuine prior interactions and is accompanied by clear, accessible privacy information about how the person's data is used.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting implies collection of personal data (e.g., tracking pixels/cookies, device identifiers) from users who see or interact with the ads. Art. 13 requires that at the point of collection the controller provides identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and profiling information. The submission contains no such information layer.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, layered privacy notice at the point of data collection (ad landing pages and cookie/consent banner) covering controller identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and the existence of profiling, with a link to the full policy.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object at any time to processing for direct marketing, including profiling related to it. A retargeting campaign must offer an effective, easily exercisable opt-out and must honour it. The campaign as described provides no visible mechanism to object to the profiling/retargeting.
findings.evidence_quote: behavioural retargeting
findings.recommendation: Implement and surface an easy opt-out from marketing profiling/retargeting (e.g., 'why am I seeing this ad' controls, unsubscribe, and suppression lists) and ensure objections stop all further targeting of that individual immediately.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation and behavioural retargeting of a group defined by "financial difficulty," which constitutes profiling of economic situation under GDPR. Nothing in the submission demonstrates a valid lawful basis, transparent information at the point of data collection, or a facilitated right to object — all of which are engaged and, as described, unlikely to be satisfied. Art. 9 (special categories) is not clearly triggered on the current text, since financial hardship is not itself a listed sensitive category, but the fairness/transparency principle and profiling obligations are squarely engaged.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The retargeting creatives use a fabricated countdown/expiry on an 'application' that the recipient never started. This is deceptive, manipulative interface/communication design on platform ads that materially distorts and impairs the recipient's ability to make a free and informed decision — precisely the conduct Art. 25 prohibits. Combined with burying the 312% APR behind a 'rates' link (false hierarchy / obscuring material information), the platform experience steers consumers toward a rushed transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove the false expiry/countdown from retargeting creatives; only display genuine, accurate deadlines tied to a real application state. Surface the representative APR (312%) and key credit terms prominently in the ad creative and landing page rather than hiding them behind a 'rates' link, so the interface does not manipulate or obscure material information.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The campaign is delivered as personalised, behaviourally retargeted advertising on online platforms (search, social, display). Art. 26(1) requires that, for each such ad, recipients can identify in a clear, real-time manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main parameters used to target them (with a way to change them). Nothing in the submission indicates the retargeted creatives carry advertiser/payer identity or meaningful targeting-parameter information.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate
findings.recommendation: Ensure every platform ad is clearly labelled as advertising and carries the advertiser's identity and (where different) the payer, and that the platform's 'why am I seeing this ad' disclosure reflects the actual targeting parameters (e.g. retargeting of prior visitors) with controls to change them. Verify these disclosures are populated correctly for the retargeting audiences before launch.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: If any of these ads are served via a Very Large Online Platform, their full content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach will be published in the public ad repository. The misleading 'guaranteed approval / no credit checks' claims, buried 312% APR and vulnerable-audience targeting would be exposed to public and regulatory scrutiny.

findings.recommendation: Assume all creatives and targeting will be publicly archived; ensure claims are substantiated and compliant, APR is disclosed, and targeting parameters would withstand public and regulator review before running on VLOPs.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs on social and display platforms using personalised/behavioural retargeting and manipulative messaging, engaging the DSA's rules for online platform advertising. The most acute DSA concern is deceptive interface/communication design (Art. 25): retargeting that fabricates an expiring "application" that was never started, combined with hidden APR, is manipulative design that distorts free and informed decision-making. Personalised platform ads also engage Art. 26(1) transparency duties (ad labelling, advertiser/payer identity, targeting parameters and how to change them). Art. 26(3) (sensitive-data targeting) is not clearly triggered, as "financial difficulty" is not a GDPR Art. 9 special category. Note that Art. 25/26 obligations bind the platform provider directly, but the advertiser designs the offending creatives and targeting and should not rely on non-compliant designs.

findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated countdown/expiry entirely. Do not display any time-limited deadline unless it is genuinely and verifiably true. A retargeting creative referencing an 'application' that was never started must not be used.

Using undue influence and time pressure to exploit a vulnerable situation significantly impairs freedom of choice and is likely an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9, where exploitation of misfortune and persistence are express factors.
findings.evidence_quote: Don't let your family go without this weekend.

findings.evidence_quote: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Reassess the entire campaign against the vulnerable-consumer standard: avoid targeting distress states, ensure all claims are true and balanced, and give due prominence to cost and risk information proportionate to the audience's vulnerability.
