triage.summary: Payday-style lender ads across search, social and display promoting 'guaranteed approval, no credit checks' loans while burying the 312% representative APR behind a link, using emotional appeals and false urgency (a 15-minute expiry for an application never started) via behavioural retargeting. The campaign explicitly targets adults in financial difficulty — a vulnerable audience — and combines misleading omissions, aggressive pressure tactics and personalised targeting.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Behavioural retargeting and the declared personalised targeting of an audience defined by 'financial difficulty' is automated processing of personal data to evaluate personal aspects (economic situation, behaviour, interests). This meets the definition of profiling under Art. 4(4), which triggers the substantive GDPR obligations (Arts. 6, 13, 21).
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes ... Retargeting creatives escalate
findings.recommendation: Document that behavioural retargeting/personalisation is profiling and map each processing operation to its purpose, data sources and lawful basis before running the campaign.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The retargeting relies on tracking individuals (e.g. site visitors / ad interactions) and re-serving personalised ads. Under Art. 6(1) this profiling for advertising requires a valid lawful basis — in practice prior consent for tracking cookies/identifiers, or a documented legitimate-interest balancing test. The submission shows no lawful basis, and a legitimate-interest balance is very difficult to pass where the audience is financially vulnerable and the tactics are manipulative, tilting the balancing test toward the data subjects' interests.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started.
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a lawful basis for the retargeting/profiling: obtain valid, freely given consent for tracking identifiers where required, or complete a legitimate-interests assessment. Given the vulnerable audience and aggressive tactics, do not rely on legitimate interests for this profiling.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness and transparency principle requires that personal data not be processed in ways individuals would not reasonably expect and that are manipulative. Deploying behavioural tracking to serve a false-urgency countdown ('application expires') to people who never applied uses their personal data unfairly and deceptively, breaching Art. 5(1)(a)'s fairness limb, and covert tracking breaches its transparency limb.
findings.evidence_quote: Retargeting creatives escalate: 'Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started.
findings.recommendation: Cease using tracking-based creatives that misrepresent the data subject's own history (no application existed). Ensure processing is fair, expected and accompanied by clear, honest information about how behavioural data is used.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected/used for profiling and retargeting, Art. 13 requires the controller to inform data subjects of its identity, purposes, lawful basis, recipients, retention and their rights (including any profiling) at the point of collection. Nothing in the campaign indicates such transparency information is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at the point of data collection (landing page, cookie/consent layer) covering purposes, lawful basis, profiling/retargeting, retention and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Direct-marketing profiling triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3): data subjects must be able to stop the processing at any time and be explicitly informed of this right. There is no evidence the campaign offers or signposts an opt-out from the behavioural targeting/retargeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Explicitly present the right to object to direct-marketing profiling at first contact, and provide an easy, effective opt-out that immediately stops retargeting for that individual.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Financial difficulty / economic situation is a profiling attribute under Art. 4(4) but is not one of the exhaustive Art. 9 special categories, so Art. 9 is not squarely engaged on the facts stated. However, if the targeting is achieved through proxies that reveal or infer Art. 9 data (e.g. health, debt/illness indicators) or if platform sensitive-interest segments are used, Art. 9's prohibition (explicit consent required) would be triggered.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Confirm the targeting/segmentation does not rely on or infer special-category data (health, etc.). If any sensitive proxy is used, stop it or obtain explicit consent; note DSA Art. 26(3) separately bans sensitive-data ad targeting on platforms.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares personalisation/targeting and uses behavioural retargeting against an audience of "adults in financial difficulty," which constitutes profiling of personal data (economic situation, behaviour) under GDPR. This engages the requirements of a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)), the fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), transparency at collection (Art. 13) and the absolute right to object to direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21). The submission provides no evidence of a lawful basis, transparency notices or opt-out mechanisms; these should be verified. Targeting by "financial difficulty" is a profiling attribute (Art. 4(4)) but not an exhaustive Art. 9 special category on the facts given, so it is flagged for attention rather than as a prohibition unless health/other sensitive proxies are used.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: A countdown claiming a non-existent application will expire is a deceptive, manipulative interface design element deployed via online-platform retargeting creatives. It materially distorts recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions by manufacturing false time pressure, squarely within the DSA Art. 25 prohibition on dark patterns (deceptive/manipulative interface design, including artificial urgency).
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove the fake expiry countdown entirely. Never display a deadline for an application or offer that does not genuinely exist. Any time-limited element must reflect a real, verifiable limitation and must not be used to pressure or deceive recipients into acting.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: The ads are presented on online platforms (social, display) using behavioural retargeting/profiling. DSA Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify in a clear, real-time manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid, plus meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The campaign as described gives no indication these transparency elements are provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all platform placements are clearly labelled as advertising with the advertiser's identity, and rely on/support the platform's mechanisms disclosing the main targeting parameters and how recipients can change them. Coordinate with the hosting platforms so per-ad transparency and targeting-parameter disclosure obligations are satisfied.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign uses profiling-based behavioural retargeting on platforms accessible to minors with no reliable age assurance. DSA Art. 28 bans presenting profiling-based advertisements to recipients reasonably known to be minors and requires appropriate measures to protect minors. Without age gating, profiled high-pressure credit ads risk reaching minors in breach of Art. 28.
findings.evidence_quote: open search/social/display channels provide no reliable age gating, so minors could plausibly be reached
findings.recommendation: Exclude minors from all profiling/retargeting audiences and apply age-assurance/age-appropriate targeting settings on each platform. Confirm with platforms that no behaviourally targeted ad in this campaign can be served to users who are, with reasonable certainty, minors.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs behaviourally retargeted ads across social and display platforms and uses a fake countdown ("Your application expires in 15 minutes" for an application never started). Under the DSA this is a clear dark pattern (Art. 25). Personalised targeting engages platform ad-transparency duties (Art. 26(1)), and the plausible reach of minors via open, un-age-gated channels with profiling-based retargeting engages the ban on profiled ads to minors (Art. 28). The sensitive-data ban (Art. 26(3)) is not clearly triggered, as "financial difficulty" is not a GDPR Art. 9 special category.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The retargeting creatives display a personalised 15-minute expiry deadline for an application the consumer never actually started. This is a false statement that the offer is available only for a very limited time, designed to elicit an immediate decision and deprive the consumer of the opportunity to make an informed choice. Annex I point 7 prohibits such false urgency claims in all circumstances, without any need to prove consumer harm — it is a per se (blacklisted) violation.
findings.evidence_quote: Your application expires in 15 minutes' although no application was started
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated countdown/expiry entirely. Never display a time-limited deadline unless the stated limitation is genuinely true and verifiable; a countdown must not be attached to an application that does not exist or reset per user session.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The representative APR is the single most material cost item for a credit product, yet it is hidden behind a secondary 'rates' link while the headline promises '€1,000 in your account in 10 minutes'. Presenting material price information in an unclear, untimely and non-prominent manner is a misleading omission under Art. 7, likely to cause consumers to take a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The vulnerability of the declared audience (adults in financial difficulty) heightens the materiality.
findings.evidence_quote: The representative APR (312%) appears only behind a 'rates' link
findings.recommendation: Display the representative APR (and total cost of credit / repayment example) prominently within the ad creative itself, with equal or greater visual weight than the headline offer, in line with UCPD Art. 7 and Consumer Credit Directive prominence requirements (raise CCD specifics with credit specialists).

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: 'Guaranteed approval' and 'everyone qualifies' are absolute claims about the main characteristics/availability of the credit product that are almost certainly false — regulated lenders cannot lawfully approve every applicant, and 'no credit checks' conflicts with responsible-lending affordability obligations. These claims deceive the average consumer about the nature of the offer and are likely to induce a transactional decision, engaging Art. 6 (misleading actions).
findings.evidence_quote: GUARANTEED approval — no credit checks, no questions, no paperwork. Bad credit? Perfect credit? Everyone qualifies.
findings.recommendation: Remove unqualified 'guaranteed approval' and 'everyone qualifies' claims. Any approval statement must be truthful and subject to clearly stated eligibility and affordability assessment; do not advertise 'no credit checks' where credit/affordability checks are legally required.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign combines an emotive appeal that exploits the misfortune of financially distressed consumers ('Don't let your family go without') with escalating behavioural retargeting and a fabricated countdown. Under Arts. 8-9, exploitation of a specific misfortune/emergency, timing pressure, and persistent retargeting can amount to undue influence that significantly impairs the consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise take — an aggressive commercial practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Don't let your family go without this weekend.
findings.recommendation: Remove emotionally coercive messaging that leverages family hardship, and stop escalating high-pressure retargeting sequences. Marketing to consumers in financial difficulty must avoid undue-influence tactics; use neutral, factual messaging without artificial pressure.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is expressly targeted at economically vulnerable consumers. Under Art. 5(3) the fairness of the practice must be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group, which lowers the threshold for finding the combined tactics (false urgency, hidden APR, deceptive approval claims, emotional pressure) contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour. Art. 5 operates as the overarching fairness safety-net reinforcing the specific findings above.
findings.evidence_quote: adults in financial difficulty
findings.recommendation: Reframe the whole campaign to meet professional-diligence standards appropriate to a vulnerable audience: prominent cost disclosure, no false deadlines, no coercive emotional appeals, and clear eligibility criteria before promoting the product to financially distressed consumers.

verdicts.notes: This payday-lender campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions. Most seriously, the "Your application expires in 15 minutes" countdown for an application that was never started is a blacklisted false-urgency practice (Annex I point 7) — unlawful in all circumstances. The campaign also buries the material 312% representative APR behind a "rates" link (misleading omission, Art. 7), makes deceptive "guaranteed approval / everyone qualifies" claims (misleading action, Art. 6), and combines relentless retargeting with emotional pressure on a financially vulnerable audience (aggressive practice, Arts. 8-9; general unfairness assessed against the vulnerable-consumer standard, Art. 5). Consumer Credit Directive APR-disclosure rules are also engaged and should be raised with credit-advertising specialists.

report.executive_summary: This campaign advertises payday-style loans to people in financial difficulty using headline promises of "guaranteed approval," "no credit checks," and "€1,000 in 10 minutes," while hiding the 312% representative APR behind a "rates" link and running escalating retargeting ads with a fake "your application expires in 15 minutes" countdown for applications that never existed. As designed, it cannot lawfully run in the EU. The fake countdown is a per se prohibited practice under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I blacklist) and a banned dark pattern under the DSA — these are automatic violations with no defence. On top of that, the "guaranteed approval / everyone qualifies" claims are misleading, the buried APR is an unlawful omission of the most important price information, and the emotional "don't let your family go without" pressure aimed at vulnerable people is an aggressive practice. The behavioural retargeting of a "financial difficulty" audience also triggers GDPR profiling obligations (lawful basis, transparency, right to object) that the submission does not address, plus DSA ad-transparency and minor-protection duties. This is not a matter of tweaking wording — the core mechanics and claims are illegal and the campaign should not launch in its current form.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign as submitted. The fake 15-minute expiry countdown is a blacklisted false-urgency practice (UCPD Annex I) and a banned DSA dark pattern — illegal in all circumstances. Remove it entirely; never attach a deadline to an application or offer that does not genuinely exist.

Delete the 'GUARANTEED approval', 'no credit checks', 'no questions', and 'everyone qualifies' claims. These are misleading and conflict with responsible-lending/affordability obligations; any approval statement must be truthful and conditional on eligibility checks.

Show the representative APR (312%), total cost of credit and a repayment example prominently in the ad creative itself, with at least equal visual weight to the headline — not hidden behind a 'rates' link. Involve credit-advertising specialists on Consumer Credit Directive prominence rules.

Remove the emotionally coercive 'don't let your family go without this weekend' messaging and stop the escalating high-pressure retargeting sequence. Marketing to financially vulnerable consumers must avoid undue-influence tactics and use neutral, factual language.

Before any retargeting/profiling runs, establish and document a valid GDPR lawful basis (consent for tracking identifiers, or a legitimate-interests assessment). Given the vulnerable audience and manipulative tactics, do not rely on legitimate interests here.

Provide a clear privacy notice at data collection covering purposes, lawful basis, profiling/retargeting, retention and rights (GDPR Art. 13), and offer an easy, effective opt-out from direct-marketing profiling (Art. 21).

Ensure all platform placements are clearly labelled as ads with the advertiser's identity and support the platform's targeting-parameter disclosures (DSA Art. 26); exclude minors from all profiled/retargeted audiences and apply age-assurance settings (DSA Art. 28).
Confirm targeting does not rely on or infer sensitive/special-category data (e.g. health or debt-illness proxies), which would trigger GDPR Art. 9 and the DSA sensitive-data ad-targeting ban.

Given the number and severity of issues, reframe the entire campaign against a vulnerable-consumer professional-diligence standard rather than patching individual lines, and obtain legal sign-off before relaunch.

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

detected_practices: fake official emblem and national colours
charging for a publicly free service
buried disclaimer in low-visibility 7pt grey text
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is low-income households — a vulnerable consumer group under UCPD Art. 5(3)/Annex I, heightening the seriousness of the misleading official-authority impersonation and undisclosed fee. Although personalisation/targeting is declared 'no', audience selection toward low-income users and the collection of application/payment data via the portal means GDPR is plausibly engaged. As a private trader posing as government (Annex I 'blacklist' practices — claiming endorsement/authorisation and posing as non-trader), DSA advertising transparency (trader identification) is engaged. AI Act relevant given declared generative AI use, including potential transparency/deepfake-style labelling obligations for the official-emblem content.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate a government energy-subsidy notice — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem and an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing — to funnel consumers to a private site charging €49 for an application that is publicly free. The ads conceal the trader's identity, bury a 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey, apply false deadline urgency, and target low-income households; generative AI is declared as used to produce content.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared as used to produce the ad content, which is styled as a government bulletin with 'national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem' and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing. Art. 50(4) requires deployers to disclose (a) AI-generated/manipulated image content constituting a deep fake — here AI-manipulated content fabricating an authentic-looking official government emblem/bulletin — and (b) AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, which an energy-subsidy 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' squarely is. No disclosure that the notice and emblem are artificially generated is present; the only footer text disclaims government affiliation, not AI origin.
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure that the ad imagery and text are artificially generated/AI-produced, at first exposure and not buried. More fundamentally, stop generating official-looking emblems and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing altogether, as the disclosure obligation cannot cure the underlying impersonation.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares generative AI use to create ad assets (images and copy). Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of generative AI systems be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. As described, the AI-generated display/search creatives carry no indication of machine-readable provenance marking, so this transparency obligation is engaged and not evidenced as met.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets embed machine-readable provenance/watermark marking (e.g. C2PA-compatible metadata) as produced by the generative AI provider, and verify the marking survives export into the ad formats used.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI that exploits vulnerabilities of a group due to a specific economic situation, with the effect of materially distorting behaviour in a way reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Generative AI is used to produce content deliberately aimed at low-income households (an economically vulnerable group) that deceptively induces them to pay €49 for a publicly free service — a distortion of behaviour likely to cause significant financial harm to those least able to bear it. Caveat: the prohibition targets exploitation performed by an AI system, and personalisation/targeting is declared 'no', so it is arguable whether the AI is 'exploiting' vulnerability or merely generating static creative; the combination of AI-produced deceptive content plus a declared vulnerable audience and real financial harm makes this a serious risk.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI-generated marketing content designed to exploit the financial situation of low-income households. Remove the deceptive official-authority framing and the paid intermediation of a free service; if any AI system is used to select or optimise delivery toward this group, discontinue it.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(a) prohibits AI systems deploying purposefully deceptive techniques with the effect of materially distorting behaviour, impairing informed decision-making and causing decisions the person would not otherwise take, in a way reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Here generative AI produces content whose whole purpose is deception (impersonating a government notice) to make consumers pay a €49 fee they would not pay if they knew the service was free and non-governmental. Caveat: 5(1)(a) requires the deceptive technique to be deployed by an AI system; as described, AI generates the creative but the deception is executed through static ad design, so the threshold that an 'AI system' deploys the technique is not clearly met — hence flagged as a risk rather than a confirmed prohibited practice.
findings.evidence_quote: The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the deceptive impersonation entirely (official emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' language). If generative or optimisation AI is involved in producing or amplifying this deception, ensure it is not used to deploy deceptive behavioural-distortion techniques, which are prohibited outright.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce the ad content, which engages the AI Act's transparency obligations (Art. 50). Most notably, AI-generated content styled as an "OFFICIAL NOTICE" with a coat-of-arms-like emblem and national colours conveys public-interest information (energy-subsidy eligibility) in a form designed to appear as an authentic official artefact, engaging Art. 50(4) disclosure and Art. 50(2) marking, neither of which is described as satisfied. Because the AI-produced deceptive content is aimed at a declared vulnerable group (low-income households) and is likely to cause financial harm (a €49 fee for a free service), the Art. 5 prohibitions on manipulative/deceptive AI and exploitation of economic vulnerability are also plausibly engaged, though their "AI system" threshold and the declared absence of targeting create some uncertainty.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data (application inputs and €49 payment data) is collected under a deceptive government-impersonation pretext. Data subjects believe they are submitting to a public authority, not a private trader. Processing personal data obtained by misleading users about the controller's identity and the nature of the service breaches the fairness and transparency principle — the collection is neither fair nor transparent, and the material clarifying information is deliberately obscured in 7pt grey.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Cease the government-impersonation framing entirely. Present the trader's true identity clearly and prominently before any data is collected, and ensure the collection context accurately reflects that this is a private paid service, so that data is processed fairly and transparently.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected directly from the data subject, the controller must provide, at the point of collection, its identity, the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The campaign conceals the trader/controller identity in the ads and funnels users to a portal whose operator is disguised behind a fake official appearance, so the Art. 13 identity and purpose information cannot be validly provided at the point of collection.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete Art. 13 privacy notice at the data-collection point on the portal, clearly stating the actual controller's legal identity and contact details, the purposes and legal basis for processing the application and payment data, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights — without any government-authority styling.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information addressed to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible using clear and plain language. Relegating the key clarifying statement to a 7pt grey footer makes essential context practically inaccessible, undermining the accessibility and intelligibility required for any accompanying privacy/transparency information provided at the same interface.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present all transparency information — including the non-affiliation statement and the privacy notice — in a legible font size and adequate contrast, positioned prominently rather than buried in a low-visibility footer.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Any processing of the application and payment data requires a valid lawful basis. Where users are deceived about who the controller is and the nature of the service, consent cannot be freely given or informed, and reliance on 'contract' is doubtful because the transaction is procured through deception. The lawful basis is therefore not securely established as described.
findings.evidence_quote: 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6(1) lawful basis for the application and payment data. If relying on contract, ensure the user genuinely and knowingly enters into the paid service with the real trader; if relying on consent, ensure it is informed and freely given, which is impossible while the government-impersonation framing persists.

verdicts.notes: GDPR is engaged because the 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu' site collects personal data — application details and €49 payment data — from data subjects. The data collection occurs in a deceptive context: consumers are led to believe they are dealing with a government authority, the trader's identity is concealed, and the only clarifying information is buried in 7pt grey text. This undermines the fairness and transparency principle and the point-of-collection information obligations. Findings focus on the transparency/fairness dimension; the misleading-practice and trader-disclosure aspects are for UCPD/DSA agents.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad presented on an online platform, recipients can identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf / who paid for it. These display and search ads are deliberately styled as a 'government bulletin' with an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing and do not identify the private trader behind them, defeating the requirement to identify both the commercial (advertisement) nature and the advertiser's identity.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Ensure the ads are clearly labelled as advertising and prominently display the identity of the trader on whose behalf they are presented (and who paid for them), as required for platform ad transparency. Remove the government/official framing so the commercial origin is unambiguous.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in ways that deceive or manipulate recipients or materially distort their ability to make free and informed decisions, and expressly covers disguised advertisements. Disguising a commercial ad as an official government notice, combined with a false deadline ('before the deadline') and a 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer buried in 7pt grey text, is deceptive/manipulative interface and communication design targeting the recipient's decision-making. This is aggravated by targeting low-income (vulnerable) consumers.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the ad creative to remove the disguised-ad tactics: eliminate the official emblem, national colours and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing; drop the artificial deadline urgency unless genuinely true; and give the 'not affiliated with any government' and the €49 fee equal prominence rather than burying them in low-visibility 7pt grey text.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs paid ads on display and search platforms, engaging the DSA's advertising-transparency and anti-dark-pattern regime that applies to the platforms presenting these ads. The ad creative is a disguised advertisement styled as an official government bulletin and does not identify the trader, undermining Art. 26(1) transparency, while the impersonation, buried 7pt disclaimer and false deadline urgency are deceptive/manipulative design engaging Art. 25. Note that Arts. 25/26 are primarily obligations on the online platform providers; the advertiser cannot satisfy them by hiding its identity and disguising the ad. Art. 26(3) (sensitive-data ad targeting) and Art. 28 (minors) are not engaged given no declared profiling and no minors reached.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: A private company presents itself as a public/government body issuing an official subsidy notice, falsely implying it is approved, endorsed or authorised by a public authority. This is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances — no assessment of consumer impact is required. The buried 7pt 'not affiliated with any government' footer does not cure the false official-authority impression created in the ads.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official framing entirely: delete national colours, the coat-of-arms-like emblem, and the 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording. The trader must not imply any public-body affiliation, endorsement or authorisation unless it genuinely holds one.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying a coat-of-arms-like emblem and official national insignia mimics an authoritative/quality mark of the state without any authorisation. Use of such an official-looking emblem without authorisation is a per se prohibited practice under the blacklist.
findings.evidence_quote: national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any state insignia. Use only the trader's own clearly commercial branding, plainly distinguishable from official government emblems.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads omit the trader's identity and conceal their commercial intent by disguising a paid commercial service as an official government communication. The only clarifying information (non-affiliation) is provided in an unclear, illegible manner (7pt grey), which is a misleading omission and hiding of material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader ... The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader in the ads themselves, state the commercial nature of the service prominently, and display the non-affiliation and the €49 fee in equally prominent, legible text before any transactional decision is prompted.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The campaign deceives the average consumer about the nature of the service and the price: it presents itself as an official eligibility check while charging €49 for an application that is publicly free. This false/deceptive information about the product's nature, price and the trader's status is likely to cause a transactional decision the consumer would not otherwise take (paying €49 for a free public service).
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State up-front and prominently that the application is free of charge through the official government channel, disclose exactly what the €49 buys (a private intermediary service), and remove any implication that payment is required to access the subsidy.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice is targeted at low-income households — a clearly identifiable vulnerable group in economic distress and precisely those most reliant on energy subsidies. Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group, which materially heightens the seriousness of the official-authority impersonation, the deadline pressure and the undisclosed €49 fee. This is contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort their economic behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not target vulnerable low-income consumers with subsidy-related commercial offers dressed as official communications. If a legitimate paid service is offered at all, ensure full transparency and that a vulnerable consumer would clearly understand it is a private, chargeable, optional intermediary service.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The ad applies deadline urgency ('before the deadline') to elicit an immediate decision. If this deadline is fabricated, artificial, or does not correspond to a genuine limitation on the €49 service, it is a false urgency claim prohibited in all circumstances under the blacklist. Even a genuine public application deadline is exploited misleadingly to pressure payment for a free service.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove urgency framing unless a real, verifiable deadline exists and is accurately attributed to the official public application (not the trader's paid service). Do not use deadline pressure to funnel consumers into the €49 payment.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages the UCPD severely, with multiple Annex I "blacklist" practices that are prohibited in all circumstances regardless of consumer impact. The ads falsely present a private €49 service as an official government energy-subsidy notice, using a coat-of-arms-like emblem and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" framing to claim government endorsement/authorisation (Annex I points 4 and 2), while concealing trader identity and burying the disclaimer (Art. 7). The "before the deadline" pressure engages false-urgency rules and the general misleading-action prohibition (Arts. 6, and Annex I point 7 if the deadline is fabricated). Targeting low-income households sharply aggravates the assessment under Art. 5(3).

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads that impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-style emblem, and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" framing — to funnel low-income households to a private site that charges €49 for an application that is free through the real government channel. This is not a borderline case: it triggers multiple EU consumer-law "blacklist" practices that are banned outright regardless of consumer harm (falsely claiming government endorsement, using an unauthorised official emblem, hiding the trader's identity and commercial intent, and applying deadline pressure). On top of that, the declared use of generative AI to create the fake official content engages the AI Act's transparency rules and, more seriously, its prohibitions on manipulative and vulnerability-exploiting AI. The platform-ad transparency and dark-pattern rules (DSA) and data-fairness rules (GDPR) are also breached, because the trader is concealed and personal/payment data is collected under a false official pretext. The buried 7pt "not affiliated with any government" footer does nothing to cure any of this. The core problem is the deception itself — no disclosure, disclaimer, or relabelling can make an impersonation-of-government campaign lawful. This campaign must not run in its current form; the deceptive concept needs to be abandoned, not tweaked.
recommendations: Do not launch this campaign. The government-impersonation concept violates outright-banned EU consumer-law practices and cannot be fixed by adding disclosures — the entire official-notice framing must be scrapped.</recommendation> Remove all government/official signalling: delete the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, and the 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording (UCPD Annex I points 2 and 4 — prohibited in all circumstances).

Stop implying that payment is needed to access the subsidy. State prominently and up-front that the application is free through the official channel and that this is an optional private paid service, clearly disclosing what the €49 buys (UCPD Arts. 6 & 7).

Identify the trader clearly in the ads themselves and label them unambiguously as advertising; give the non-affiliation notice and the fee equal, legible prominence — not a 7pt grey footer (DSA Arts. 25 & 26; UCPD Art. 7; GDPR Art. 12).

Remove the 'before the deadline' urgency unless a real, verifiable deadline exists and is accurately tied to the official public application — do not use it to pressure payment (UCPD Annex I point 7).

Cease using generative AI to produce deceptive official-looking content aimed at low-income households; this risks the AI Act's outright prohibitions on manipulative and vulnerability-exploiting AI (Art. 5), which cannot be cured by disclosure.
If any legitimate AI-generated creative is retained, ensure AI-origin disclosure and machine-readable provenance marking (AI Act Art. 50(2) & 50(4)).

On the portal, provide a complete, legible Art. 13 privacy notice with the real controller's identity, purpose and lawful basis before collecting any application or payment data, and establish a valid lawful basis that does not depend on the deceptive framing (GDPR Arts. 5, 6 & 13).

Given the vulnerable low-income target audience, escalate this to legal/compliance leadership before any subsidy-related marketing is attempted, as targeting this group sharply aggravates liability (UCPD Art. 5(3)).

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads
campaign.text: Display and search ads styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'. The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.

detected_practices: fake official emblem and national colours
charging for a publicly free service
concealed disclaimer in illegible 7pt grey text
failure to identify the trader in advertising
triage.audience_notes: Explicitly targets low-income households — a potentially vulnerable group under UCPD Art. 5(3), heightening the aggressive/misleading assessment. Government-impersonation framing exploits trust and financial pressure. Although personalisation/targeting is declared "no", the portal will collect application/personal data (likely including financial/eligibility data), so GDPR review is warranted; AI Act review flagged due to declared generative AI use and potential manipulative/deceptive design concerns.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, "OFFICIAL NOTICE" wording) to funnel low-income households to a private site charging €49 for a service that is publicly free. The trader is not identified in the ads and the non-affiliation disclaimer is buried in illegible 7pt grey text. Generative AI is declared as used in creating the material.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The ad creative (government-bulletin styling, coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, notice text) is generated by generative AI and is therefore synthetic image/text content. Art. 50(2) requires providers of generative AI systems to ensure such outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. Nothing in the submission indicates the AI-generated assets carry any provenance marking, and the synthetic content is being used precisely to fabricate an air of official authenticity.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets carry machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g. C2PA / watermarking) as required of the generative-AI provider, and verify with the AI tool vendor that outputs are marked. Independently, the deceptive use of synthetic 'official' imagery should be discontinued (see UCPD assessment).

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: Generative AI is the instrument used to produce purposefully deceptive material — a fake official government notice with a coat-of-arms-like emblem and manufactured deadline urgency — designed to make recipients believe they are dealing with a public authority and pay €49 for a publicly free service. This deploys deceptive techniques via an AI system with the effect of materially distorting the recipient's decision (impairing their ability to make an informed decision and causing a payment they would not otherwise make) in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant financial harm, engaging the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition. Note the underlying deception is also, and primarily, a UCPD matter.
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Do not use AI to generate content that impersonates official government communications or deploys manufactured urgency to distort consumer decisions. Remove the emblem, national-colour styling, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing and 'deadline' pressure, and clearly present the service as a private paid offering.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The campaign is directed at low-income households — a group vulnerable due to their specific economic situation — using AI-generated official-looking content that exploits their reliance on public subsidies and financial pressure to distort their behaviour (paying €49 for a free application), likely causing significant harm. This engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting economic-situation vulnerability. The AI-system nexus is weaker here because personalised/AI-driven targeting is declared 'no' (the exploitation runs through AI-generated creative rather than AI targeting), so the vulnerable-audience concern is chiefly a UCPD Art. 5(3) matter.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting low-income households with content that exploits their economic vulnerability. Ensure no AI system is used to identify, reach or tailor content to financially distressed groups in a way that could distort their decisions; redesign the offer so it does not prey on eligibility anxiety.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to create ad creative styled as an official government bulletin. This primarily engages the AI Act's transparency obligation for synthetic content (Art. 50(2)), which appears unmet. The deceptive, government-impersonating design produced via AI and aimed at low-income households also touches the Art. 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(b) prohibitions, though these prohibitions turn on the AI *system* deploying manipulative techniques / exploiting vulnerability — the core misleading/aggressive-practice and vulnerable-audience concerns are more squarely UCPD/DSA matters covered by other agents. Flagged as risks given the AI-generation nexus with clearly deceptive, harm-causing content.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data collected via an eligibility check that is deliberately disguised as an official government notice is not processed 'fairly' or 'transparently'. Consumers are induced to disclose their data on the false belief they are dealing with a public authority; the whole data-collection context is misleading, which is precisely what the fairness/transparency principle prohibits (covert or misleadingly-framed collection).
findings.evidence_quote: OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove all government-impersonation framing (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'). Any data collection must occur in a context that honestly identifies the private trader and the true nature of the service before the data subject provides data.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected (the eligibility application), the controller must provide, at the point of collection, its identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The advertising does not identify the trader at all, and the only reference to the operator is a 7pt grey non-affiliation line — this cannot satisfy the Art. 13 identity/information obligation that anchors the subsequent data collection.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the controller (legal entity name and contact details) and provide a complete, prominent privacy notice covering purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and rights before any data is submitted on the portal.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, intelligible and easily accessible in clear, plain language. Presenting the material clarifying information in 7pt grey footer text is the opposite of easily accessible and legible, undermining any transparency the operator claims to provide around who is processing the data and why.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present all data-subject-facing information (controller identity, non-affiliation status, privacy notice) in legible, prominent text with adequate contrast and size, at the point where users decide to submit data.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: If the operator relies on 'performance of a contract' as its lawful basis for processing the applicant's data, that basis is fragile where the contract itself is procured through deception (impersonating officialdom and charging for a free service). Consent obtained under a false impression of dealing with a government body would likewise not be freely given or informed. The validity of the claimed lawful basis is therefore in serious doubt.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a genuine, valid lawful basis for processing under a truthful service description; do not rely on a contract or 'consent' obtained through the misleading official-notice framing.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Energy/social-subsidy eligibility data reveals financial hardship and, depending on the questions asked, may reveal or allow inference of special-category data (e.g. health/disability status, household composition) that determines eligibility. If such data is collected, Art. 9's prohibition applies unless a valid exception (e.g. explicit consent) is met — which is questionable in a deceptive context. Flagged for verification of the actual application form fields.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility
findings.recommendation: Audit the application form; if any special-category data is collected, minimise it and secure a valid Art. 9(2) condition (e.g. explicit, informed consent) obtained in a non-deceptive context, or remove such fields.

verdicts.notes: The campaign funnels low-income households to a private site that collects personal data (an "energy subsidy eligibility" application, which will foreseeably include financial-hardship and possibly special-category data) under a deliberately deceptive government-impersonation pretext. This engages GDPR core principles: personal data obtained through a misleading, disguised-as-official context is not processed fairly, lawfully or transparently (Art. 5(1)(a)), and the ads/site fail the identity and information duties of Arts. 13/12 (the trader is not identified and the only disclaimer is buried in illegible 7pt grey). Whether the €49 "application" contract can constitute a valid lawful basis (Art. 6(1)) is doubtful where the underlying premise is deceptive. Eligibility data for energy/social subsidies may reveal financial hardship and, by inference, protected attributes, warranting Art. 9 caution. Note: much of the collection detail lives on the landing site rather than the ad text, so several findings are risk/attention pending the site's actual data flows.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that, for each advertisement presented on an online platform, recipients can identify in a clear, unambiguous manner that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented and who paid for it. These display/search ads are presented on online platforms yet actively conceal the advertiser's identity and their commercial (advertising) nature — they are disguised as an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' from government. The trader's refusal to identify itself makes it impossible for the platform to satisfy, and for recipients to exercise, the Art. 26(1) transparency required, and the ad is not identifiable as an advertisement at all.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the advertising trader (legal name of the private company operating energy-subsidy-portal.eu) and the paying party in every ad creative, and ensure the ad is recognisable as a paid advertisement rather than an official government notice, so the platform's Art. 26 transparency panel reflects accurate advertiser information.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially distorts their ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including disguised advertisements. The ad and landing interface disguise a commercial ad as an official government bulletin, add a false deadline to induce urgency, and bury the material 'not affiliated with any government' disclaimer in 7pt grey text (false hierarchy / concealment). This is precisely the disguised-ad and deceptive-design conduct Art. 25 targets on online-platform interfaces. Caveat: Art. 25 binds providers of online platforms rather than the advertiser directly, so applicability to the trader depends on whether it operates the interface; the equivalent all-trader prohibition sits in the UCPD.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Redesign the creative and landing page to remove government/official styling (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'), remove the false 'deadline' urgency, and present the non-affiliation disclaimer with equal prominence and legibility rather than in illegible 7pt grey, so the interface does not deceive or materially distort user decisions.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs as display and search ads on online platforms, engaging DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern rules. The ads explicitly fail to identify the advertiser ("ads do not identify the trader"), which conflicts with the Art. 26(1) requirement that recipients can identify on whose behalf and who paid for each ad — the trader must supply this information for the platform's transparency scheme to function. The disguised-ad framing (styled as a government bulletin) plus the illegible 7pt grey non-affiliation disclaimer are deceptive interface design of the type Art. 25 addresses. Note: the primary DSA obligations bind the platform providers, but the trader's conduct directly undermines them; the strongest misleading/impersonation findings fall under UCPD (covered by another agent).

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads are designed to convey that the offer is an official government notice / that the trader is approved or authorised by a public body, when the operator is a private company 'not affiliated with any government'. Falsely claiming public-body approval/authorisation, including fake government affiliation and official-looking notices, is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances — no proof of consumer effect is required.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government/official framing entirely: delete the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, and the words 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'. The ad must not imply any governmental origin, approval or authorisation. Rebuild the creative to be unmistakably a private commercial offer.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying an official-looking coat-of-arms-like emblem and national colours amounts to displaying a trust/quality mark or official emblem without authorisation, presented as an independent official indicator. This is prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Remove the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any state insignia or national-colour styling that suggests official endorsement. Use only the trader's own clearly commercial branding.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The campaign deceives the average consumer as to the nature of the service, the price, and the existence of a price advantage: it charges €49 for a service that is publicly free, while presenting itself as an official eligibility check. This is likely to cause consumers to take a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take, constituting a misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Prominently and truthfully disclose that the underlying application is available free of charge from the public authority, and clearly state that €49 is a fee for an optional private processing service. Do not present the paid service as the only or official route.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads fail to identify the trader and hide the commercial intent behind a government-notice styling, and the only non-affiliation disclosure is buried in illegible 7pt grey footer text. Material information (trader identity, commercial nature, non-governmental status, that the service is otherwise free) is omitted or provided in an unclear and untimely manner, engaging misleading omissions and failure to identify commercial intent.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader (legal name/identity) within the ads themselves and label the material as advertising. Move the non-affiliation and 'the official application is free' information to a prominent, legible position (adequate size/contrast) at the point of decision, not a 7pt grey footer.

findings.title: Blacklist: misuse of 'free'
findings.rationale: To the extent the campaign presents access to the subsidy/application as available at no cost while the consumer must actually pay €49 (beyond any unavoidable response/delivery cost), any 'free'/no-cost framing of the underlying benefit misuses the concept of a free offer. If the ad/site conveys a 'free eligibility check' that then requires the €49 payment to proceed, point 20 is engaged.
findings.evidence_quote: charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Do not describe any part of the service or the subsidy application as 'free' or 'no charge' where the consumer must pay €49. State the €49 charge upfront and unavoidably before any commitment.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The practice is contrary to professional diligence and is deliberately aimed at low-income households — a clearly identifiable group whose economic situation makes them more susceptible to official-authority framing and deadline pressure around energy subsidies. Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that vulnerable group, heightening the material distortion of their economic behaviour. Art. 5 operates as the fairness safety-net reinforcing the specific breaches above.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the campaign in its current form. Any lawful version must not exploit financial vulnerability or subsidy-related anxiety; assess targeting and messaging from the perspective of the vulnerable audience and remove all pressure and official-authority cues.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures time pressure to elicit an immediate decision. If there is no genuine, imminent deadline that limits availability (the ad implies the trader's paid service is time-constrained, or misrepresents the public application deadline to pressure payment), this is a false urgency claim, prohibited in all circumstances.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove the deadline/urgency wording unless a specific, genuine and verifiable deadline exists and is accurately described as the public authority's deadline (not a pressure to purchase the €49 service). Do not imply the paid service is time-limited when it is not.

verdicts.notes: This campaign is a textbook multi-breach of the UCPD. Ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national colours, coat-of-arms-like emblem, "OFFICIAL NOTICE") to funnel low-income households to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free application. This triggers at least two blacklisted (per se prohibited) practices — false claim of public-body approval/authorisation (Annex I pt 4) and unauthorised display of an official emblem/trust mark (Annex I pt 2) — plus misleading action (Art. 6), misleading omission/failure to identify the trader with a concealed 7pt disclaimer (Art. 7), and the general Art. 5 fairness prohibition assessed against a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (low-income households). This is high-harm consumer deception; several findings are per se prohibited regardless of consumer effect.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up as an official government bulletin — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem and "OFFICIAL NOTICE" wording — to push low-income households to a private site that charges €49 for a subsidy application that is actually free from the government. This is not a borderline case: it triggers per se prohibited practices under EU consumer law (falsely claiming government approval and displaying an official emblem without authorisation), which are banned outright regardless of whether any consumer is actually harmed. On top of that, it is a clear misleading action and omission (hiding the trader, hiding the commercial nature, burying the "not affiliated with any government" line in 7pt grey text, charging for a free service), and it deliberately targets a financially vulnerable audience. It also breaches AI Act rules (deceptive AI-generated "official" content, missing provenance marking), GDPR (data collected under a false official pretext, no trader identity or proper privacy notice), and DSA advertising-transparency and dark-pattern rules. The core problem — government impersonation to sell a free service — cannot be fixed with disclaimers or tweaks. The verdict is critical: the campaign must not run in its current form and requires a fundamental redesign or withdrawal.
recommendations: STOP the campaign in its current form immediately. It contains multiple per se prohibited (blacklisted) practices under the UCPD that are unlawful regardless of consumer impact, so no amount of fine-tuning makes the current creative usable.

Remove ALL government/official cues entirely: the coat-of-arms-like emblem, national-colour styling, and the words 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'. The ad must be unmistakably a private commercial offer with no implied governmental origin, approval or authorisation.

Identify the trader clearly and prominently within the ads themselves (legal entity name operating energy-subsidy-portal.eu) and label the material as advertising, so both consumers and the platforms' DSA transparency panels reflect who is behind it and who paid.

Tell the truth about price: state upfront and unavoidably that the underlying application is available free of charge from the public authority, and that €49 is an optional fee for a private processing service. Never present the paid route as the only or official one, and never frame any part of it as 'free'.
Remove the manufactured 'before the deadline' urgency unless a genuine, verifiable public-authority deadline exists and is described accurately as such — not as pressure to buy the €49 service.

Stop exploiting the vulnerability of low-income households. Reassess targeting and messaging from the perspective of that audience and strip out all official-authority cues and eligibility-anxiety pressure.

Fix the data-protection failures on the landing site: identify the data controller, provide a complete and legible privacy notice (purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention, rights) BEFORE any data is submitted, and present the non-affiliation disclosure in prominent, legible text rather than 7pt grey.

Establish a genuine, valid lawful basis for processing under a truthful service description; do not rely on a contract or 'consent' obtained through the deceptive official-notice framing. Audit the application form and minimise or remove any special-category data fields.

Ensure all AI-generated assets carry machine-readable provenance/watermarking as required by the AI Act, and confirm with the AI vendor that outputs are marked — while noting that the deceptive use of synthetic 'official' imagery must be discontinued regardless.

campaign.title: 'Energy Subsidy Portal' notice ads

The link leads to 'energy-subsidy-portal.eu', a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application. The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.
