charging a fee for a publicly free service
trader failing to identify itself in ads
triage.audience_notes: Explicitly targets low-income households — a potentially vulnerable audience under UCPD Art. 5(3), heightening the seriousness of the misleading government-impersonation and hidden-fee practices. No indication minors are targeted.
triage.summary: Display and search ads impersonate an official government energy-subsidy notice (national emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') to funnel low-income households to a private site charging €49 for a publicly free application, with only a tiny buried non-affiliation disclaimer and no trader identification. This is a strong candidate for a misleading/aggressive commercial practice exploiting vulnerable consumers, using generative-AI creative.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The ad creative (government-style bulletin, coat-of-arms-like emblem, national colours, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' copy) is produced with generative AI. Art. 50(2) requires providers of AI systems generating synthetic image/text content to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated. Nothing in the campaign indicates the AI-generated visuals or copy carry any provenance marking, and the synthetic origin is material here because it is used to fabricate the appearance of an authentic official government notice.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure all AI-generated campaign assets carry machine-readable provenance/watermark marking as required by Art. 50(2), and obtain confirmation from the generative-AI provider that outputs are marked as artificially generated. Independently, reconsider using AI to synthesise official-looking government imagery at all.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: The AI-generated assets manipulate imagery (a coat-of-arms-like emblem and national colours) to make private commercial material falsely appear to be authentic government content, and the accompanying text informs the public on a matter of public interest (2026 energy subsidy eligibility). Art. 50(4) requires disclosure that such content is artificially generated or manipulated. No such disclosure is present; the only footnote ('not affiliated with any government') is buried in 7pt grey and does not address AI generation.
findings.evidence_quote: 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear and prominent disclosure that the imagery and text are artificially generated/manipulated, distinct from and not buried like the affiliation disclaimer. Do not use AI-manipulated official-emblem imagery to convey public-interest information in a way that appears authentic.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The campaign uses generative AI to produce purposefully deceptive creative (fabricated official-government branding) whose effect is to appreciably impair recipients' ability to make an informed decision — leading them to pay €49 for a service that is publicly free. This maps to the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition of deploying AI systems using manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and are reasonably likely to cause significant (here financial) harm. Applicability is somewhat attenuated because the deceptive design originates in trader intent and the AI functions as a content-generation tool, but the deceptive-technique-plus-harm structure is squarely present.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'
findings.recommendation: Cease using AI-generated deceptive government-impersonation creative. If generative AI is used to produce or optimise persuasive creative, ensure it does not deploy deceptive or manipulative techniques that distort consumer decisions; document a manipulation/harm assessment for AI-produced marketing aimed at the general public.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The AI-generated deceptive creative is directed at low-income households — a group vulnerable due to their specific economic/social situation — with the effect of distorting their behaviour into paying a €49 fee for a publicly free application, a significant harm relative to their means. This engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI systems exploiting economic-situation vulnerabilities. The fit is a risk rather than a clear breach because targeting is declared as 'no' (so the exploitation is via the AI-generated deceptive content and audience selection rather than AI-driven vulnerability profiling), but the vulnerable-audience-plus-harm elements are present and heighten seriousness.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy AI-generated deceptive or high-pressure creative to audiences defined by economic vulnerability. If any AI system tailors or selects content toward low-income segments, conduct and document an Art. 5(1)(b) vulnerability-exploitation assessment and remove the deceptive government-impersonation and hidden-fee elements.

verdicts.notes: The campaign declares use of generative AI to produce display/search ad creative, engaging the AI Act's transparency obligations for synthetic content. The AI-generated assets (fake coat-of-arms emblem, national colours, "OFFICIAL NOTICE" text) are the very medium of the deception, which also brings the manipulative-AI and vulnerability-exploitation prohibitions into play, though these are attenuated because the deception stems from trader design rather than autonomous AI behaviour and no AI-driven targeting is declared. Primary AI Act exposure is the failure to mark AI-generated content (Art. 50(2)/(4)); the Art. 5 prohibitions are secondary risks worth flagging given the vulnerable audience and clear financial harm.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Collecting personal data through an application process while presenting the site as an official government 'Energy Subsidy Portal' (national colours, coat-of-arms emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE') means data subjects are misled about the controller's identity and the true nature of the processing. Processing personal data obtained by deception is neither fair nor transparent, directly breaching the Art. 5(1)(a) fairness and transparency principle. Targeting low-income households heightens the unfairness.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: Do not collect personal data under a false government identity. Present the trader's real commercial identity clearly before any data is entered, remove the official-notice styling, and ensure the data-collection context is truthful so consumers understand who is processing their data and why.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When personal data is collected via the application form, Art. 13 requires the controller to provide, at the point of collection, its true identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights. The ads and portal actively conceal the controller's identity (no trader named, false government affiliation), so the mandatory point-of-collection disclosures cannot be satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete, prominent Art. 13 privacy notice at the point the application is submitted, clearly naming the actual controller company, its contact details, the purposes and lawful basis of processing, recipients, retention period and data-subject rights.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information relating to processing to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible in clear and plain language. Burying the key identity/affiliation information in 7pt grey footer text defeats accessibility and intelligibility, so even where information exists it is not provided in the manner Art. 12 demands.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey
findings.recommendation: Present identity, affiliation and privacy information in a legible size and prominent position, not hidden in tiny grey footer text, so a reasonable consumer can readily access and understand it before submitting data.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: If the portal relies on consent or contract as its lawful basis for processing application data, that basis is undermined because the data subject is deceived about who they are dealing with and the nature/urgency of the service. Consent or contractual willingness obtained under a false government-notice pretext and false urgency is not freely and validly given, leaving processing without a sound Art. 6(1) legal basis.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Re-establish a valid lawful basis by removing the deceptive framing and false deadline urgency, truthfully identifying the commercial service before collecting any data, and obtaining any consent on a fully informed, non-deceptive footing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign funnels consumers to a portal that collects personal data to "submit... an application" for an energy subsidy (necessarily including identity and household/economic details). Because the entire journey is built on impersonating a government body and concealing the trader's true identity, any personal-data processing that follows is neither fair nor transparent, the Art. 13 identity/purpose disclosures are absent or buried, and any "consent" obtained is vitiated by deception. GDPR is engaged even though targeting/personalisation is declared "no", because data is collected at the application stage.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that, for each advertisement presented on an online platform, recipients can identify in a clear, concise and unambiguous manner that it is an advertisement and on whose behalf it is presented. These display and search ads neither disclose that they are advertisements (they are dressed as an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' government bulletin) nor identify the trader running them, defeating both core disclosure requirements. The audience is explicitly low-income households, magnifying the harm of the concealment.
findings.evidence_quote: ads do not identify the trader
findings.recommendation: Redesign the ads so they are unmistakably labelled as advertising and clearly state the identity of the advertiser/payer (the private company). Remove the government styling that conceals commercial nature, and ensure the platform's ad-transparency labels can be populated with a truthful advertiser name.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that deceives or manipulates recipients or materially impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions; disguised advertisements are an identified form of dark pattern. Presenting a commercial ad as an official government notice, combined with hiding the material 'not affiliated with any government' disclosure in 7pt grey footer text, is a deceptive interface design that steers vulnerable consumers into paying €49 for a publicly free service.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE'
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the disguised-ad / false-officialdom design (no emblem, national colours or 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing) and surface the non-affiliation and fee information with equal prominence to the call to action, so the interface no longer deceives or distorts the user's decision-making.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA's advertising-transparency and dark-pattern rules. The display/search ads are deliberately disguised as an official government bulletin and fail to identify that they are advertisements or the trader on whose behalf they run, which cannot satisfy DSA Art. 26(1) when presented on online platforms; the disguised-ad design plus the 7pt buried non-affiliation disclaimer are a textbook dark pattern under DSA Art. 25. The special-category-targeting ban (Art. 26(3)), minor-profiling ban (Art. 28), recommender-transparency (Art. 27) and VLOP ad-repository (Art. 39) provisions are not engaged on the facts (no sensitive-data profiling, no minors, no owned recommender/platform). Note that DSA obligations bind platform providers, but the campaign as designed makes compliant presentation impossible and would be flagged/removed by any compliant platform.

findings.title: Blacklist: false claims of approval or endorsement by a body
findings.rationale: The ads create the impression that a private company is approved, endorsed or authorised by, or affiliated with, a public/government body — using an 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' label, national colours and a coat-of-arms-like emblem. In reality the site is 'not affiliated with any government'. Falsely claiming official approval/affiliation is blacklisted and prohibited in all circumstances, regardless of consumer impact.
findings.evidence_quote: styled as a government bulletin — national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem, 'OFFICIAL NOTICE: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline'
findings.recommendation: Remove all government styling entirely: no coat-of-arms/emblem, no national colours, no 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording, and no language implying an official subsidy channel. The company must present itself unambiguously as an independent private commercial service.

findings.title: Blacklist: displaying a trust mark without authorisation
findings.rationale: Displaying an official/quality mark or equivalent emblem (here a coat-of-arms-like government emblem) without authorisation is a per se prohibited practice. The emblem is used to lend official legitimacy to a private commercial service that has no such authorisation.
findings.evidence_quote: national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem
findings.recommendation: Delete the coat-of-arms-like emblem and any state insignia from all creative. Use only the company's own clearly commercial branding.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: The campaign deceives the average consumer about the nature of the service and the price/existence of a price advantage: consumers are led to believe they are accessing an official subsidy process when in fact they are paying €49 for something that is publicly free. This is likely to cause a transactional decision (paying €49) they would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: a private company charging €49 to submit a publicly free application
findings.recommendation: State clearly and prominently in the ad and on the landing page that the underlying government application is free of charge, that the €49 is a separate private assistance fee, and where the free official service can be accessed directly.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Material information is hidden or provided unclearly: the trader's identity is omitted from the ads, and the critical non-affiliation disclaimer is buried in 7pt grey footer text — unclear, untimely and effectively concealed. The commercial intent (a paid private service) is not apparent from the government-bulletin context, breaching the duty to make commercial intent clear and to provide material information intelligibly.
findings.evidence_quote: The site footer says 'not affiliated with any government' in 7pt grey; ads do not identify the trader.
findings.recommendation: Clearly identify the trader (legal name/company identity) in every ad, and present the non-affiliation and paid-service disclosures in prominent, legible text at the point of the claim — not buried in tiny footer type.

findings.title: Blacklist: false urgency and scarcity claims
findings.rationale: The 'before the deadline' framing manufactures artificial time pressure to elicit an immediate decision, especially where the service is a paid intermediary for an application consumers could make freely at their own pace. If no genuine binding deadline applies to using this private service (as opposed to the underlying public scheme), this is a blacklisted false urgency claim.
findings.evidence_quote: Check your 2026 energy subsidy eligibility before the deadline
findings.recommendation: Remove urgency/deadline language unless a specific, genuine and verifiable official deadline exists and is accurately stated with its true source; never imply the private service must be used to meet any deadline.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: The campaign is expressly aimed at low-income households — a clearly identifiable vulnerable group in the context of an energy-subsidy offer. Under Art. 5(3) the practice is assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group, whose economic behaviour is especially likely to be materially distorted by an official-looking notice charging €49 for a free service. This safety-net provision reinforces and aggravates the seriousness of the misleading/impersonation findings.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: low-income households
findings.recommendation: Do not exploit financial vulnerability: cease the deceptive government-impersonation tactic entirely and ensure any offer to this audience is transparent about cost, the free public alternative, and the private nature of the service.

verdicts.notes: This campaign engages multiple UCPD prohibitions, including several blacklisted (per se unfair) practices under Annex I. The core violation is impersonation of a government authority to make consumers believe a private €49 service is an official subsidy channel — a false claim of official endorsement/authorisation (Annex I point 4) and misuse of an official emblem/trust mark (point 2). It is compounded by misleading actions on the free/official nature of the service (Art. 6), misleading omissions of trader identity and commercial intent (Art. 7), and a false 'deadline' urgency claim (point 7). Because the campaign deliberately targets low-income households — a vulnerable group under Art. 5(3) — the seriousness of every finding is heightened.

report.executive_summary: This campaign runs display and search ads dressed up as an official government bulletin — using national colours, a coat-of-arms-like emblem and 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' wording — to drive low-income households to a private site that charges €49 for a subsidy application that is actually free from the government. This is not a fixable labelling problem; it is impersonation of a public authority, which EU consumer law bans outright. The campaign breaks multiple blacklisted rules under the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (false claim of official endorsement, unauthorised use of an official emblem, and a fake deadline), all of which are prohibited in every circumstance regardless of intent. It also fails the Digital Services Act's ad-transparency and anti-dark-pattern rules (the ads don't reveal they are ads or who paid for them), and any personal data collected on the fake portal breaches GDPR because it's gathered under a false identity with the trader hidden in 7pt grey text. The AI-generated official-looking creative additionally lacks the AI Act's required 'artificially generated' marking and edges toward its prohibited manipulation and vulnerability-exploitation provisions. Deliberately targeting financially vulnerable people makes every issue more serious and increases regulatory and reputational exposure. Verdict: do not run this campaign as designed — it requires fundamental redesign, not tweaks.
recommendations: STOP — do not launch this campaign in its current form. The government-impersonation concept is per se illegal under UCPD Annex I and cannot be made compliant by adding disclaimers.</br>
Remove ALL official/government styling: no coat-of-arms or state emblem, no national colours, no 'OFFICIAL NOTICE' framing, and no wording implying an official subsidy channel.
Identify the trader clearly in every ad — the real company name — and make each ad unmistakably recognisable as a paid advertisement (DSA Art. 26 and UCPD Art. 7).

State prominently, up front (not in a footer), that the government subsidy application is FREE, that your €49 is a separate optional private assistance fee, and where consumers can access the free official service directly.
Delete the false 'before the deadline' urgency unless a genuine, verifiable official deadline exists and is stated accurately with its true source (UCPD Annex I point 7).

Move the 'not affiliated with any government', fee, and privacy information out of the 7pt grey footer into legible, prominent placement with equal weight to the call to action (UCPD Art. 7, DSA Art. 25, GDPR Art. 12).

Before collecting any personal data, present the true controller identity and a full GDPR Art. 13 privacy notice (purposes, lawful basis, retention, rights); do not collect data under a false government identity.

For any AI-generated assets, ensure machine-readable provenance marking and a clear disclosure that content is artificially generated (AI Act Art. 50(2)/(4)); do not use AI to synthesise official-emblem/government imagery.

Given the low-income target audience, conduct and document a vulnerability/harm assessment before targeting this group, and avoid any high-pressure or deceptive tactics aimed at them (UCPD Art. 5(3); AI Act Art. 5(1)(a)/(b)).

campaign.title: HomeSecure winter blitz — purchased list
campaign.text: Email campaign for home alarm systems sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available). The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

detected_practices: purchased/third-party data list with no consent records
uploading purchased list to Meta/Google to build lookalike audiences
cold follow-up phone calls to non-openers using broker-appended numbers
triage.audience_notes: Declared target is homeowners aged 30-65, so minors are not the intended audience; however, lookalike audiences and a purchased list of unknown provenance mean actual reach is uncontrolled. No generative AI declared or detected, but the platform lookalike-audience targeting engages DSA online advertising/profiling provisions in addition to core GDPR and UCPD (misleading/aggressive practices) review.
triage.summary: Multi-channel (email, social, phone) marketing campaign for home alarm systems targeting EU homeowners aged 30-65, built on a 400,000-address list purchased from a data broker with no valid consent records. The list is reused for Meta/Google lookalike audiences, emails lack any unsubscribe mechanism or privacy policy reference, and non-openers receive cold follow-up calls using broker-appended numbers. Serious GDPR concerns (lawful basis, consent, transparency, data broker sourcing) plus consumer-protection and platform-targeting issues.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Email direct marketing and profiling generally require a valid lawful basis — for unsolicited email marketing typically prior consent (or a carefully balanced legitimate interest that cannot cure the absence of consent for the broker source). With no consent records and only a vague broker assertion, there is no demonstrable lawful basis for the email send, the platform uploads, or the follow-up calls. All processing is therefore unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Cease using the purchased list. Only market to individuals for whom a valid, documented lawful basis exists (e.g. genuine opt-in with records). Conduct due diligence on any data source and retain evidence of the basis before any processing.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Where consent is the basis relied upon, the controller must be able to demonstrate it. An undated, unverifiable broker claim with no consent records fails Art. 7's demonstrability requirement; consent cannot simply be inherited from an unknown third-party collection point.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Do not rely on unverifiable third-party consent. Obtain fresh, documented consent directly, storing the time, wording, and scope of each opt-in so consent can be demonstrated on demand.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Valid consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, and specific to the controller and purposes. A generic 2019 opt-in 'somewhere' is neither specific to HomeSecure nor informed as to these purposes (email, lookalike audiences, follow-up calls), so it does not meet the definition of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker
findings.recommendation: Collect purpose- and controller-specific consent that names HomeSecure and the intended uses (email marketing, social advertising, phone contact) via a clear affirmative action.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently. Repurposing a broker list for uses individuals never anticipated, with no privacy information provided, is covert and unfair processing that breaches the core lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Ensure all processing is lawful, limited to reasonably expected purposes, and accompanied by clear privacy information; abandon covert repurposing of undisclosed data.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Because the data was obtained from a source other than the data subject and no privacy information is provided, the controller fails to supply the mandatory information (identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients such as Meta/Google, retention, rights, profiling) required when processing personal data. (Art. 14 obligations for third-party-sourced data are engaged; the campaign provides none of this.)
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete privacy notice at first contact identifying the controller, purposes, legal basis, the fact data came from a broker, recipients (Meta/Google), retention and data-subject rights, and link it in every communication.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and every marketing communication must facilitate opt-out. Emails with no unsubscribe mechanism (and cold follow-up calls) fail to provide an easy, effective means to exercise this right.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a functioning one-click unsubscribe link in every email and an opt-out on calls; honour objections immediately and suppress objecting contacts across all channels.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading the list to build lookalike audiences and targeting non-openers constitutes automated processing to evaluate/predict personal aspects, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4). This profiling shares the same lack of lawful basis and transparency as the underlying list, compounding the breach.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Do not upload personal data to build lookalike/custom audiences without a valid lawful basis and transparency; if profiling for marketing is pursued, base it on validly consented data and disclose it, honouring the right to object under Art. 21.

verdicts.notes: This campaign presents multiple serious and interlocking GDPR breaches. It is built on a 400,000-address list purchased from a data broker with no consent records, then reused for platform lookalike audiences and broker-appended phone calls — none of which has a demonstrable lawful basis. Emails carry no opt-out mechanism and no privacy information is provided at any point, defeating the transparency and right-to-object obligations. The processing is unlawful, unfair and non-transparent as described and should not proceed in its current form.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Building lookalike audiences on Meta/Google from an unvetted broker list for home alarm/security products constitutes profiling-based platform advertising. DSA Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits presenting ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including where sensitive attributes are inferred via proxies. Security/anxiety-driven lookalike segments carry a real risk of inferring or correlating with sensitive attributes (e.g. health/vulnerability, victimisation), and the marketer has no visibility into how the platform derives lookalike similarity from an opaque source list. While the text does not prove targeting on an Art. 9 category, the uncontrolled provenance makes this a genuine compliance risk the advertiser cannot exclude.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Do not seed lookalike/custom audiences from the purchased list. Only use platform audiences built from data with a verified lawful basis, and configure targeting to exclude any parameters that directly or by inference rely on GDPR Art. 9 sensitive categories. Document the audience-construction logic so you can demonstrate no sensitive-attribute profiling is used.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Presenting the ads on Meta/Google engages DSA Art. 26(1), which requires that each ad clearly identify that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf and who paid for it, plus meaningful information about the main targeting parameters. Although the disclosure obligation sits with the platform, the advertiser must supply accurate advertiser/payer identity and cannot obscure who is behind the campaign; the reliance on an opaque broker-sourced list weakens the ability to give meaningful targeting-parameter information.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the campaign is set up with accurate advertiser and payer identity in the platform ad tools, and that the targeting parameters declared to the platform are truthful and explainable so the platform can surface them to recipients as Art. 26(1) requires.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Meta and Google are designated VLOPs and must maintain public ad repositories under DSA Art. 39, archiving ad content, advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. The campaign's targeting choices — including any lookalike/audience parameters — will therefore be publicly inspectable, exposing the questionable data sourcing and targeting to regulator and public scrutiny.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Assume every ad and its targeting parameters will be permanently public in the platforms' ad repositories; only run targeting you can defend in the open, and remediate the data-sourcing issues before launch to avoid a publicly documented compliance trail.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The declared audience excludes minors, so the Art. 28 prohibition on profiling-based ads to minors is not deliberately engaged. However, lookalike audiences seeded from a list of unknown provenance mean actual reach is uncontrolled and could include minors, in which case profiled ads to them would be prohibited.
findings.evidence_quote: homeowners 30-65
findings.recommendation: Apply platform age controls and exclude minors from all audience definitions; verify that lookalike expansion cannot serve profiled ads to users the platform knows with reasonable certainty are minors.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged through the reuse of the purchased list to build Meta/Google lookalike audiences, i.e. profiling-based platform advertising. The primary DSA obligations (Arts. 26, 28, 39) bind the platforms (Meta/Google) rather than the advertiser directly, but the campaign's design creates concrete DSA exposure: platform ad-transparency duties are engaged, VLOP ad repositories will publicly archive the targeting, and there is a material risk that lookalikes seeded from an unvetted security-product list rely on inferred sensitive attributes. No dark-pattern (Art. 25) finding is made because the missing-unsubscribe/no-privacy-policy issues concern email communications (ePrivacy/GDPR/UCPD), not online-platform interface design. Minors are not the declared audience, so Art. 28 is a low-level caution only.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media (outside enforcement of a contractual obligation). The recipients are strangers on a purchased list with no consent records who never asked to be contacted; the emails provide no way to stop the messages, and non-openers — who by definition showed no interest — are then re-contacted by cold phone call. This multi-channel, opt-out-less re-solicitation of unwilling recipients is exactly the blacklisted conduct: continued/scripted contact ignoring the consumer's lack of consent, with no mechanism to refuse.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') ... Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Stop the campaign as designed. Only market to individuals with a demonstrable lawful basis/valid opt-in; include a functioning one-click unsubscribe in every email and honour it immediately; do not phone non-openers or anyone who has not consented to phone contact, and screen against opt-out/objection and national do-not-call registers before any call.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat as aggressive any practice that, through harassment, persistence or undue influence, significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Escalating from unsolicited email to unsolicited phone calls specifically targeted at people who did not engage (non-openers), combined with the absence of any opt-out and the fear/security framing of home-alarm marketing, constitutes persistent harassment that pressures consumers into a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. This reinforces the point 26 breach and applies even where point 26's per-se test is contested.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the non-opener phone follow-up sequence and any relentless cross-channel re-contact. Cap contact frequency, obtain prior consent for calls, and ensure consumers can easily refuse or stop further solicitation at any point.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that material information not be omitted or hidden. While the commercial intent of an alarm-system advertisement is apparent from context (so the 'hidden commercial intent' limb is not strongly engaged), the total absence of a privacy-policy reference or any indication of how recipients can find data-handling/opt-out information deprives the average consumer of information they need to respond informedly. The core deficiency is a GDPR transparency matter, but it compounds the UCPD unfairness of the communication.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, accessible privacy-policy link and identify the sender in every communication, alongside a plain opt-out route, so recipients have the material information needed to make an informed choice.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the UCPD primarily through unwanted, unstoppable solicitations across email and phone. Sending marketing to a 400,000-address purchased list with no consent and no unsubscribe mechanism, then placing cold follow-up calls to non-openers using broker-appended numbers, matches the per-se blacklisted practice in Annex I point 26 (persistent and unwanted solicitations) and also amounts to an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. Consent/lawful-basis and privacy-transparency deficiencies are primarily GDPR matters and are not scored here except where they compound the UCPD unfairness. No misleading claims (false urgency, cures, reviews, endorsements) are present in the described material.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems to 400,000 people on a purchased broker list across email, social and phone. As designed, it is not lawful to run in the EU and should not launch. The core problem is that there is no valid, documented consent for anyone on the list — a vague "opted-in somewhere in 2019" broker claim does not meet EU consent standards, so every downstream use (emailing, uploading to Meta/Google for lookalikes, and cold-calling non-openers) has no legal basis. On top of that, the emails have no unsubscribe link and no privacy notice, and the follow-up calls to people who didn't open constitute a blacklisted "persistent and unwanted solicitation" and an aggressive practice under consumer-protection law. Seeding platform lookalike audiences from this security-product list also creates real risk of sensitive-attribute profiling and will be publicly visible in the platforms' ad repositories. In short: multiple critical GDPR and UCPD breaches that expose the marketer to enforcement, fines, and reputational harm. Do not proceed with the campaign in its current form.
recommendations: Do not launch the campaign as designed and stop any use of the purchased broker list — there is no demonstrable lawful basis for emailing, platform uploads, or calls.
Delete the broker list from your systems and remove/withdraw the lookalike and custom audiences already uploaded to Meta and Google.
Cancel the phone follow-up sequence to non-openers entirely — cold-calling uninterested recipients is a blacklisted, per-se unfair practice and an aggressive commercial practice.
Only market to individuals for whom you hold fresh, documented, purpose- and controller-specific opt-in (recording time, wording, and scope so consent is demonstrable on demand).

Add a functioning one-click unsubscribe to every email and an opt-out on any call; honour objections immediately and suppress across all channels; screen against national do-not-call registers before phoning.

Provide a complete privacy notice at first contact (controller identity, purposes, legal basis, that data came from a broker, recipients such as Meta/Google, retention, and data-subject rights) and link it in every communication.

If you pursue platform advertising later, build audiences only from validly consented data, exclude any targeting that could infer sensitive attributes, apply age controls to exclude minors, and document your audience-construction logic — assume it will be publicly inspectable in VLOP ad repositories.
Conduct and retain due-diligence documentation on any future data source before processing.

The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

detected_practices: purchased marketing list with no verifiable consent records
no privacy policy reference in emails
uploading purchased list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
cold follow-up phone calls to non-openers using broker-appended phone numbers
personal data (email addresses, phone numbers) sourced from third-party data broker
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is homeowners 30-65 in the EU, so minors are unlikely to be a primary target; however, purchased broker lists offer no reliable age verification. Core concern is the absence of any lawful basis or consent records for processing, the lack of opt-out mechanisms, and unsolicited direct marketing (email and phone) under GDPR and ePrivacy principles.
triage.summary: A cross-channel (email, social, phone) marketing campaign for home alarm systems targeting EU homeowners aged 30-65, built on a 400,000-address list purchased from a data broker with no verifiable consent records. The campaign uploads the list to Meta and Google for lookalike audiences, sends emails lacking any unsubscribe link or privacy policy reference, and cold-calls non-openers via broker-appended phone numbers.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Processing personal data (email addresses, appended phone numbers) for direct marketing requires a valid lawful basis. The controller cannot rely on consent because no consent records exist, and cannot readily rely on legitimate interests for email/phone marketing built on a purchased broker list where individuals never had a relationship with the sender and had no reasonable expectation of contact. There is therefore no valid Art. 6(1) basis for any of the email, phone or lookalike processing.
findings.evidence_quote: purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Stop processing this list immediately. Do not use broker-sourced data without documented, verifiable, purpose-compatible consent obtained by the source. Rebuild marketing audiences from first-party data collected with a clear lawful basis, or delete the list.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that the data subject consented. With no consent records and only a vague broker assertion ('opted-in somewhere in 2019'), consent cannot be demonstrated for any of the 400,000 individuals. The 2019 'somewhere' opt-in is also not specific to this controller or this purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Obtain and retain granular, auditable consent records tied to each data subject and to the specific processing purpose (this sender's direct marketing) before any contact. Absent such records, the list cannot lawfully be used.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Even if some opt-in occurred, consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A generic broker opt-in 'somewhere' is not specific to this controller's home-alarm marketing nor informed about onward sharing to third parties, so it fails the Art. 4(11) standard as a basis for this campaign.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019'
findings.recommendation: Rely only on consent that names the controller and the specific marketing purposes; discard non-specific third-party opt-ins as invalid for this campaign.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to direct marketing, and every marketing communication must facilitate opt-out. Emails with no unsubscribe mechanism (and manual reply handling) fail to provide an effective, easy means to exercise this right; cold-calling non-openers compounds the failure to respect objection rights.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a functioning, one-click unsubscribe in every marketing email and an equivalent easy opt-out for phone contact; suppress objecting individuals across all channels and the lookalike source list immediately and permanently.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data are obtained (including from a third-party broker), the controller must provide identity, purposes and legal basis, recipients (Meta/Google), the source of the data, retention and data-subject rights, and information about profiling. None of this is provided; there is no privacy notice reference at all.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete Art. 13/14 privacy notice at or before first contact, including that data was obtained from a broker, the recipients (Meta, Google), profiling activities, retention and how to object; link it prominently in every email.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Transparency information must be concise, intelligible and easily accessible. With no privacy policy referenced anywhere in the emails, data subjects cannot access the required information, breaching the transparency-communication obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Make the privacy information easily accessible via a clear link in every communication, in plain language.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The processing is neither lawful (no valid basis), fair (individuals had no expectation of being marketed to or profiled by this sender), nor transparent (no privacy notice). This breaches the overarching lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle.
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Remediate lawful basis, transparency and opt-out issues before any processing; treat covert use of broker data for onward profiling as inherently unfair and cease it.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading personal data to build lookalike audiences is automated processing to evaluate/predict personal preferences and behaviour, i.e. profiling under Art. 4(4). This profiling is carried out on data with no lawful basis and no transparency, engaging the definition and triggering the associated Art. 6(1)/Art. 21 obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Do not upload the purchased list for audience-matching or lookalike modelling; any profiling for advertising needs a valid lawful basis, transparency and an easy objection route.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Broker-appended phone numbers are additional personal data processed for direct marketing calls with no consent and no expectation of contact, so there is no lawful basis for this processing either. Marketing calls generally require prior consent under GDPR read with ePrivacy.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker
findings.recommendation: Cease cold-calling based on appended broker numbers; only call individuals who have given prior consent (subject to national ePrivacy/telemarketing rules and do-not-call registries).

verdicts.notes: This campaign is built on a 400,000-address list purchased from a data broker with no verifiable consent records ('opted-in somewhere in 2019', no records available), used for email, phone and social (lookalike) marketing across the EU. It engages multiple core GDPR obligations that are almost certainly breached: there is no demonstrable lawful basis (Art. 6(1)), consent cannot be demonstrated and does not meet the informed/specific/unambiguous standard (Arts. 4(11), 7), emails carry no opt-out and no privacy information (Arts. 21, 12, 13, 5(1)(a)), and uploading the list for lookalike audiences constitutes profiling without a basis (Arts. 4(4), 6(1), 21). Overall risk is very high; the underlying processing should be halted pending remediation.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media (except to enforce a contractual obligation). Here recipients never requested contact (purchased list, no consent), emails deliberately omit any unsubscribe link so there is no way to refuse, and the campaign then escalates by placing follow-up phone calls to those who did not open the email. This scripted, multi-channel re-contact of people who cannot opt out is exactly the blacklisted 'persistent and unwanted solicitation' — a per-se unfair practice regardless of effect on the average consumer.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') ... Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Stop contacting individuals for whom there is no valid consent/opt-out record. Provide a working, one-click unsubscribe in every email and honour it immediately; suppress from all channels anyone who does not open, objects, or unsubscribes, and never escalate non-openers to phone calls. Maintain a do-not-contact suppression list and screen phone numbers against it before any calling.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, through harassment or undue influence, and taking account of timing, persistence and onerous barriers to exercising rights, it impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Persisting across channels (unsolicited email, then cold calls to non-openers) while providing no means to object combines persistence with the removal of the consumer's ability to make it stop, which meets the aggressive-practice factors of persistence and onerous barriers to exercising the right to be left alone.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate the escalation logic that re-targets non-openers by phone. Any calling must be based on prior consent, must present clear caller identity, must stop on first refusal, and must offer an immediate, cost-free way to be removed from all contact.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the average consumer needs, including failing to make the commercial intent and identity/context clear. Emails to a cold purchased list that reference no privacy policy and provide no identity or opt-out information deny recipients the material information needed to understand who is contacting them and how to stop, which supports a misleading-omission finding (overlapping with, but distinct from, the pure data-protection obligations).
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: In every communication clearly identify the trader, state that it is a marketing message, reference/link the privacy policy, and give clear instructions and a functioning mechanism to opt out of further contact.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's primary defects (no consent, no lawful basis for the broker list) fall under GDPR/ePrivacy, but the design of the outreach independently engages the UCPD. Sending unsolicited email with no unsubscribe mechanism to a purchased list and then cold-calling non-openers is a scripted, multi-channel solicitation with no functioning opt-out — a practice blacklisted in all circumstances under Annex I point 26 and reinforced by the aggressive-practices standard in Arts. 8-9. The failure to identify the trader/commercial context and provide a way to stop contact also engages the misleading-omission rule in Art. 7.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems by email, social lookalike audiences, and follow-up phone calls to 400,000 people from a purchased broker list that has no usable consent records — just a vague claim that people "opted in somewhere in 2019." That single fact undermines the entire campaign. Under GDPR there is no valid lawful basis to email, call, or profile these individuals, consent cannot be demonstrated, no privacy information is provided, and the emails have no unsubscribe link. Uploading the list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences is unlawful profiling. On top of the data-protection problems, cold-emailing with no opt-out and then escalating to phone calls to non-openers is a "persistent and unwanted solicitation" that is banned outright under EU consumer law (UCPD Annex I) and also qualifies as an aggressive commercial practice. This is not a campaign that can be fixed with tweaks — the underlying data and outreach design are unlawful. Do not launch; halt processing of the list and rebuild from properly consented first-party data.
recommendations: Do not launch the campaign. Immediately stop all processing of the purchased list — no emails, no calls, no uploads — pending remediation.
Remove the list from Meta and Google and delete any lookalike audiences already built from it; this profiling has no lawful basis.

Delete or quarantine the broker list unless the broker can supply granular, auditable, per-person consent records that specifically name your company and the home-alarm marketing purpose (the 2019 'opted-in somewhere' claim does not qualify).

Cease all follow-up phone calls to non-openers; cold-calling appended broker numbers is unlawful and, combined with the no-opt-out emails, is a per-se banned 'persistent and unwanted solicitation' under UCPD Annex I point 26.
Rebuild your marketing audience from first-party data collected directly with clear, documented, purpose-specific consent under a valid GDPR lawful basis.
Add a functioning one-click unsubscribe to every marketing email and an equivalent easy opt-out for phone contact; honour objections immediately and suppress across all channels permanently.

Provide a complete Art. 13/14 privacy notice at or before first contact — identify your company, state it is marketing, disclose the broker source and the Meta/Google recipients, describe the profiling, retention, and how to object — and link it prominently in every message.
Establish and screen against a do-not-contact suppression list before any future outreach, and identify the trader and commercial intent clearly in every communication.

campaign.title: HomeSecure winter blitz — purchased list
campaign.text: Email campaign for home alarm systems sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available). The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences. Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') and the privacy policy is not referenced. Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.

detected_practices: purchased marketing list with no verifiable consent
no privacy policy reference in communications
uploading purchased list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
unsolicited follow-up phone calls to non-openers
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is homeowners 30-65, so minors are not intentionally targeted; however the source list has no consent provenance, so actual recipients cannot be verified. No generative AI declared or detected. GDPR is central (unlawful processing, absent consent for purchased list and phone appends, missing lawful basis/transparency, ePrivacy-adjacent unsolicited direct marketing without opt-out). UCPD applies to the consumer-facing nature and potential aggressive/misleading practices. DSA is included for the use of Meta/Google platform advertising and lookalike/behavioural targeting.
triage.summary: A cross-channel (email, social, phone) marketing campaign for home alarm systems targeting EU homeowners aged 30-65, built on a 400,000-address list purchased from a data broker with no verifiable consent records. The list is used for direct email (with no unsubscribe link or privacy policy reference), uploaded to Meta/Google for lookalike audience building, and used for unsolicited follow-up calls to non-openers. The campaign presents serious lawful-basis, transparency, and direct-marketing consent issues.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All processing (email marketing, phone appends, platform upload) requires a valid Art. 6 lawful basis. The list was purchased with no consent records and no verifiable provenance; consent cannot be relied on, and legitimate interest cannot cure email/phone direct marketing to individuals who were never informed and never opted in. There is no demonstrable lawful basis for any of the processing operations.
findings.evidence_quote: sent to 400,000 addresses purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available)
findings.recommendation: Cease processing the purchased list immediately. Do not send, call, or upload any records lacking documented, valid consent. Only process contacts for whom a lawful basis (typically prior GDPR-standard opt-in consent for email/phone marketing) can be evidenced.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to be able to demonstrate that consent was given. Vague broker assertions with no consent records make it impossible to demonstrate consent, and consent must be as easy to withdraw as to give — which is impossible here given no unsubscribe mechanism.
findings.evidence_quote: 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' per the broker, no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Obtain and retain auditable consent records (timestamp, wording, scope, source) for every contact before any marketing. Where records cannot be produced, treat the contact as having no consent and suppress it.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A generic third-party opt-in 'somewhere in 2019' cannot be specific or informed as to marketing by HomeSecure for home alarm systems, nor to onward transfer to Meta/Google for lookalike profiling. Such bundled/broad broker consent does not qualify.
findings.evidence_quote: purchased from a data broker ('opted-in somewhere in 2019'
findings.recommendation: Re-collect fresh, specific, informed opt-in consent naming HomeSecure as controller and each processing purpose (email, phone, platform matching) before contacting individuals.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing is absolute and every marketing communication must facilitate opt-out. The absence of an unsubscribe link means recipients cannot easily exercise this right; manual reply handling does not satisfy the requirement to enable and honour objection at any time and at no cost.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually')
findings.recommendation: Include a clear, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out mechanism in every email and an opt-out route in phone calls; suppress objecting individuals across all channels immediately and permanently.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is obtained (including from a third party), controllers must provide identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients (Meta/Google), retention, data subject rights and profiling information. Recipients received no such information, so Art. 13/14 transparency obligations are unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Provide a complete privacy notice at first contact, linked in every communication, covering controller identity, source of data, purposes, lawful basis, recipients (platforms), retention and data subject rights.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. With no privacy policy reference in any communication, the accessibility requirement is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: the privacy policy is not referenced
findings.recommendation: Reference and link an accessible, plain-language privacy notice in all emails, social ads and provide it verbally/on request in phone contact.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle is breached: processing lacks a lawful basis (unlawful), individuals were never informed (not transparent), and using data from an unverified broker source for purposes recipients never anticipated is unfair.
findings.evidence_quote: no consent records available
findings.recommendation: Rebuild the campaign on lawfully sourced, transparently informed data; conduct a data-protection review before relaunch.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Uploading the list to build lookalike audiences constitutes profiling — automated processing to evaluate and predict personal aspects/interests of individuals. This engages profiling rules and compounds the lawful-basis and transparency failures, as no consent covers this onward use.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Do not upload the purchased list for lookalike/behavioural profiling without a valid lawful basis and prior disclosure of platform recipients; obtain specific consent for platform matching or drop the practice.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Automated segmentation of non-openers for follow-up is profiling-driven targeting. While it likely does not produce legal or similarly significant effects (so Art. 22's core prohibition may not bite), it is worth flagging as automated profiling-based decisioning within the marketing flow.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers
findings.recommendation: Confirm no solely-automated significant decisions are made; ensure any profiling-based follow-up is disclosed and covered by a lawful basis.

verdicts.notes: This campaign presents serious and multiple GDPR breaches. The entire operation is built on a 400,000-address purchased list with no verifiable consent, meaning there is no demonstrable lawful basis for the email/phone direct marketing, the phone appends, or the upload to Meta/Google for lookalike profiling. Consent cannot be demonstrated (Art. 7) and does not meet the standard of freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous (Art. 4(11)). Transparency obligations (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13) are unmet as recipients were never informed, and the absolute right to object to direct marketing (Art. 21) is defeated by the missing unsubscribe mechanism.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Building lookalike/behavioural audiences on Meta and Google constitutes profiling-based advertising presented on online platforms. Art. 26(1) requires that each ad be clearly identifiable as an advertisement, disclose on whose behalf and who paid for it, and provide meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how recipients can change them. The advertiser must ensure its platform ads carry accurate advertiser-identity information and that the lookalike targeting parameters it selects are disclosable; a covertly seeded, broker-sourced lookalike audience makes meaningful parameter transparency difficult to satisfy.
findings.evidence_quote: The same list is uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences.
findings.recommendation: When running the Meta/Google ads, use each platform's paid-partnership/advertiser-disclosure tools so the ad is clearly labelled with the correct advertiser and payer identity, and configure targeting so the 'why am I seeing this ad' parameters shown to recipients are accurate. Do not build audiences from lists that cannot be lawfully sourced, since undisclosed broker-seeded lookalikes undermine parameter transparency.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) prohibits platform ads based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special-category data (health, religion, sexual orientation, etc.), directly or by inference. Home-alarm marketing to homeowners 30-65 does not inherently rely on sensitive attributes, so no breach is evident from the text. Flagged for awareness: if lookalike seed lists or targeting proxies were ever derived from sensitive attributes, the ads would be prohibited regardless of consent.
findings.evidence_quote: uploaded to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences
findings.recommendation: Confirm that neither the seed list nor the lookalike/interest targeting relies on or infers GDPR Art. 9 categories. Document the targeting parameters to demonstrate no sensitive-attribute profiling is used.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 bans profiling-based advertising to minors on online platforms. The declared audience excludes minors, so the provision is not intentionally engaged. However, the seed list has no consent provenance and recipients cannot be verified, so a residual risk exists that minors could be reached by lookalike expansion. No evidence in the text shows minors are actually targeted.
findings.evidence_quote: homeowners 30-65
findings.recommendation: Apply age-gating/exclusions in the Meta/Google campaigns to ensure no profiling-based ads are served to users under 18, and avoid list-based audiences whose provenance cannot confirm adult-only composition.

verdicts.notes: The DSA is engaged because the campaign uploads a 400,000-address purchased list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences — i.e. profiling-based advertising delivered through online platforms. Most DSA advertising obligations bind the platforms (Meta/Google) rather than the advertiser directly, but the advertiser's targeting choices determine whether platform ad-transparency and ad-repository requirements (Art. 26, 39) can be satisfied, and the advertiser must supply accurate advertiser-identity and targeting-parameter information. The core unlawfulness here (no consent, no lawful basis, no opt-out) sits under GDPR/UCPD/ePrivacy; on the DSA axis the practices are transparency risks rather than clear prohibitions. No profiling-based advertising to minors and no evident sensitive-category (Art. 9) targeting is described.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits making persistent and unwanted solicitations by telephone, e-mail or other remote media in all circumstances. Recipients are on a purchased list with no verifiable consent, so the solicitations are 'unwanted' by default. The campaign then escalates across channels — emailing people, and where the email is ignored, telephoning them on broker-appended numbers — which is a scripted re-contact pattern. Removing the standard unsubscribe link and routing opt-outs to unreliable 'manual reply' handling means the marketing continues without an effective way for the consumer to refuse, reinforcing the 'persistent and unwanted' character. This is not justified by any contractual obligation, the only exception in the provision.
findings.evidence_quote: Emails have no unsubscribe link ('replies handled manually') ... Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Only contact individuals with a verifiable, documented lawful basis/consent to be marketed by each specific channel. Restore a one-click unsubscribe link in every email and an equivalent opt-out on calls, honour objections immediately across all channels, and suppress any contact whose consent cannot be evidenced. Do not follow up non-openers on a second channel absent affirmative consent for that channel.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, by harassment or undue influence — assessed by factors including timing, persistence and the presence of onerous barriers to exercising rights — it impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. Sending marketing with no functioning opt-out and then telephoning consumers who simply did not open an email exhibits persistence and pressure directed at people who gave no indication of interest, while the absence of an easy stop mechanism is an onerous barrier. Combined with the home-security subject matter (which can play on safety anxieties), this cross-channel escalation risks crossing into an aggressive practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Follow-up calls are placed to non-openers using phone numbers appended by the broker.
findings.recommendation: Eliminate cold follow-up calling to non-openers. Ensure any telephone marketing is preceded by clear consent, capped in frequency, and stops on first request. Avoid framing that exploits fear about home safety to pressure a purchase decision.

verdicts.notes: The campaign's consumer-facing tactics engage the UCPD through its solicitation model rather than through misleading claims. Recipients on a purchased list with no verifiable consent receive marketing emails that provide no opt-out mechanism, and non-openers are then chased by follow-up phone calls using broker-appended numbers. Contacting people who never asked to be contacted, offering no means to stop it, and escalating to a second channel is close to the Annex I point 26 blacklist (persistent and unwanted solicitations) and may also amount to an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. The consent/data-provenance issues themselves fall to GDPR/ePrivacy, but the harassment-by-design pattern is a genuine UCPD risk.

report.executive_summary: This campaign markets home alarm systems by email, social ads, and phone to 400,000 people on a purchased broker list with no consent records, then uploads that same list to Meta and Google to build lookalike audiences and cold-calls people who don't open the emails. In plain terms, the entire campaign is built on data you have no legal right to use. The specialists found critical GDPR breaches: there is no lawful basis for any of the processing, consent cannot be demonstrated or shown to be valid, recipients were never informed, there is no privacy notice, and — because there is no unsubscribe link — people cannot exercise their absolute right to stop marketing. On top of that, the cross-channel chase (email then phone to non-openers with no way to opt out) is close to an outright banned practice under EU consumer law and risks being treated as an aggressive practice, especially given the fear-based nature of home-security selling. The lookalike upload also creates ad-transparency risks under the DSA. The AI Act does not apply. The verdict: do not launch this campaign in its current form — it exposes the business to regulatory enforcement, fines, and complaints, and needs to be rebuilt from lawfully sourced, consented data.
recommendations: Do not launch. Immediately stop all use of the purchased list — do not send emails, place calls, or upload it to Meta/Google — as there is no lawful basis for any of it.

Suppress and delete any contact for whom you cannot produce an auditable, GDPR-standard opt-in consent record (timestamp, wording, scope, source, naming HomeSecure and each purpose). A broker's 'opted-in somewhere in 2019' assertion does not qualify.

Stop the cross-channel escalation: do not phone people who simply didn't open an email. This is close to a blacklisted 'persistent and unwanted solicitation' and risks being an aggressive practice; only phone people who gave specific consent for phone marketing.

Add a clear one-click unsubscribe link to every email and an equivalent opt-out on every call, and honour objections instantly and permanently across all channels — replace the unreliable 'manual reply' handling.

Provide a complete, accessible privacy notice at first contact and link it in every communication, covering controller identity, data source, purposes, lawful basis, recipients (Meta/Google), retention and data-subject rights.

Do not upload lists to Meta/Google for lookalike profiling without a valid lawful basis and prior disclosure to individuals; if you do run platform ads, use the platforms' advertiser-disclosure tools and apply an under-18 exclusion so no profiling-based ads reach minors.
Avoid marketing framing that exploits fear about home safety to pressure a purchase decision.
Rebuild the campaign on freshly collected, consented, first-party data and run a data-protection review before any relaunch.

campaign.title: SleepWell mattress radio spot
campaign.text: A 30-second radio and podcast spot uses an AI-cloned voice of a nationally famous talk-show host: 'Hi, it's me — you know I only recommend what I use, and I sleep on a SleepWell every night.' The host has no relationship with the brand and never consented. No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears in the spot or the podcast description. The media plan notes the clone 'tested 40% better than an actor'.

detected_practices: impersonation of a public figure without consent
misleading claim of personal use ('I sleep on a SleepWell every night')
triage.summary: A 30-second radio/podcast spot uses an AI-cloned voice of a famous talk-show host who never consented, falsely implying a personal endorsement and use of the SleepWell mattress, with no disclosure that the voice is synthetic. This raises serious issues of deceptive fake endorsement, unauthorised impersonation, and undisclosed deepfake audio content targeting general adult consumers across the EU.

findings.title: Transparency: disclosure of deep fakes and AI-generated text
findings.rationale: An AI-cloned voice of a real, identifiable public figure is a deep fake — AI-generated/manipulated audio depicting a real person in a way that would falsely appear authentic (listeners believe the host actually spoke). Art. 50(4) requires deployers of AI systems generating or manipulating audio constituting a deep fake to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. The campaign provides no such disclosure in either the spot or the podcast description, so the deployer disclosure obligation is unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: uses an AI-cloned voice of a nationally famous talk-show host ... No disclosure that the voice is synthetic appears in the spot or the podcast description.
findings.recommendation: Do not run the spot in its current form. If any synthetic voice is used, add a clear, timely audible disclosure that the voice is AI-generated (e.g., a spoken statement that the voice is artificially generated) and a written note in the podcast description. Separately, using a specific real person's cloned voice without consent is unlawful on other grounds and should be dropped entirely rather than merely disclosed.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The spot is synthetic AI-generated audio. Art. 50(2) requires that outputs of AI systems generating synthetic audio be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Nothing in the campaign indicates the audio output carries any provenance/machine-readable marking, so this obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: A 30-second radio and podcast spot uses an AI-cloned voice ... Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Ensure any AI-generated audio asset embeds machine-readable provenance marking identifying it as artificially generated (e.g., watermarking/metadata per emerging standards), and confirm the generative-AI provider applies such marking to its outputs.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system is used to deploy a deceptive technique: a cloned voice falsely presenting a genuine personal endorsement and personal use, with the effect of distorting consumers' purchasing decisions by impairing their ability to make an informed choice. This engages the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition on deceptive AI techniques. The prohibition additionally requires the practice to cause or be reasonably likely to cause 'significant harm'; for a mattress purchase this high threshold may not be met, so the deception is more squarely addressed under the transparency obligations and consumer-protection law, but the manipulative/deceptive AI dimension is worth flagging.
findings.evidence_quote: 'Hi, it's me — you know I only recommend what I use, and I sleep on a SleepWell every night.'
findings.recommendation: Remove the fabricated personal-endorsement framing generated via AI voice cloning. Any endorsement must be genuine, consented and truthful; do not use AI to impersonate a real person to manufacture trust and steer purchase decisions.

verdicts.notes: The spot uses an AI-cloned voice of a real, identifiable talk-show host — this is a deep fake (AI-manipulated audio depicting a real person) and AI-generated synthetic audio. It is deployed with no disclosure of its synthetic nature, breaching the AI Act's transparency obligations. Art. 50(4) (deep fake disclosure) is very likely violated; Art. 50(2) (machine-readable marking of synthetic output) is engaged and apparently unmet. The deceptive fake-endorsement dimension also touches the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibition, though the "significant harm" threshold makes that a secondary concern best handled under transparency and UCPD.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing

Under the AI Act, the AI-generated impersonation of a real person is a "deep fake" that must be disclosed, which it is not. The verdict is clear: this campaign cannot run in its current form, and the problem cannot be fixed by simply adding a disclosure — the non-consented impersonation itself must be removed.
