findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing personal data (device, visit history, behaviour) to set individualised prices while telling users prices merely 'reflect live market availability' is covert and misleading processing. This directly breaches the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle — the personalisation is hidden and its stated explanation is false.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised; the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'.
findings.recommendation: Stop misrepresenting the pricing logic. Clearly and truthfully disclose that displayed prices are personalised based on device type, prior visits and browsing behaviour, and correct the FAQ so it no longer attributes price variation solely to 'live market availability'.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of device type, prior visits and a 'hesitation index' to evaluate a user's behaviour and likely price tolerance is profiling within the meaning of Art. 4(4). This classification triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 22).
findings.evidence_quote: adjusts displayed hotel prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index')
findings.recommendation: Recognise the pricing engine as profiling, document it in the record of processing, and apply the full set of profiling safeguards (lawful basis, transparency, objection rights) described below.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Profiling users for personalised pricing needs a valid legal basis. A generic analytics-cookie banner does not establish consent for behavioural profiling that drives commercial pricing decisions, and legitimate interest is hard to sustain for covert price discrimination that consumers would not reasonably expect. As described, no adequate lawful basis exists.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis for the personalised-pricing profiling. If relying on consent, obtain separate, specific, informed consent (not bundled with analytics); if relying on legitimate interests, conduct and document a balancing test — though the covert, disadvantaging nature of the processing makes this basis difficult to rely on.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. A generic, bundled analytics banner is neither specific nor informed as to behavioural profiling for pricing, so any consent purportedly covering the pricing personalisation is invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Replace the generic banner with granular consent options that separately and clearly describe profiling for personalised pricing, allowing users to accept or refuse it independently of analytics cookies.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes and, importantly, of the existence of automated decision-making including profiling and its logic. Here the profiling and its use to set prices is entirely undisclosed, so the Art. 13 information duty (especially the automated-decision-making disclosure) is not met.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear privacy notice at the point of data collection explaining that browsing/device data is used to profile users and personalise prices, including meaningful information about the logic and consequences of that automated processing.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Solely-automated dynamic pricing that systematically produces materially different (higher) offers for an identifiable segment can 'similarly significantly affect' individuals, engaging Art. 22. As described there is no exception basis established (no explicit consent, and the processing is not obviously necessary for the contract) and no Art. 22 safeguards.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the pricing decision is 'solely automated' with significant effect; if so, secure an Art. 22 exception (e.g. explicit consent) and implement safeguards such as meaningful information, the ability to obtain human intervention, and a route to contest the personalised price.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Information to data subjects must be transparent, intelligible and not misleading. Burying/misstating the basis of pricing in an FAQ that gives an inaccurate explanation fails the requirement for clear, transparent communication.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Present accurate, plain-language information about personalised pricing prominently in the user journey rather than an incorrect FAQ statement.

verdicts.notes: The pricing engine processes personal data (device type, prior-visit history, a behavioural 'hesitation index') to evaluate and predict individuals' behaviour and price sensitivity — this is profiling under GDPR Art. 4(4). The personalised pricing is entirely undisclosed and actively misdescribed as reflecting 'live market availability', breaching the transparency/fairness principle and the Art. 13 duty to inform about automated decision-making. The generic analytics-only consent banner cannot lawfully cover profiling-based personalised pricing, undermining lawful basis and valid consent. Solely-automated dynamic pricing that systematically disadvantages a segment (returning iOS users) also engages Art. 22 safeguards. Note: Art. 9 special-category data is NOT engaged — device/behaviour signals are not sensitive data as described.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: UCPD Art. 6 covers false information deceiving the average consumer regarding the price or the manner in which the price is calculated. Prices in fact vary ±12% based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural 'hesitation index' — i.e. personalised profiling of the individual consumer, not market availability. Telling consumers prices 'reflect live market availability' is a false statement about the manner of price calculation that is liable to cause a transactional decision (e.g. accepting a higher personalised quote as if it were an objective market rate) the consumer would not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Remove or correct the FAQ statement. Do not attribute personalised price variation to 'live market availability'; accurately state that displayed prices may be individually adjusted based on device and browsing behaviour, and ensure any explanation of price-setting is truthful.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: UCPD Art. 7 prohibits omitting material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision, or hiding it. Whether a displayed price is personalised on the basis of automated profiling of the consumer's device and behaviour is material information (also expressly required to be disclosed under the Consumer Rights Directive as amended). Here the personalisation is entirely undisclosed, and its commercial intent (charging the same consumer more based on inferred hesitation/device) is concealed, so the average consumer cannot appreciate that the quote is individually tailored.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point the price is displayed stating that the price has been personalised on the basis of automated decision-making/profiling (device type, prior visits, browsing behaviour), as required for personalised pricing. Make the disclosure timely and intelligible, not buried in an FAQ.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, Art. 5 treats as unfair practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer. Systematically presenting higher first quotes to returning users identified by device, and exploiting an inferred 'hesitation index', combined with the concealment and the misleading 'market availability' explanation, may amount to an unfair practice contrary to professional diligence even where consumers are not a specially vulnerable group. This reinforces the Art. 6/7 findings rather than standing wholly alone.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the pricing methodology is transparent and does not exploit behavioural signals in a way that distorts consumer choice; document a professional-diligence justification and disclose the personalisation so consumers can make an informed comparison (e.g. offer a non-personalised reference price).

verdicts.notes: The campaign applies undisclosed personalised/dynamic pricing (±12%) driven by device type, prior visits and a behavioural "hesitation index", while the FAQ states prices "reflect live market availability". This engages UCPD Art. 7 (misleading omission of material information about how the price is set and hidden commercial intent of the profiling) and Art. 6 (misleading action, because the FAQ statement is false/deceptive as to the manner of price calculation). The Art. 5 fairness safety-net is also engaged. No urgency/scarcity or blacklisted urgency practice is present (the text states no urgency messaging is used), so Annex I point 7 does not apply.

report.executive_summary: This campaign uses a pricing engine that quietly adjusts hotel prices by up to ±12% based on each visitor's device, past visits, and how long they spend comparing (a "hesitation index"), with returning iOS users systematically shown higher first quotes. The core problem is that this personalisation is completely hidden — and worse, actively misdescribed. The FAQ tells consumers prices "reflect live market availability" when in fact they reflect a profile of the individual. Two separate bodies of EU law are likely breached. Under consumer law (UCPD), the false "market availability" explanation is a misleading action and the failure to disclose personalised pricing is a misleading omission. Under data protection law (GDPR), profiling people to set individual prices without transparency, without a valid lawful basis (a generic analytics cookie banner does not cover this), and without required disclosures breaches the fairness, transparency, lawful-basis and information duties, and may also trigger automated decision-making safeguards. Notably, prices are honoured as shown and no urgency tactics are used, which limits some risks — but the concealment and the false explanation are the serious issues. Overall this is a high-risk campaign that should not run in its current form until the pricing logic is truthfully disclosed and properly consented.
recommendations: Fix the FAQ immediately: stop stating prices 'reflect live market availability'. This single sentence is the clearest and most defensible violation (misleading action under UCPD Art. 6 and a false statement under GDPR fairness/transparency). Replace it with an accurate explanation that prices may be individually adjusted based on device and browsing behaviour.

Disclose the personalisation prominently at the point the price is shown — not buried in an FAQ. Tell consumers clearly that the displayed price has been personalised using automated profiling of device type, prior visits and browsing behaviour. This is material information required under UCPD Art. 7 and the GDPR Art. 12/13 information duties.

Establish and document a valid lawful basis for the profiling. A generic analytics-cookie banner does not cover behavioural profiling for pricing. If relying on consent, obtain separate, specific, granular consent that users can accept or refuse independently of analytics cookies.
Replace the generic consent banner with granular options that separately describe profiling for personalised pricing (GDPR Art. 4(11) valid consent).

Assess whether the pricing decision is 'solely automated' with a significant effect on individuals (GDPR Art. 22). If so, secure a valid exception (e.g. explicit consent) and add safeguards: meaningful information about the logic, human intervention on request, and a route to contest the personalised price.

Reconsider or justify the practice itself: systematically showing returning iOS users higher first quotes and exploiting an inferred 'hesitation index' may be unfair even if disclosed (UCPD Art. 5). Consider offering a non-personalised reference price so consumers can make an informed comparison, and document a professional-diligence justification.
Record the pricing engine as profiling in your record of processing activities and apply the full set of profiling safeguards.

campaign.title: TravelDeal adaptive pricing
campaign.text: An online travel agency's pricing engine adjusts displayed hotel prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index'). Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes. Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised; the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'. Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically. Prices are honoured as displayed and no urgency messaging is used.

detected_practices: personalised/adaptive pricing based on behavioural signals
price steering by device type (iOS users shown higher quotes)
behavioural profiling via 'hesitation index' (time spent comparing)
non-disclosure of personalised pricing to consumers
potentially misleading FAQ statement ('prices reflect live market availability')
generic consent banner covering analytics cookies
triage.summary: An online travel agency operates an adaptive pricing engine that varies displayed hotel prices by up to ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and behavioural signals (a 'hesitation index'), with returning iOS users systematically shown higher first quotes. The personalisation is undisclosed and the FAQ arguably misrepresents pricing as reflecting 'live market availability', while consent for the underlying tracking is only generically covered by an analytics cookie banner.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automatically processing device type, visit history and a behavioural 'hesitation index' to evaluate a person's economic situation and behaviour is textbook profiling under Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the downstream obligations (transparency, lawful basis, Art. 22).
findings.evidence_quote: adjusts displayed hotel prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index')
findings.recommendation: Formally document the pricing engine as a profiling operation, map exactly which personal data feed it, and record the purpose so that the corresponding transparency and lawful-basis obligations can be met.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The displayed price is a decision based solely on automated processing/profiling. Personalised pricing that systematically raises the price a specific individual must pay can 'similarly significantly affect' them, bringing the practice within Art. 22, which permits it only under an exception (explicit consent or contract necessity) with safeguards — none of which are described here.
findings.evidence_quote: Returning iOS users see systematically higher first quotes.
findings.recommendation: Establish a valid Art. 22 exception (most realistically explicit consent) before running individual-level automated pricing, and implement the required safeguards: meaningful information about the logic, and the ability to obtain human intervention, express a view and contest the outcome. Absent this, disable individual-level automated price adjustment.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing personal data to set individualised prices while concealing that fact — and giving an affirmatively misleading explanation ('live market availability') — breaches the fairness and transparency limb of Art. 5(1)(a). Covert, misleading processing is precisely what this principle prohibits.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised; the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'.
findings.recommendation: Disclose clearly and prominently that prices are personalised based on user data, remove or correct the misleading 'live market availability' FAQ statement, and align public-facing explanations with what the pricing engine actually does.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at the point of data collection the controller inform data subjects of the purposes of processing and, specifically, of the existence of automated decision-making including profiling together with meaningful information about the logic involved. Consumers here are given no information that their data drives personalised pricing.
findings.evidence_quote: Nothing on the site indicates prices are personalised
findings.recommendation: Add an Art. 13-compliant notice at the point of collection covering the personalised-pricing purpose, the profiling logic and its significance, retention, recipients and data-subject rights; link it from the pricing pages, not only a buried privacy policy.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and informed. A generic 'analytics cookies' banner cannot constitute valid consent for behavioural profiling used to set individualised prices — the purpose is neither disclosed nor separately agreed, so any consent is not specific or informed and bundling makes it invalid.
findings.evidence_quote: Consent banner covers analytics cookies generically.
findings.recommendation: Obtain granular, separately toggled, informed consent specifically for personalised-pricing profiling, described in plain language and distinct from generic analytics; ensure it is opt-in and as easy to withdraw as to give.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: The profiling requires a valid Art. 6(1) legal basis. Consent is not validly obtained (see Art. 4(11) finding). Legitimate interest is difficult to sustain for covert individualised pricing given the intrusive nature and consumer detriment, and contract necessity does not cover raising prices via profiling. As described, the processing likely lacks a valid lawful basis.
findings.evidence_quote: based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index')
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis. If relying on legitimate interest, complete and record a legitimate interests assessment (LIA); given the covert detriment this is unlikely to pass, so obtain valid consent instead. Do not process pricing data until a lawful basis is secured.

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to data subjects to be concise, transparent, intelligible and accurate. Presenting personalised-pricing logic as 'live market availability' is neither transparent nor intelligible; it obscures rather than communicates the real processing.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Rewrite consumer-facing pricing explanations in clear, plain, accurate language that reflects the actual personalisation, and make the relevant privacy/pricing information easily accessible at the moment prices are shown.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Where profiling is related to direct marketing/commercial targeting, data subjects have an absolute right to object. Nothing indicates a mechanism to object to the profiling-based pricing exists.
findings.evidence_quote: based on device type, prior visits, and time spent comparing ('hesitation index')
findings.recommendation: Provide a clear, easy mechanism for users to object to profiling-based pricing and, on objection, stop applying personalised pricing to that individual.

verdicts.notes: TravelDeal's adaptive pricing engine constitutes profiling within the meaning of GDPR Art. 4(4) — it uses automated processing of personal data (device type, prior visits, behavioural "hesitation index") to evaluate economic situation and behaviour, and then makes an automated decision (the price shown) that arguably significantly affects the individual under Art. 22. The processing is materially non-transparent: consumers are not told prices are personalised, the FAQ actively misrepresents the basis of pricing, and consent for the underlying tracking is only generically bundled into an analytics cookie banner. This engages breaches of the transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)), the Art. 12/13 information duties, the consent standard (Art. 4(11)/6(1)), and Art. 22 safeguards. The lawful basis and consent deficiencies are the most serious.
Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

This is false/deceptive information about the price and the manner in which the price is calculated (Art. 6 covers deception as to the price or manner of price calculation), and is liable to cause the average consumer to accept a quote they would otherwise have questioned or rejected. The claim actively misdirects consumers away from the true (personalised) basis of the price, going beyond mere omission into a positive misleading action.
findings.evidence_quote: the FAQ says prices 'reflect live market availability'
findings.recommendation: Correct or remove the FAQ statement so it accurately describes how prices are set. If dynamic personalisation is used, state plainly that displayed prices are individually calculated using behavioural and device signals, rather than framing variation as neutral 'live market availability'.

verdicts.notes: The campaign runs an adaptive/personalised pricing engine that varies displayed prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural 'hesitation index', with returning iOS users systematically quoted higher — yet nothing on the site discloses that prices are personalised. No false urgency/scarcity or fake-discount blacklist practices are present, and prices are honoured as displayed, so the blacklist provisions are not triggered.

report.executive_summary: Your TravelDeal adaptive pricing campaign shows returning iOS users higher hotel quotes and adjusts prices ±12% based on device type, prior visits and a behavioural "hesitation index" — but never tells consumers that prices are personalised, and the FAQ actively claims prices "reflect live market availability." Immediately correct or remove the FAQ statement that prices 'reflect live market availability' — it is factually false and a misleading action under UCPD Art. 6.

Add a clear, prominent disclosure at the point prices are shown stating the price is personalised via automated decision-making and explaining the main parameters (device, visit history, comparison behaviour). Do not bury this in a cookie banner or privacy policy.
Obtain granular, separately-toggled, informed opt-in consent specifically for personalised-pricing profiling, distinct from analytics cookies and as easy to withdraw as to give.
Provide the Art. 22 safeguards: meaningful information about the logic, and the ability to get human intervention, express a view and contest the price outcome.

Add an Art. 13-compliant notice at the point of data collection covering the personalised-pricing purpose, retention, recipients and data-subject rights, and give users an easy way to object to profiling-based pricing.

Document the pricing engine as a profiling operation and, if any reliance on legitimate interest is contemplated, complete a legitimate interests assessment (likely to fail here given the covert consumer detriment).

opt-out friction (deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking) — dark pattern
bundled total obscuring add-on costs until final screen

The design raises misleading/drip-pricing and dark-pattern concerns under the UCPD (and pre-ticked-box rules), and generative AI is declared. findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: Generative AI is declared as used in the campaign content. Under Art. 50(2), providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable, detectable format. Any AI-generated visuals or copy in the web/email assets fall within this transparency obligation, and nothing in the submission indicates that machine-readable provenance marking has been applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm which campaign assets (images, video, audio, text) were AI-generated and ensure the generating system applies machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. watermarking/metadata per emerging C2PA-style standards). findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The total price and its composition are material information. Pre-ticking optional paid extras and hiding their individual cost inside collapsed accordions, while displaying only a bundled total until the last screen, provides material pricing information in an unclear and untimely manner and effectively hides costs the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision. This is a misleading omission under Art. 7, and the pre-selection is a 'sneaking' dark pattern.
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking. The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen.

Make deselection unnecessary by not pre-selecting; if choices are offered, disclose the full itemised price and total on the same screen before the consumer commits, not only at the final step.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Advertising the bare fare in promotional emails while the booking flow automatically pre-selects paid add-ons (€26.98 of extras) means the headline price and the actual price the consumer will be led to pay diverge. findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure headline fares reflect the price a consumer following the standard flow will actually see; since add-ons will be opt-in and not pre-selected, the advertised '€39' should match the default checkout starting price. findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, the overall design — defaulting consumers into paid extras and adding friction (collapsed accordions, extra clicks) to remove them — is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of the average consumer by exploiting inertia and time pressure at checkout, causing them to purchase extras they did not actively choose. This constitutes an unfair commercial practice under the general prohibition even where no specific blacklist item applies.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Redesign the checkout so that acquiring an add-on requires a deliberate affirmative action of equal or lesser effort than declining it. Avoid asymmetric friction (hidden accordions, buried unticking) that steers consumers toward paid options.

verdicts.notes: The AeroFly booking flow engages the UCPD through deceptive checkout design rather than any blacklisted (Annex I) practice. Pre-selecting three paid add-ons with obstructive opt-out ("sneaking" dark pattern) and showing only a bundled total until the final screen are misleading omissions (Art. 7) and contrary to professional diligence (Art. 5). Advertising the bare "from €39" fare while the checkout defaults extras in engages Art. 6 (price/manner of price calculation) and Art. 7 (untimely disclosure of total price). Note: the EU pre-ticked-box prohibition itself lives in CRD Art. 22, outside this Directive; the UCPD angle is the misleading/unfair-design overlay. No false urgency or "free" misuse is present.

report.executive_summary: The AeroFly campaign advertises a bare "Lisbon from €39" fare while the booking flow pre-selects three paid add-ons (Cancellation Cover, Priority Boarding and a "carbon contribution", totalling €26.98) and makes them deliberately awkward to remove — you must open each accordion and untick, and only a bundled total is shown until the final screen. This is the campaign's core and most serious problem: under EU consumer law it is a "sneaking" dark pattern combined with drip pricing that hides material price information and steers consumers into paying for extras they did not actively choose. It creates high risk of breaching the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (misleading omissions, misleading price actions, and the general fairness duty), and separately the EU pre-ticked-box ban under the Consumer Rights Directive. The AI Act and GDPR are only peripherally engaged: because you declared use of generative AI, any AI-generated images/copy must carry machine-readable provenance marking, and your marketing emails must have a documented lawful basis and an easy unsubscribe link. There are no data-targeting or profiling concerns since personalisation is declared as not used. Bottom line: the checkout design must be fixed before this campaign goes live — the pricing/dark-pattern issues are the priority, the AI and email items are straightforward compliance housekeeping.

Confirm and document a valid lawful basis for the marketing emails (prior opt-in consent, or the ePrivacy soft opt-in for existing customers), and ensure every email carries a clear, free, one-click unsubscribe honoured immediately via a suppression list.

obstructing deselection via collapsed accordions (dark pattern / obstruction)
headline 'from' price advertising bare fare in emails
pre-selected additional payment for optional services
triage.summary: An airline's own booking flow pre-selects paid add-ons (cancellation cover, priority boarding, a carbon contribution) that require effort to deselect via collapsed accordions, and displays a single bundled total until the final screen while promo emails advertise only the bare fare. This raises consumer-protection concerns around pre-ticked boxes, drip/partitioned pricing and obstruction dark patterns. The campaign declares generative AI use and, being conducted over web and email, likely processes consumer contact/booking data.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The submission declares generative AI use, and the campaign consists of web and email marketing assets (e.g. the promo email copy 'Lisbon from €39'). Where campaign audio, image, video or text is produced by a generative AI system, Art. 50(2) obliges the provider to ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Nothing in the submission indicates such marking is applied.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Identify which campaign assets (email copy, banners, imagery) were generated or manipulated by generative AI and ensure those outputs carry machine-readable provenance/marking (e.g. C2PA metadata or watermarking) as required by Art. 50(2). Document the generation tool and marking method for audit.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The pre-selected add-ons and obstructive collapsed accordions are manipulative interface design, but Art. 5(1)(a) only applies where such manipulative/deceptive techniques are deployed by an AI system and are reasonably likely to cause significant harm. The campaign describes static booking-flow UI with no indication the manipulation is AI-driven, and the harm is ordinary over-payment on genuine services rather than 'significant harm'. The prohibition therefore does not appear engaged; the dark-pattern substance falls to UCPD/DSA.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: No AI Act action required for the design tactics as described. If the booking flow later introduces AI-driven personalised nudging or adaptive persuasion, reassess against Art. 5(1)(a). Address the pre-ticked boxes and obstruction under the consumer-protection frameworks.

verdicts.notes: The core issues in this campaign (pre-ticked add-ons, drip pricing, obstructive accordions) are dark-pattern/consumer-protection matters best addressed under UCPD/DSA — not the AI Act, because nothing indicates these manipulative design choices are driven by an AI system, and Art. 5(1)(a) additionally requires a likelihood of significant harm. The only AI Act hook is the campaign's declared use of generative AI: if any email or web copy/imagery is AI-generated, Art. 50(2) requires machine-readable provenance marking, and there is no indication such marking is applied. No deep fakes, synthetic personas or public-interest AI text are present, so Art. 50(4) is not engaged.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The campaign sends promotional emails to consumers, which constitutes direct marketing. Art. 21(2)-(3) grants an absolute right to object to direct marketing that every such communication must respect and facilitate (e.g. a working unsubscribe/opt-out). The submission describes the marketing emails but gives no evidence of an opt-out mechanism or how objections are handled and suppressed.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure every promotional email includes a clear, one-click unsubscribe/opt-out, and that objections are honoured immediately by suppression. Document the opt-out flow and confirm it is as easy to exercise as it was to sign up.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Email direct marketing generally requires prior consent (Art. 6(1) in conjunction with the ePrivacy Directive Art. 13), unless a narrow soft opt-in for own similar products from an existing customer applies. The campaign relies on promotional email but does not document a valid legal basis (consent or applicable soft opt-in) for those sends.
findings.evidence_quote: Channels: web, email
findings.recommendation: Identify and document the lawful basis for the promo emails: obtain prior opt-in consent, or rely on the soft opt-in only where recipients are existing customers who received an opt-out at data collection and in every message, for similar products/services.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: The booking flow and email channel collect personal data (contact and booking details). Art. 13 requires that identity of controller, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and data-subject rights be provided at the point of collection. The submission does not evidence a privacy notice at the point of data capture.
findings.evidence_quote: An airline's own booking flow
findings.recommendation: Provide a concise, layered Art. 13 privacy notice at the point of data collection in the booking flow and at email sign-up, linking to the full privacy policy and clearly stating marketing purposes, legal basis and the right to object.

A booking flow that hides information behind collapsed accordions and single bundled totals raises a broader design-transparency concern; to the extent privacy information is presented in the same obstructive manner, it would fall short of Art. 12. This is flagged for review as the text does not describe how privacy information is presented.

findings.recommendation: Verify that privacy/data-processing information in the booking flow is presented clearly and accessibly (not buried in collapsed accordions), consistent with the Art. 12 clear-and-plain-language and easy-accessibility standard.

The only genuine GDPR touchpoints are the promotional emails (direct marketing) and the processing of booking/contact data over web and email. The text is silent on the email marketing legal basis, opt-out mechanism, and point-of-collection privacy information, so the relevant obligations are engaged but their satisfaction cannot be verified. findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Presenting only a single bundled total until the final payment screen, while the email advertised 'Lisbon from €39', means the price and its manner of calculation (the added €14.99 + €9.99 + €2 in pre-selected extras) is provided in an unclear and untimely manner. Total price and any unavoidable/optional-yet-defaulted charges are material information the average consumer needs to make an informed transactional decision; hiding the breakdown until the last step is a misleading omission under Art. 7.
findings.evidence_quote: The summary shows one bundled total until the final screen.
findings.recommendation: Show an itemised, real-time price breakdown from the first checkout step, clearly separating the bare fare from each optional add-on, and update the running total as items are selected/deselected — not only on the final screen.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Pre-ticking optional paid add-ons so the consumer must take active steps to remove them ('sneaking into the basket'), combined with obstruction that forces the user to open each collapsed accordion and untick, is contrary to professional diligence and is likely to materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour by causing them to pay for extras they did not choose. This is the UCPD safety-net application of the dark-patterns concept (sneaking + obstruction), which the graph links to Art. 5 for all traders.
findings.evidence_quote: pre-selects 'Cancellation Cover (€14.99)', 'Priority Boarding (€9.99)' and a €2 'carbon contribution' on the payment page; deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Present all add-ons unselected by default (opt-in) and make selecting an add-on no harder than declining it. Remove the accordion obstruction so each optional item can be seen and toggled directly without extra clicks; ensure the default state adds nothing beyond the fare and mandatory taxes.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Advertising 'from €39' in emails while the booking flow then defaults the consumer into ~€27 of pre-selected add-ons risks deceiving the average consumer about the price and manner of its calculation. While a genuine 'from' bare-fare headline is permissible, the discrepancy between the advertised entry price and the amount the consumer is steered to actually pay (via defaults) can cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take, engaging the misleading-actions prohibition on price.
findings.evidence_quote: Promo emails advertise the bare fare: 'Lisbon from €39'.
findings.recommendation: Ensure the 'from' price reflects the amount a consumer actually pays when no optional extras are added, and that no paid extras are auto-added to reach checkout. If mandatory unavoidable charges exist, include them in or clearly next to the headline price.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Onerous barriers to declining or removing optional charges can amount to undue influence/obstruction under the aggressive-practices provisions, which list 'onerous barriers to exercising contractual rights' as a factor. Here the friction is moderate rather than coercive (no pressure language is used), so the risk is lower than under Arts. 5/7, but the obstruction dimension should still be remedied.
findings.evidence_quote: deselecting requires opening each accordion and unticking
findings.recommendation: Make removing or declining any add-on a single, clearly visible action of equal prominence to accepting it, eliminating the multi-step accordion friction.

verdicts.notes: The AeroFly checkout flow engages several UCPD prohibitions. The core problems are pre-selected paid add-ons that consumers must actively opt out of ("sneaking into basket"), obstruction of deselection via collapsed accordions, and drip/partitioned pricing that hides the true bundled total until the final screen. These practices are contrary to professional diligence and constitute misleading omissions on price under Arts. 5 and 7, and the interface design is a classic obstruction/sneaking dark pattern. No blacklisted false-urgency or 'free'-misuse issue arises (the campaign uses no pressure language and does not use the word 'free'), and the add-ons are genuine services, but the opt-out architecture and price presentation are the substantive violations.

report.executive_summary: The AeroFly checkout campaign advertises a low "from €39" fare but then pre-selects three paid add-ons (Cancellation Cover €14.99, Priority Boarding €9.99 and a €2 carbon contribution) on the payment page, hides the breakdown behind a single bundled total until the final screen, and makes removing each extra harder than accepting it. These are textbook dark patterns — sneaking items into the basket, drip pricing and obstruction — and they are the campaign's main compliance problem. Under EU consumer law (UCPD) this is a likely violation: it risks misleading consumers about the real price and steering them into charges they did not choose. There are also secondary GDPR issues around the promo emails: you must have a valid lawful basis (consent or soft opt-in), a working one-click unsubscribe, and a clear privacy notice at the point of data collection — none of which are evidenced. Because you declared use of generative AI, any AI-generated email or web copy/imagery must carry machine-readable provenance marking under the AI Act. The AI Act's manipulation prohibition and the DSA are not engaged here. Overall verdict: high risk, driven mainly by the checkout design, which should be fixed before the campaign runs.
recommendations: Turn off all pre-selected paid add-ons: Cancellation Cover, Priority Boarding and the carbon contribution must be unticked by default so consumers actively opt in rather than opt out. This is the single most important fix (UCPD Art. 5).

Show an itemised, real-time price breakdown from the first checkout step, separating the bare fare from each optional extra and updating the running total as items are toggled — do not reveal the true total only on the final screen (UCPD Art. 7).
Remove the accordion obstruction: make declining or removing any add-on a single, clearly visible action of equal prominence to accepting it (UCPD Arts. 5, 8-9).
Ensure the 'Lisbon from €39' headline reflects what a consumer actually pays with no optional extras added; include any genuinely unavoidable charges in or next to the headline price (UCPD Art. 6).

For the promo emails, confirm and document a valid lawful basis — prior opt-in consent or the soft opt-in for existing customers with similar products — and include a clear one-click unsubscribe that is honoured immediately (GDPR Art. 6/21).

Provide a concise, layered privacy notice at the point of data collection in the booking flow and at email sign-up, and make sure privacy information is not buried in collapsed accordions (GDPR Arts. 12-13).

Identify which email/web assets were produced by generative AI and apply machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. C2PA metadata or watermarking); document the tool and method for audit (AI Act Art. 50(2)).

campaign.title: ShoeVault 'we saw you looking' sequence
campaign.text: After a signed-in user abandons a cart, ShoeVault triggers: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days, three emails ('We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back'), and an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.'). Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users. The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup; the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes.

detected_practices: unsubscribe/opt-out not fully honoured (pushes continue after email unsubscribe)
anthropomorphising/pressure copy ('they're watching you back', 'Still up? Your cart is too.')
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is signed-in, adult shoppers in the EU; no indication of minors being reached, though age verification/segmentation basis is unstated. Personalisation is based on signed-in behavioural/cart data.
triage.summary: ShoeVault runs a cart-abandonment retargeting sequence for signed-in adult shoppers across display, email, and app-push in the EU, using behavioural personalisation with 30-day cross-site retargeting, late-night pushes, and disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users. No generative AI is declared. Notable concerns include partial opt-out (unsubscribe stops emails but not pushes), reliance on a broad 'marketing communications' consent, and pressuring/anthropomorphising copy.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing under Art. 21(2)-(3) is absolute and covers all direct marketing channels and related profiling, not just email. A user who unsubscribes has objected to direct marketing; continuing to send app-push marketing after that objection means data is still processed for a purpose the user objected to, breaching the absolute opt-out right.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out channel-agnostic: a single unsubscribe/objection must suppress all direct-marketing channels (email, display retargeting audiences, and app-push). Route the objection to a central suppression list and stop all cart-abandonment marketing on receipt.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that withdrawal of consent be as easy as giving it and that consent be demonstrable. Where the campaign relies on consent, allowing withdrawal to stop only one channel while another continues means withdrawal is not effective and not as easy as the original opt-in, undermining valid consent.
findings.evidence_quote: the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Ensure the preference centre lets users withdraw consent for each processing purpose and channel, and that withdrawal is honoured across all channels including app-push. Provide clear per-channel controls with immediate effect.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific, informed and unambiguous; bundled or overly broad consent does not qualify. A single blanket 'marketing communications' opt-in at signup is unlikely to constitute specific, informed consent for behavioural profiling and 30-day cross-site display retargeting, which are distinct and more intrusive processing operations.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Collect separate, granular consent for each purpose (email marketing, app-push, behavioural profiling, cross-site retargeting) with plain-language descriptions of what each entails, rather than relying on one broad 'marketing communications' checkbox.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and behavioural profiling require a valid legal basis. Cross-site retargeting on third-party news sites for 30 days generally requires consent (and ePrivacy consent for the underlying tracking); a broad signup consent is unlikely to validly cover this. If relying on legitimate interest instead, a documented balancing test is required and the intrusive, sustained retargeting may not pass it.
findings.evidence_quote: triggers: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Identify and document a valid lawful basis specific to the cross-site retargeting and behavioural profiling. If consent-based, obtain purpose-specific consent; if legitimate interest is claimed for any element, complete and record a legitimate-interests assessment and honour objections.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Scoring users as 'high-intent' from cart and behavioural data to determine treatment is automated evaluation of personal aspects (behaviour, interests) and therefore profiling under Art. 4(4). This triggers the associated transparency, lawful-basis and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Recognise 'high-intent' scoring as profiling and ensure it is covered by a lawful basis, disclosed to users, and subject to the opt-out mechanism.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that, at the point of collection, users be informed of the purposes and legal basis of processing, recipients (e.g. display/retargeting partners on third-party news sites), retention (e.g. the 30-day retargeting window) and the existence of profiling. The campaign shows behavioural profiling and third-party retargeting but no indication that this transparency information is provided.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Provide layered Art. 13 information at signup and in the privacy notice covering the behavioural profiling, the 30-day cross-site retargeting, the ad/retargeting recipients, retention periods, and the right to object, and link it from the preference centre.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a) constrains how personal data is used, not just its lawfulness. Combining behavioural data with deliberately disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, anthropomorphising surveillance-suggestive copy ('they're watching you back') and late-night pressure pushes uses personal data in a manner that pressures and unsettles data subjects, which is difficult to reconcile with fair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.')
findings.recommendation: Apply reasonable frequency caps to all users regardless of intent score, avoid surveillance-suggestive/pressuring copy, and avoid late-night send windows. Ensure the use of personal data for messaging is proportionate and does not exploit the individual's inferred state.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data of signed-in users for behavioural profiling and multi-channel direct marketing, so GDPR clearly applies. The most serious issue is that objecting/unsubscribing only stops emails but not late-night app pushes, breaching the absolute right to object (Art. 21) and the "as easy to withdraw as to give" rule (Art. 7). Reliance on a single broad "marketing communications" consent to justify 30-day cross-site retargeting and behavioural profiling is unlikely to meet the specific/informed/granular standard (Arts. 4(11), 6(1)), and transparency about the profiling appears unaddressed. Disabled frequency caps plus manipulative copy also raise a fairness concern under Art. 5(1)(a).

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating online interfaces in a way that materially distorts or impairs users' ability to make free and informed decisions, expressly including repeatedly requesting/ignoring a choice already made and making it harder to withdraw than to opt in. A user who unsubscribes has made a clear choice to stop marketing; continuing to send app-push notifications after that opt-out is a form of obstruction/nagging that overrides the user's expressed decision. This is compounded by the surrounding pressure tactics below.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Route unsubscribe/opt-out to suppress ALL marketing channels (email, push and retargeting) — or provide a single, equally prominent global marketing off switch that reliably stops push notifications, and honour it in real time.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Deliberately removing frequency limits for a targeted segment produces repetitive, high-pressure exposure (nagging) designed to wear down resistance rather than inform. Combined with anthropomorphising pressure copy ('they're watching you back'; 'Still up? Your cart is too.') and 21:30 timing that exploits vulnerability, the interface/communication design manipulates rather than enables free and informed choice, engaging the Art. 25 prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Reinstate reasonable frequency caps for all users regardless of intent score, remove pressuring/anthropomorphising and late-night ('Still up?') framing, and avoid timing designed to exploit reduced consumer resistance.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Where the ads are presented on online platforms, Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad the recipient can identify, clearly and in real time, that it is an advertisement, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main targeting parameters and how to change them. The 30-day behaviourally-targeted retargeting campaign gives no indication these disclosures (advertiser identity, targeting-parameter explanation and controls) are provided.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Ensure retargeting creative/placements carry a clear ad label with ShoeVault as advertiser/payer, and that the platforms used surface the main targeting parameters (e.g. 'because you viewed items on ShoeVault') and a control to change them, as required for platform-served ads.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: Art. 28 bans profiling-based advertising to recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign is declared adults-only and there is no indication minors are reached, so no breach is identified. However, the basis for the adult segmentation / age assurance is unstated while the campaign relies on behavioural profiling, so the assumption should be verified.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared target audience: signed-in shoppers, adults
findings.recommendation: Document and verify the age-assurance basis for the 'adults' segment so that profiled retargeting/push messaging is never served to users who could reasonably be identified as minors.

verdicts.notes: ShoeVault operates its own app/website interfaces and runs cross-site display retargeting, so the DSA's dark-pattern and ad-transparency rules are engaged. The strongest DSA concern is Art. 25: the interface/communication design distorts free and informed decision-making by not honouring a choice already made (unsubscribe stops emails but not pushes), by disabling frequency caps for 'high-intent' users (nagging), and by manipulative, pressuring copy and late-night timing. Ad-transparency (Art. 26(1)) is engaged by the 30-day cross-site display retargeting. No evidence of sensitive-data targeting (Art. 26(3)) or minor-targeted ads (Art. 28); Art. 27/39 are not engaged.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, persistent and unwanted solicitations by remote media except to enforce a contractual obligation. Once a user unsubscribes they have refused marketing; continuing to send app-push notifications is a solicitation the consumer has expressly declined. This is a blacklisted per-se unfair practice — no case-by-case distortion test is needed. The marketing win-back nature (cart abandonment) is not a contractual-enforcement exception.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make unsubscribe/opt-out global across ALL channels. A single opt-out action (or the preference centre) must immediately stop emails, app-push and any other marketing solicitation. Ensure suppression lists are shared across channels so a refusal in one stops all.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: A practice is aggressive where, by harassment or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. The relevant factors — timing, persistence and onerous barriers to exercising rights — are all present: relentless uncapped retargeting for 30 days across news sites, three emails, and pushes deliberately timed for 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.') targeting users when they are winding down. Removing frequency caps specifically for those flagged 'high-intent' intensifies pressure precisely on the consumers already inclined to buy, and pushes surviving unsubscribe adds an onerous barrier to escaping the solicitation.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Apply reasonable frequency caps to all users (including 'high-intent'), avoid marketing pushes during late-night/rest hours, cap retargeting duration, and ensure consumers can easily stop the whole sequence. Remove the pressuring/anthropomorphising framing that plays on the consumer's psychological state rather than product merits.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a fairness safety-net, Art. 5 catches practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort economic behaviour. The anthropomorphising, mildly unsettling copy ('the Air Runners — they're watching you back'; 'Still up? Your cart is too.') combined with late-night timing and uncapped nagging is designed to manufacture pressure and FOMO rather than inform, which departs from the standard of professional diligence expected of a trader and can distort a consumer's transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: they're watching you back
findings.recommendation: Rework copy to be informational rather than pressuring or surveillance-suggestive, and document that the overall sequence design respects professional diligence (reasonable cadence, honest framing, easy exit).

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence engages several UCPD prohibitions. Most seriously, app-push notifications continue after the user unsubscribes — a per-se blacklisted practice under Annex I point 26 (persistent and unwanted solicitations ignoring the consumer's refusal). The combination of disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users, 30-day cross-site retargeting, a three-email drip, and deliberately timed 21:30 pushes with pressuring/anthropomorphising copy also risks qualifying as an aggressive practice under Arts. 8-9. Note: consent/opt-out mechanics also engage GDPR (covered by another agent); here they are assessed only for UCPD fairness.

report.executive_summary: This campaign triggers a 30-day cross-site retargeting drive, three "we saw you looking" emails, and a late-night (21:30) app push after a shopper abandons their cart, with frequency caps switched off for "high-intent" users. The single biggest problem is that unsubscribing only stops the emails, not the app pushes — meaning you keep messaging people who have clearly told you to stop. That is a per-se banned practice under EU consumer law (an outright prohibited "persistent and unwanted solicitation"), and it also breaches the absolute right to object under GDPR. On top of that, disabling frequency caps, using pressuring/surveillance-style copy ("they're watching you back", "Still up?"), and deliberate late-night timing add up to an aggressive and manipulative design that regulators treat as an illegal dark pattern under both the UCPD and the DSA. Your legal basis is also shaky: a single broad "marketing communications" tick at signup does not validly cover behavioural profiling and 30-day cross-site retargeting, and required transparency about the profiling and ad-targeting appears to be missing. The AI Act does not apply. Overall this is a critical-risk campaign that should not launch in its current form.
recommendations: Make opt-out global and immediate across ALL channels. A single unsubscribe or preference-centre action must stop email, app-push AND retargeting audiences in real time via a shared suppression list. Continuing pushes after unsubscribe is a banned practice (UCPD Annex I pt 26) and breaches GDPR Art. 21 — fix this before any launch.

Turn frequency caps back on for everyone, including 'high-intent' users. Uncapped nagging aimed at users you've flagged as most susceptible is treated as aggressive/manipulative (UCPD Arts. 8-9; DSA Art. 25).
Remove the late-night send window (21:30) and the 'Still up?' timing that exploits users winding down; move sends to reasonable daytime hours.

Rewrite the copy to be informational, not pressuring or surveillance-suggestive. Drop 'they're watching you back' and similar anthropomorphising/FOMO framing (UCPD Art. 5; GDPR fairness Art. 5(1)(a)).

Replace the single broad 'marketing communications' consent with granular, purpose-specific consent (email, app-push, behavioural profiling, cross-site retargeting), and ensure withdrawal is as easy as opt-in per channel (GDPR Arts. 4(11), 6(1), 7).

Provide the required transparency: layered Art. 13 notice covering the profiling, the 30-day retargeting window, ad/retargeting recipients and retention, plus DSA Art. 26 ad labelling (advertiser/payer identity and main targeting parameters with a control to change them).
Cap and shorten the 30-day retargeting duration and document a valid lawful basis (or a recorded legitimate-interests assessment) for the profiling and cross-site tracking.
Recognise 'high-intent' scoring as profiling and verify the age-assurance basis for the 'adults' segment so profiled ads are never served to anyone reasonably identifiable as a minor (DSA Art. 28).

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Art. 21(2)-(3) grants an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, including profiling. App-push notifications triggered by the abandonment profile are direct marketing. When a user unsubscribes they are objecting to marketing; continuing to send 21:30 pushes means the objection is only partially honoured, so personal data continues to be processed for a purpose the user has objected to. The right is absolute and must stop ALL direct marketing channels, not just email.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out global: a single unsubscribe/objection must suppress all direct-marketing channels (email, display retargeting audiences, and app-push) tied to that user. Wire the preference centre and the push-notification system to the same suppression flag, and provide an easy in-app opt-out for pushes.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and informed (Art. 4(11)). A single broad 'marketing communications' opt-in taken at signup is not specific to 30-day cross-site behavioural retargeting on third-party news sites, multi-channel push, and behavioural profiling. Bundled, generic consent does not qualify as a valid indication of wishes for these distinct and more intrusive processing operations.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Replace the generic bundled opt-in with granular, purpose-specific consent options (e.g. separate toggles for email marketing, app-push, and cross-site behavioural retargeting/profiling), each described in plain language, so each processing purpose has its own valid consent.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires the controller to demonstrate valid consent and that withdrawal is as easy as giving it. A signup-time blanket consent that cannot be effectively withdrawn for the push channel means withdrawal is not as easy as consent — the user cannot switch off pushes via the same simple mechanism. It also risks being conditional/bundled rather than distinguishable per purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: consented to 'marketing communications' at signup; the preference centre works and unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Ensure every channel/purpose consent can be withdrawn as easily as it was given, from the same preference centre, with immediate effect across all systems. Keep auditable records demonstrating what each user consented to and when.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing cart-abandonment behaviour and scoring users as 'high-intent' to tailor ad frequency and messaging is automated processing to evaluate personal aspects (interests, behaviour) and therefore profiling under Art. 4(4). This confirms the campaign involves profiling, which triggers the transparency, lawful-basis and objection obligations.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days ... Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Document the profiling activity (behavioural scoring, 'high-intent' segmentation) in the record of processing and privacy notice, and confirm a valid lawful basis for it; treat the 'high-intent' scoring as profiling subject to the Art. 21 objection right.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised advertising and cross-site behavioural retargeting generally require consent or a carefully documented legitimate-interests balancing test. The only stated basis is a broad signup consent that is unlikely to be valid for these purposes (see Art. 4(11)), leaving the lawful basis for the 30-day cross-site retargeting and profiling uncertain and probably unsatisfied as described.
findings.evidence_quote: ShoeVault triggers: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days, three emails ... and an app push
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis for each processing operation: obtain specific consent for cross-site retargeting/tracking (also required under ePrivacy) or complete a documented legitimate-interests assessment where appropriate, and align retention (the 30-day window) with that basis.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at the point of data collection users are told the purposes and legal basis, recipients (e.g. third-party ad networks/news sites), retention period, and information about profiling. Nothing in the campaign indicates the signed-in users were informed that their cart behaviour would drive 30-day cross-site retargeting and behavioural profiling, so the information obligation appears unmet.
findings.evidence_quote: triggers: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Provide a layered privacy notice at signup and on cart pages disclosing the behavioural retargeting purpose, the 30-day retention, third-party recipients/ad networks, the profiling logic, and the right to object, with a link to full details.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires processing that is not deceptive or unduly manipulative and where tracking is transparent. Messaging that emphasises covert surveillance ('we saw you looking', 'they're watching you back') signals behavioural tracking that users may not have transparently agreed to, undermining fair and transparent processing of their personal data.
findings.evidence_quote: 'We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back'
findings.recommendation: Ensure the underlying tracking is transparently disclosed and consented, and avoid framing that highlights surveillance without a clear, upfront explanation of what data is collected and why; align messaging with the disclosed processing.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data of signed-in, identified users to build a behavioural cart-abandonment retargeting sequence across display, email and app-push — this is profiling and personalised direct marketing squarely within GDPR. Two serious issues stand out: (1) the legal basis rests on a broad, bundled "marketing communications" consent obtained at signup, which is unlikely to be the specific, informed and unambiguous consent required for 30-day cross-site behavioural retargeting; and (2) the opt-out is not fully honoured — unsubscribing stops emails but not the 21:30 push notifications, breaching the absolute right to object to direct marketing. Additional transparency and consent-withdrawal concerns also arise.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that materially distorts or impairs users' free and informed decisions, expressly including making cancellation harder than it should be and repeatedly requesting/overriding a choice already made. Where a signed-in user opts out via the preference centre yet the 21:30 app pushes continue, the interface effectively defeats the user's exercised choice — a classic obstruction-of-opt-out dark pattern. The anthropomorphic pressure messaging ('they're watching you back', 'Still up? Your cart is too.') combined with disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users reinforces the manipulative-design concern.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out global and effective: unsubscribing (or any preference-centre suppression) must stop ALL marketing channels including app-push, not just email. Provide a clear, equally easy per-channel and all-channels opt-out, respect it in real time, re-enable frequency caps, and drop coercive/anthropomorphic push copy and late-night timing that pressures rather than informs.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(1) requires that, for each advertisement presented on an online platform, the recipient can identify in a clear, unambiguous, real-time manner that it is an ad, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main parameters used to target them (and how to change them). ShoeVault's 30-day behavioural retargeting served on third-party news-site platforms is precisely such platform advertising; the submission gives no evidence that these transparency elements (advertiser identity, 'why am I seeing this' targeting-parameter disclosure) are provided.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Ensure every retargeted display placement is clearly labelled as an advertisement, names ShoeVault as advertiser/payer, and exposes meaningful 'why you are seeing this' information (e.g. abandoned-cart / behavioural retargeting parameters) with a link to change or stop that targeting. Confirm the ad-serving platform surfaces these Art. 26(1) disclosures in real time.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages the DSA mainly through its interface-design tactics and cross-site advertising. The pressure-toned messaging and — critically — the fact that unsubscribing stops emails but not the 21:30 pushes reflect exactly the obstruction-of-cancellation / nagging conduct that DSA Art. 25 prohibits for online-platform interfaces (ShoeVault's app). The 30-day cross-site display retargeting on news-site platforms engages DSA Art. 26(1) ad-transparency duties (identifiable-as-ad, advertiser identity, main targeting parameters and how to change them). Note a scope caveat: core DSA obligations attach to "online platform" providers, and a pure retail advertiser may not itself qualify; the identical conduct is squarely covered by the UCPD (handled separately). Art. 26(3) (special-category data) and Art. 28 (minors) are not engaged on the facts as described.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, persistent and unwanted solicitations by e-mail or 'other remote media' except where justified to enforce a contractual obligation. App-push notifications are a remote medium. Once a user unsubscribes they have signalled refusal of marketing contact, yet the 21:30 pushes continue — a scripted re-contact of a user who has refused. Cart-abandonment win-back messaging is a commercial solicitation, not enforcement of a contractual obligation, so the exception does not apply. Disabling frequency caps for 'high-intent' users compounds the persistence.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Route the unsubscribe (and any channel-level opt-out) so that it suppresses ALL marketing channels including app-push, or provide an equally accessible push opt-out that is honoured immediately. Never treat a marketing unsubscribe as covering only email.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, by harassment or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice. The listed factors — timing, persistence, and onerous barriers to exercising rights — are all present: deliberately timed 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.') pushes, uncapped frequency for the very segment identified as most susceptible, 30 days of cross-site retargeting, and pushes that keep coming after the consumer tries to stop them. Targeting 'high-intent' users with removed limits is designed to wear down resistance rather than inform, pressing a transactional decision the consumer might not otherwise take.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Reinstate frequency caps for all segments (including 'high-intent'), avoid marketing pushes during late-night hours, cap the retargeting window well below 30 days, and ensure opt-out is fully effective across channels so the practice cannot be characterised as harassment.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a safety-net, Art. 5 catches practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort the average consumer's economic behaviour. The anthropomorphic, surveillance-toned copy ('they're watching you back', 'Still up? Your cart is too.') is a communication-design nudge that leverages the consumer's sense of being watched and late-night vulnerability to pressure a purchase, sitting alongside the dark-pattern nagging effect of uncapped, cross-channel repetition. Even if no individual message is misleading, the cumulative design is likely to distort economic behaviour and falls short of professional diligence.
findings.evidence_quote: We saw you looking at the Air Runners — they're watching you back
findings.recommendation: Drop surveillance/pressure framing in favour of neutral, informative reminders; limit reminder volume; and document that the sequence respects consumer autonomy rather than exploiting it.

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence engages the UCPD's aggressive-practices regime rather than its misleading-practices rules. The most serious issue is that unsubscribing stops emails but not the 21:30 app pushes, combined with disabled frequency caps for 'high-intent' users — this is continued remote solicitation of a consumer who has partially refused, engaging the Annex I point 26 blacklist and the Arts. 8-9 aggressive-practice test (timing, persistence, onerous barriers to exercising the right to stop contact). The anthropomorphic pressure messaging and relentless 30-day retargeting reinforce an undue-influence concern under the general fairness safety-net. No misleading-action (Art. 6) violation is clearly made out on the text.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: The right to object to direct marketing (including profiling for marketing) is absolute: once a data subject objects, personal data must no longer be processed for that purpose across all channels. Here the opt-out only suppresses email while app-push direct marketing (and presumably the underlying profiling/retargeting) continues, so the objection is not fully honoured. This is a direct failure of Art. 21(2)-(3).
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
