findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 requires that withdrawing consent be as easy as giving it. A user who consented once at signup cannot switch off pushes at all through the working preference centre, so withdrawal is harder than the original opt-in and effectively unavailable for that channel. The controller must also be able to demonstrate that consent covered each processing purpose.
findings.evidence_quote: consent must be as easy to withdraw as to give
findings.recommendation: Provide per-channel toggles (email, push, cross-site retargeting) in the preference centre so each can be withdrawn as easily as given, and ensure withdrawal is immediately effective. Log granular consent records to demonstrate compliance.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: Consent must be specific and informed. A single blanket 'marketing communications' checkbox at signup is unlikely to validly cover distinct, more intrusive purposes such as 30-day cross-site display retargeting, behavioural profiling and late-night app pushes. Bundled, non-granular consent does not meet the Art. 4(11) standard for these specific processing operations.
findings.evidence_quote: The user consented to 'marketing communications' at signup
findings.recommendation: Collect separate, specific consents for each processing purpose/channel (email marketing, app-push, cross-site behavioural retargeting) with clear descriptions, rather than one bundled 'marketing communications' opt-in. Do not rely on the generic signup checkbox for cross-site tracking.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Cross-site behavioural retargeting and cart-abandonment profiling require a valid lawful basis. Given the doubts over consent scope, and that cross-site tracking generally requires consent (also under ePrivacy), the campaign as described has not established a demonstrably valid Art. 6(1) basis for the profiling and 30-day cross-site advertising.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Document the lawful basis for each processing operation. For cross-site retargeting rely on specific consent (aligned with ePrivacy); if legitimate interests are invoked for any first-party processing, conduct and record a balancing test and honour objections.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Analysing a user's browsing and cart-abandonment behaviour to target tailored ads and messages is profiling within Art. 4(4). This triggers the connected obligations on lawful basis (Art. 6), transparency (Arts. 12-13) and the right to object (Art. 21), which must all be satisfied for the retargeting sequence.
findings.evidence_quote: personalisation based on browsing/cart behaviour
findings.recommendation: Treat the retargeting sequence as profiling: ensure it is grounded in a lawful basis, disclosed transparently, and fully covered by the objection mechanism.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at collection users are informed of processing purposes, legal basis, and the existence of profiling and its logic/consequences. Segmenting users into a 'high-intent' category that receives uncapped messaging is a profiling-driven decision that must be transparently disclosed; nothing indicates users were informed of this profiling and its intensity.

findings.recommendation: Disclose in the privacy notice at signup that behavioural profiling (including 'high-intent' scoring) is used to determine ad frequency and messaging, describe the purposes and lawful basis, and clearly signpost the right to object.

verdicts.notes: The campaign processes personal data of signed-in shoppers through behavioural profiling and multi-channel direct marketing, but relies on a single broad "marketing communications" checkbox and provides an opt-out that fails to stop all channels. The most serious GDPR issue is that unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night app pushes, which breaks the absolute right to object under Art. 21 and undermines valid consent under Art. 7. Consent validity (specificity/granularity), the lawful basis for 30-day cross-site profiling, and profiling transparency are also engaged and appear unsatisfied as described.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing online interfaces in a way that materially distorts or impairs recipients' ability to make free and informed decisions, and expressly lists making a choice already made ineffective / obstructing opt-out. ShoeVault's preference centre lets a user express an opt-out ('unsubscribe') that the system then partially ignores by continuing 21:30 app pushes. An opt-out that does not actually stop all the solicitations it appears to govern is a deceptive, choice-obstructing interface design falling within Art. 25.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the opt-out honour the user's expressed choice across all channels: unsubscribing (and the preference centre) must be able to stop app-push marketing as well as email, with clearly labelled, granular per-channel controls that take effect immediately.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 names 'repeatedly requesting that the recipient make a choice already made' and pressure-through-repetition as manipulative interface patterns. Removing frequency caps for users scored as 'high-intent' engineers relentless, uncapped exposure specifically at those most susceptible, which is capable of materially distorting their ability to make a free decision — the essence of a nagging dark pattern.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Apply reasonable frequency caps to all users regardless of intent score, and never remove caps as a manipulation lever; document that repetition levels do not exploit or pressure identified high-propensity users.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that ads presented on online platforms be clearly identifiable as advertising, with the advertiser/payer and main targeting parameters disclosed to the recipient in real time. The obligation rests on the platform presenting the ad (here the third-party news sites), not on ShoeVault as advertiser, but ShoeVault should ensure its retargeting creatives can be properly labelled and that it supplies accurate advertiser and targeting-parameter information to those platforms.
findings.evidence_quote: display retargeting across news sites for 30 days
findings.recommendation: Ensure display creatives are deliverable as clearly labelled ads and provide the hosting platforms with complete advertiser-identity, payer and targeting-parameter data so the platforms can meet their Art. 26(1) transparency duties; keep the targeting logic ('saw you looking'/cart behaviour) explainable to recipients.

verdicts.notes: The DSA's core relevance here is Art. 25's prohibition of dark patterns in online-interface design, which applies to ShoeVault as the operator of its own app/site interface. Two design choices — disabling frequency caps for "high-intent" users and an opt-out mechanism where unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night app pushes — engage Art. 25's examples of repeatedly nagging users and obstructing/not honouring a choice already made. The advertising-transparency duty (Art. 26) falls primarily on the third-party platforms presenting ShoeVault's retargeting rather than on ShoeVault itself, so it is flagged only for context. Art. 26(3) (sensitive-data ads) and Art. 28 (minors) are not engaged on the facts.

findings.title: Blacklist: persistent and unwanted solicitations
findings.rationale: Annex I point 26 prohibits, in all circumstances, making persistent and unwanted solicitations by e-mail or other remote media, except to enforce a contractual obligation. App-push marketing is a remote medium, and continuing to send late-night pushes after the consumer has used the preference centre to unsubscribe is textbook continued solicitation after opt-out. The marketing purpose (recovering an abandoned cart) is not enforcement of any contractual obligation, so no exception applies. This is a per-se blacklisted unfair practice.
findings.evidence_quote: unsubscribing stops emails but not the late-night pushes
findings.recommendation: Make the preference centre/unsubscribe stop ALL marketing channels including app-push, not just email. Provide a single, effective opt-out that suppresses the entire win-back sequence across display, email and push once the consumer objects.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, by harassment or undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice, with relevant factors including persistence, timing and onerous barriers to exercising rights. Deliberately removing frequency caps for the most susceptible ('high-intent') segment, combined with 30-day cross-site retargeting, a three-email sequence and 21:30 pushes that cannot be switched off, amounts to relentless, uncapped pressure designed to wear the consumer down into completing a purchase they had abandoned. The broken push opt-out is itself an onerous barrier to exercising the right to be left alone.
findings.evidence_quote: Frequency caps are disabled for 'high-intent' users
findings.recommendation: Reinstate reasonable frequency caps for all users (do not exempt 'high-intent' segments), cap the total campaign duration/volume, and ensure the opt-out is easy and effective across every channel so consumers can readily stop contact.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Timing is an express aggressiveness factor under Arts. 8-9. Deliberately timing pushes to late evening, with copy playing on the consumer being awake and vulnerable ('Still up?'), together with the surveillance-style 'they're watching you back' framing, uses undue influence and psychological pressure to push a transactional decision rather than communicating a neutral reminder. Assessed cumulatively with the uncapped, unstoppable contact, this reinforces the aggressive-practice finding.
findings.evidence_quote: an app push at 21:30 ('Still up? Your cart is too.')
findings.recommendation: Avoid late-night send windows for marketing pushes and drop coercive, surveillance-flavoured copy ('they're watching you back', 'Still up? Your cart is too.'). Use neutral, non-pressuring reminder messaging within reasonable hours.

verdicts.notes: The ShoeVault sequence engages the UCPD's aggressive-practices regime rather than its misleading-practices regime. The combination of disabled frequency caps for "high-intent" users, 30-day cross-site retargeting, and late-night pushes that continue after unsubscribe most seriously implicates Annex I point 26 (persistent and unwanted solicitations — a per-se blacklisted practice) and Arts. 8-9 (aggressive practices via persistence, timing and an onerous/broken opt-out). The "they're watching you back" copy adds a coercive, surveillance-style pressure element reinforcing the aggressiveness assessment. Fixes are straightforward: honour opt-out across all channels, restore frequency caps, and avoid deliberately unsettling late-night contact.

report.executive_summary: This campaign triggers a multi-channel win-back sequence (30-day cross-site display retargeting, three emails, and a 21:30 app push) for signed-in shoppers who abandon a cart, with frequency caps switched off for "high-intent" users. It carries serious compliance problems and should not run in its current form. The single most damaging issue: when a user unsubscribes, emails stop but the late-night app pushes keep coming. That broken opt-out is a per-se prohibited "persistent and unwanted solicitation" under the UCPD (an automatic blacklist violation), and it also breaches the GDPR's absolute right to object and its rule that consent be as easy to withdraw as to give. Disabling frequency caps for your most susceptible users, combined with late-night timing and coercive "they're watching you back" / "Still up?" copy, adds up to an aggressive commercial practice and a DSA dark-pattern (nagging plus an opt-out that ignores the user's choice). On top of that, a single blanket "marketing communications" checkbox at signup is too broad to lawfully cover cross-site behavioural retargeting and profiling. The good news is that the fixes are concrete and mostly about honouring choices you already offer.
recommendations: Make the opt-out global and immediate: one unsubscribe/objection in the preference centre must stop ALL channels — email, app-push AND cross-site display retargeting — plus the underlying marketing profiling. This alone resolves the critical UCPD blacklist violation and the core GDPR Art. 21 breach.

Restore reasonable frequency caps for every user and never disable them for 'high-intent' segments; cap total campaign duration and volume. Removing caps for susceptible users is both an aggressive practice (UCPD) and a DSA dark pattern.
Stop late-night marketing sends and drop the coercive, surveillance-style copy ('they're watching you back', 'Still up? Your cart is too.'). Use neutral reminders within reasonable hours.

Replace the single blanket 'marketing communications' checkbox with separate, specific, granular consents per channel/purpose (email, app-push, cross-site behavioural retargeting), and provide per-channel toggles in the preference centre.

Document a valid lawful basis for the 30-day cross-site retargeting and cart-abandonment profiling (consent aligned with ePrivacy for cross-site tracking) and keep granular consent/withdrawal records.
Update the signup privacy notice to disclose the behavioural profiling, including 'high-intent' scoring used to set ad frequency, and clearly signpost the right to object.

Supply the third-party news-site platforms with accurate advertiser, payer and targeting-parameter information so they can meet their DSA Art. 26 ad-transparency duties, and keep the targeting logic explainable.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: behavioural profiling (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history)
targeting users during inferred low-mood/distressed windows
delivery of betting/gambling ads to vulnerable emotional states
no user disclosure of emotional inference
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users in the EU; minors are excluded from the pilot per the submission, though exclusion effectiveness is unverified. Key concern is targeting users in inferred emotionally distressed/vulnerable states.
triage.summary: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, without informing users. Internal data notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed, and advertisers can toggle a 'receptivity boost'. This raises serious concerns around emotion recognition/manipulative AI, profiling of sensitive inferred data, opaque online-platform advertising, and exploitation of consumer vulnerability.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: This is an AI system deploying purposefully manipulative techniques operating beyond users' awareness ('Users are not informed'). By timing betting and impulse-purchase ('retail therapy') ads to inferred low-mood/distressed windows, the system has the objective or effect of materially distorting users' behaviour, appreciably impairing their ability to make an informed decision and causing them to take decisions (gambling, impulse spending) they would not otherwise take. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences both the manipulative effect and the reasonable likelihood of significant financial and psychological harm, satisfying the harm threshold in Art. 5(1)(a). This is a prohibited practice, not a merely regulated one.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue the emotional-state inference and mood-timed ad delivery entirely. Do not use inferred emotional/low-mood states to trigger, time or boost ad delivery. Any personalisation must not covertly exploit inferred psychological states to distort purchasing/gambling decisions; remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle that operationalises this.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The system deliberately identifies users in a vulnerable state — a 'specific social or economic situation' of momentary emotional distress/low mood — and exploits that vulnerability to materially distort their behaviour. Directing betting/gambling and impulse-spending ads at users the system has classified as distressed is reasonably likely to cause significant harm (gambling losses, financial harm, worsened mental state). The advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and the documented uplift in conversion among distressed users show the exploitation is purposeful and effective, squarely engaging the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition. That minors are excluded does not cure the exploitation of vulnerability among adults in distress.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Stop targeting or boosting ad delivery based on inferred vulnerability/distress states. Prohibit gambling/betting and impulse-purchase advertising from being coupled to any emotional-state inference. Conduct an Article 5 compliance review before any further pilot and document that no vulnerability-based targeting occurs.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: The AI Act's dedicated emotion-recognition prohibition in Art. 5(1)(f) is confined to the workplace and education institutions. This campaign operates on a consumer social platform, so Art. 5(1)(f) is not directly breached. It is flagged for completeness because the same emotion-inference conduct is captured by Art. 5(1)(a)-(b) and by GDPR sensitive/inferred-data rules handled by other agents.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state
findings.recommendation: No action required under Art. 5(1)(f) specifically, but ensure the emotion-inference model is never deployed in workplace or educational contexts, where it would become an outright prohibited use.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deploys an in-house AI system that covertly infers users' momentary emotional/low-mood state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and impulse-purchase ('retail therapy') ads during those windows. This engages two Article 5 prohibitions of the AI Act: manipulative AI techniques (Art. 5(1)(a)) and exploitation of vulnerability arising from a specific situation (Art. 5(1)(b)), both of which carry the highest severity as outright prohibited practices. The company's own review noting 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is strong evidence of the intended/actual behaviour-distortion effect and likely harm. Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition) is scoped to workplace/education and does not apply to this consumer platform.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's momentary emotional/mental state — and specifically identifying users as 'distressed' or in 'low-mood windows' — constitutes processing of data concerning a person's mental health, which is a special category under Art. 9. Art. 9 covers inferred attributes, not just declared ones. Processing such data is prohibited unless an exception (e.g. explicit consent) applies. Here users are not informed and give no explicit consent, so no exception is met and the prohibition is breached.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring and processing emotional/distress states for ad delivery absent a valid Art. 9 exception. Because marketing personalisation cannot rely on 'substantial public interest' or the other narrow exceptions, this would require prior, specific, explicit opt-in consent — and even then targeting inferred distress raises fairness concerns. Realistically, discontinue the emotional-state inference feature entirely.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Inferring emotional state and exploiting inferred distress covertly — with no disclosure and only 'standard sponsored labels' that reveal nothing about the mood inference — is covert processing that breaches the transparency and, crucially, the fairness limb of Art. 5(1)(a). Exploiting 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is the antithesis of fair processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Do not process personal data in ways users cannot reasonably foresee. Provide clear disclosure of any behavioural inference used to time or select ads, and eliminate targeting that exploits inferred vulnerability, which cannot be made 'fair' by disclosure alone.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated evaluation of personal aspects (emotional state, behaviour) from behavioural signals to tailor ad delivery is textbook profiling under Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 22, Art. 21) below.
findings.evidence_quote: behavioural profiling (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history)
findings.recommendation: Recognise the operation as profiling and apply the full GDPR profiling regime; document a DPIA given the scale (28M users) and the sensitivity/vulnerability involved.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: This profiling and personalised ad delivery requires a valid lawful basis. Consent is absent (users are not informed), and legitimate interests cannot succeed: a balancing test would fail where the processing exploits inferred emotional distress for commercial gain, and in any event special-category data cannot be processed on a legitimate-interests basis. No lawful basis is present.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Establish a valid Art. 6 basis before any such processing. For this type of intrusive profiling that basis would need to be consent; given the Art. 9 issue and fairness concerns, the feature should not proceed on any basis as designed.

findings.title: Conditions for consent
findings.rationale: There is no consent mechanism at all for the emotional-inference targeting; any consent that were relied upon would have to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous per Arts. 4(11)/7 and, for Art. 9 data, explicit. Silent enrolment of users into MoodMatch cannot meet these conditions.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers can tick 'receptivity boost'.
findings.recommendation: If the feature continues in any form, implement a granular, explicit opt-in consent flow (clearly distinguishable, plain language, as easy to withdraw as to give) specifically covering emotional-state inference — noting that lawful design likely still fails on fairness/Art. 9 grounds.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting/processing personal data the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes, legal basis, and — importantly — the existence of automated decision-making/profiling and meaningful information about the logic involved. None of this is provided; the mood-inference processing is entirely undisclosed.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Provide layered privacy information (via Art. 12 clear, accessible notice) disclosing the behavioural inference, its purposes, the profiling logic, and users' rights, at or before the processing begins.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: This is profiling for direct marketing purposes, which triggers an absolute right to object under Art. 21(2)-(3), and users must be explicitly informed of this right at the latest at first communication. Because users are not informed of the processing at all, the right to object cannot be meaningfully exercised.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads
findings.recommendation: Explicitly present the right to object to direct-marketing profiling, clearly and separately, and provide an easy opt-out that immediately stops the profiling-based ad delivery.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: MoodMatch makes solely-automated decisions about which users receive betting/'retail therapy'/comfort-food ads based on inferred distress. Automated allocation targeting a vulnerable emotional state — especially with gambling ads — plausibly 'similarly significantly affects' individuals, engaging Art. 22 and its requirements for a valid basis and safeguards, none of which are present.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'.
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated targeting significantly affects users; if so, either obtain explicit consent with Art. 22 safeguards (human intervention, contest the decision) or discontinue. Given the exploitation of vulnerability, discontinuation is the safer course.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch infers users' momentary emotional/mental state from behavioural signals and targets ads during inferred "low-mood/distressed" windows. This is clearly profiling (Art. 4(4)); the inferred emotional/distress state is very likely health/special-category data engaging the Art. 9 prohibition, which is unmet because users are not informed and give no explicit consent. Covert inference with "Users are not informed" breaches the lawfulness/fairness/transparency principle (Art. 5(1)(a)) and the Art. 13 duty to inform, and there is no valid lawful basis (Art. 6) or valid consent (Art. 7). The absence of disclosure also undermines the Art. 21 right to object to direct-marketing profiling.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, including by inference. MoodMatch infers users' momentary emotional/mental state ('low-mood', 'distressed') from behavioural signals and uses that inferred state to determine which ads are delivered. Inferred emotional/mental-health state falls within Art. 9 health data, so targeting ad delivery on this basis is prohibited regardless of any consent, and the 'receptivity boost' toggle operationalises exactly this sensitive-inference targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Cease using inferred emotional/mood state as an ad-delivery or targeting signal entirely. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and any pipeline that routes emotional-state inferences into ad selection. If mood inference is used for non-advertising product features, ring-fence it fully from advertising systems.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits platforms from designing or operating their online interface in a way that manipulates recipients or materially distorts or impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. Timing the delivery of impulse-purchase, comfort-food and gambling ads to coincide with algorithmically inferred moments of emotional distress is designed to exploit a diminished decision-making state; the internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences that the design materially distorts autonomous decisions rather than merely informing them.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Disable mood-contingent ad delivery so that ad selection and timing do not vary with inferred emotional vulnerability. Introduce safeguards preventing high-risk categories (e.g. gambling/betting, impulse-purchase) from being boosted by any affect/receptivity signal, and document an anti-manipulation review of delivery logic.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify, in real time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine the recipient it is presented to, and how to change them. A standard 'sponsored' label discloses that content is an ad but omits the actual main parameter driving delivery here — the inferred emotional-state / 'receptivity' signal. Because users 'are not informed', the meaningful-parameters requirement is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide per-ad transparency that discloses the real main targeting parameters (i.e. behavioural/affect-based delivery signals) and offer users controls to change them. Given the sensitive nature of the parameter, the correct fix is to eliminate the emotional-inference parameter rather than merely disclose it.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: Art. 27 requires platforms using recommender/delivery systems to set out in plain language the main parameters used and any options to modify them. MoodMatch is a delivery-ranking system whose main parameters include inferred emotional state derived from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, none of which are disclosed to users in plain language or made adjustable.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Update the platform's recommender-system disclosures to describe the parameters actually used in ad/content delivery in plain language and provide user options to influence them, while removing affect-based parameters from the delivery logic.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: With 28M EU users the platform is very likely a Very Large Online Platform (>45M threshold should be confirmed, but scale is significant). Under Art. 39 a VLOP must maintain a public ad repository including the targeting parameters and reach of each ad. The undisclosed emotional-inference / receptivity targeting would have to be published, and cannot lawfully be recorded because it relies on prohibited sensitive-data profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Confirm VLOP status. Ensure any ad-repository entries accurately reflect targeting parameters; since the MoodMatch parameters could not survive public disclosure or the Art. 26(3) ban, remove them from the delivery system before any launch.

verdicts.notes: The MoodMatch pilot engages multiple DSA obligations, several likely breached. The platform (28M EU users, a probable VLOP) infers users' momentary emotional/distressed state and preferentially delivers betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows without informing users. This most seriously implicates the Art. 26(3) ban on profiling ad targeting using Art. 9 special-category data (inferred mental/health state), the Art. 25 prohibition on interfaces that manipulate or materially distort users' ability to make free and informed decisions, and the Art. 26(1)/27 transparency duties, which are not met because the emotional-inference parameter and 'receptivity boost' are undisclosed. As a likely VLOP, Art. 39 ad-repository obligations also apply.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 treat a practice as aggressive where, by undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. Timing and exploitation of the consumer's misfortune/emotional state are named factors. Here the platform deliberately times ads to inferred low-mood/distressed windows and the internal review records 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' — direct evidence that the timing materially distorts economic behaviour by exploiting a moment of weakened resistance. Serving betting/gambling and impulse 'retail therapy' ads to people in inferred distress makes the resulting harm significant.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue timing or boosting ad delivery based on inferred emotional/mood states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and any 'low-mood window' logic; do not use distress inference as a targeting or optimisation signal for any advertiser, and especially exclude high-risk categories (betting/gambling, impulse purchases) from any behavioural timing.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 is the general fairness safety-net: a practice is unfair if contrary to professional diligence and likely to materially distort economic behaviour, and vulnerable groups are assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group (Art. 5(3)). Users algorithmically identified as being in a momentary distressed/low-mood state are a clearly identifiable vulnerable group in that moment; deliberately intensifying commercial pressure on them is contrary to professional diligence and, on the platform's own conversion data, distorts their transactional behaviour.
findings.evidence_quote: Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Adopt a professional-diligence standard that prohibits exploiting inferred negative emotional states as a commercial-optimisation variable; document this in advertising policy and suppress rather than boost ad pressure when distress is inferred.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the consumer needs for an informed decision, including where information is provided in an unclear or untimely manner. While the ads are labelled 'sponsored', the material fact that the ad has been specifically selected and timed to the user's inferred emotional/distressed state is concealed. A standard sponsored label does not reveal this emotional-targeting mechanism, so consumers cannot appreciate why they are seeing the ad at that moment — a material omission affecting their transactional decision.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: If any emotion-linked targeting were retained (not recommended given the Arts. 8-9 exposure), it would need clear, timely disclosure that ad delivery is influenced by inferred emotional state, plus a user control to opt out — but the safest course is to cease the practice entirely rather than attempt to cure it with disclosure.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch times commercial messages to moments when users are algorithmically inferred to be in a distressed/low-mood state, and internal data confirms "elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed" — i.e. the tactic works precisely because it exploits transient vulnerability to impair free choice. This engages the UCPD as an aggressive practice by undue influence (Arts. 8-9), reinforced by the Art. 5 vulnerability safety-net, and as a misleading omission (Art. 7) because the emotional-targeting mechanism is deliberately concealed from users. The gambling/betting and "retail therapy" ad categories heighten the likelihood of significant transactional harm.

report.executive_summary: The 'MoodMatch' pilot uses an AI model to secretly infer when your 28M EU users are feeling low or distressed (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions), then preferentially serves them gambling, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads at exactly those vulnerable moments. Your own internal review confirms it works — conversions rise among users inferred as distressed — which is precisely the problem: it exploits a moment of emotional weakness for commercial gain, and users are never told. All four specialist reviews (AI Act, GDPR, DSA, UCPD) returned 'violation likely', with the most serious hitting the highest severity. This is not a feature that can be fixed with a better disclosure label or a consent checkbox: inferring emotional state is special-category health data, and both the AI Act and DSA flatly prohibit this kind of manipulation and sensitive-data ad targeting regardless of consent. The realistic verdict is that the pilot cannot lawfully launch in the EU as designed. The clear path forward is to discontinue emotional-state inference as an ad-delivery signal entirely and remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle. Continuing risks prohibited-practice enforcement under the AI Act, DSA VLOP penalties, and GDPR fines.
recommendations: STOP the pilot as designed — it cannot launch lawfully in the EU. Discontinue all emotional/low-mood state inference used to time, select or boost ad delivery. This is a prohibited manipulative and vulnerability-exploiting practice under AI Act Art. 5(1)(a) and (b), which no consent or disclosure can cure.

Remove the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and dismantle any pipeline that routes emotional-state inferences into ad selection. Inferred emotional/mental state is Art. 9 special-category (health) data, and DSA Art. 26(3) flatly bans ad targeting on such data — even by inference, even with consent.

Immediately cease coupling gambling/betting and impulse-purchase ('retail therapy') ads to any affect or timing signal — these categories create the greatest risk of significant financial and psychological harm to distressed users (UCPD Arts. 5, 8-9; AI Act Art. 5(1)(b)).

Do not attempt to salvage the feature via consent or a disclosure label. Even a valid opt-in would still fail on fairness (GDPR Art. 5(1)(a)), the AI Act prohibitions, and the DSA dark-patterns ban (Art. 25). Disclosure of the emotional-targeting mechanism is legally insufficient to make it lawful.

Preserve and escalate the internal review noting 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' to your DPO and legal team — this document is direct evidence of the harmful effect and must inform the decision to halt, not be treated as a performance win.

Confirm the platform's VLOP status (28M users; the >45M threshold should be verified) and ensure ad-repository entries (DSA Art. 39) and recommender-system disclosures (Art. 27) accurately reflect targeting parameters once the prohibited affect-based signals are removed.

If mood/affect inference is used for any legitimate non-advertising product feature, fully ring-fence it from all advertising and delivery-ranking systems, and conduct a DPIA given the scale and sensitivity involved.

Before any future personalisation pilot, run an AI Act Article 5 pre-launch screen plus a GDPR lawful-basis and fairness assessment, and document that no vulnerability- or emotion-based targeting occurs.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: emotional state inference from behavioural signals
mood-based ad targeting during inferred vulnerability (low-mood windows)
behavioural retargeting using reaction history and dwell time
targeting inferred-distressed users with betting/gambling ads
targeting inferred-distressed users with 'retail therapy' impulse-purchase ads
non-disclosure of emotional profiling to users
standard sponsored labelling only (no disclosure of mood-based delivery)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users in the EU; minors excluded per submission, though inference-based exclusion reliability should be verified. The core concern is targeting of emotionally vulnerable/distressed adults, which raises AI Act emotion-recognition and manipulation/exploitation-of-vulnerability concerns, GDPR issues around profiling and possible special-category (health/mental-state) data plus lack of transparency and lawful basis, DSA restrictions on advertising and profiling on a very large online platform, and UCPD concerns over aggressive/unfair commercial practices exploiting consumer vulnerability.
triage.summary: A large social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves comfort-food, betting and impulse-purchase ads during inferred low-mood windows, with advertisers able to opt into a 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed of the emotional profiling, and internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed. Minors are declared excluded from the pilot.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The AI system covertly detects emotional state and times ad delivery to exploit inferred low-mood windows, without user awareness. This is a purposefully manipulative technique operating beyond the user's consciousness with the objective/effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing informed decision-making and causing users to make purchases (betting, impulse spending) they would not otherwise make. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences both the manipulative effect and the reasonably likely significant harm (financial loss, gambling harm). This falls squarely within the Art. 5(1)(a) prohibited practice.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Discontinue emotion-state inference for ad timing/selection. Remove any delivery logic keyed to inferred mood or distress. Ad optimisation must not be conditioned on covertly detected emotional vulnerability; if personalisation is retained, base it only on transparent, non-manipulative signals with user awareness and control.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: The system exploits a vulnerability arising from users' specific emotional/situational state (distress, low mood) by intensifying delivery of harmful product categories (gambling/betting and impulse purchases) precisely when users are least able to make sound decisions. The 'receptivity boost' toggle and the documented conversion uplift among distressed users show the objective/effect of materially distorting their behaviour in a manner reasonably likely to cause significant harm (financial and gambling-related). This engages the Art. 5(1)(b) prohibition on AI exploiting vulnerabilities.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Advertisers ... can tick 'receptivity boost' ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Prohibit any targeting or delivery uplift ('receptivity boost') tied to inferred emotional vulnerability, and specifically block high-harm categories such as betting/gambling and impulse-purchase ads from any mood-conditioned logic. Document a risk assessment demonstrating the model cannot key delivery to inferred distress.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: The pilot clearly performs emotion inference, but Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion recognition only in the workplace and education-institution contexts. MoodMatch targets general adult platform users, so this specific prohibition is not directly triggered. Flagged for context because the emotion-inference activity remains highly relevant to Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) and to GDPR special-category-data assessment handled by other agents.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: No action required under Art. 5(1)(f) in the current consumer context; however, note that deploying MoodMatch on any employee- or student-facing surface (e.g., internal tools, education partnerships) would trigger this prohibition. Keep emotion inference out of any workplace/education deployment.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI model to covertly infer users' momentary emotional state and preferentially deliver betting, comfort-food and impulse-purchase ('retail therapy') ads during inferred low-mood windows, without informing users. This engages two AI Act Article 5 prohibitions: covert AI-driven manipulation materially distorting behaviour (5(1)(a)) and exploitation of vulnerability arising from a person's situation causing likely significant harm (5(1)(b)). Both are 'prohibited practices' carrying the highest enforcement tier; the internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is direct evidence of behavioural distortion and harm. Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition) is not directly applicable here because it is confined to workplace/education contexts, but is noted for context.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring users' momentary emotional/mental state and identifying users 'inferred as distressed' processes data revealing mental-health condition, which is special-category health data under Art. 9 — including where inferred rather than declared. Processing is prohibited absent an Art. 9(2) exception (here, explicit consent), which is entirely absent since users are not informed. The inference of psychological/emotional state to select ad delivery falls squarely within the Art. 9 prohibition.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease processing inferred emotional/mental-state data for ad delivery unless you obtain valid explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a) for that specific purpose. Given the covert and exploitative design, this processing cannot be lawfully continued as described; discontinue mood-inference targeting.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Covertly inferring emotional state and preferentially serving betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows — while users remain uninformed — breaches the fairness and transparency principle. Exploiting inferred distress to boost conversion is the paradigm of unfair processing under Art. 5(1)(a).
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide full, prominent disclosure of the emotional-inference processing and its purpose, and redesign so processing is fair — i.e. do not exploit inferred vulnerability to drive conversions. Absent both, the practice violates Art. 5(1)(a).

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: When collecting personal data the controller must inform data subjects of the purposes and legal basis, and specifically about the existence of automated decision-making/profiling and its logic and consequences (Art. 13(2)(f)). Users are given only standard sponsored labels and are not told that behavioural signals are used to infer mood and time ad delivery. This is a clear failure to provide the mandatory Art. 13 information.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Add a layered privacy notice at data collection covering the mood-inference purpose, the behavioural signals used, the legal basis, and meaningful information about the profiling logic and consequences, in line with Art. 13(2)(f).

findings.title: Transparent information and communication
findings.rationale: Art. 12 requires information to be concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible. A generic 'sponsored' label does not communicate the emotional-profiling and mood-based delivery in clear plain language, so even to the extent any notice exists it fails the Art. 12 accessibility/clarity standard.
findings.evidence_quote: the ads carry standard sponsored labels
findings.recommendation: Ensure any disclosure about mood-based delivery is presented clearly and accessibly at the relevant moment, not buried, so users can genuinely understand the processing.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: All personal-data processing needs a valid Art. 6(1) basis. Behavioural profiling for personalised advertising generally requires consent or a carefully balanced legitimate-interest assessment. No consent is obtained (users are uninformed), and a legitimate-interests basis cannot survive a balancing test where the processing infers distress and exploits it for commercial gain — the data subjects' interests and fundamental rights clearly override. No valid lawful basis is apparent.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid Art. 6(1) basis before processing; for this intrusive, vulnerability-exploiting profiling, only freely given specific consent could suffice, and given the design a legitimate-interests basis is not viable.

findings.title: Definition of consent
findings.rationale: If consent were relied upon for this profiling, it must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous (Art. 4(11)), with the conditions of Art. 7 met. Since users are not informed and give no affirmative indication for mood inference, no valid consent exists for the special-category and profiling processing.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: If proceeding, obtain separate, informed, unbundled, affirmative consent specifically for emotional-state inference and mood-based ad delivery, meeting Art. 4(11) and Art. 7 conditions (including easy withdrawal).

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated processing of behavioural data to evaluate personal aspects (behaviour, and here inferred emotional/health state) is profiling within Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the associated GDPR obligations (lawful basis, transparency of profiling logic, right to object), which the campaign does not satisfy.
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Treat MoodMatch as profiling and apply the full profiling compliance stack: DPIA, lawful basis, Art. 13(2)(f) transparency, and Art. 21 opt-out.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: Ad delivery is decided solely by automated profiling of inferred emotional state. Where such solely-automated profiling of individuals inferred as 'distressed' materially affects them (e.g. steering vulnerable users toward gambling/betting during low-mood windows), it may 'similarly significantly affect' them under Art. 22, requiring an exception plus safeguards (right to human intervention, to contest). No such safeguards are described.
findings.evidence_quote: Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'
findings.recommendation: Assess whether the automated mood-based delivery significantly affects users (targeting distressed users with betting ads strongly suggests it does); if so, ensure an Art. 22 exception applies and implement the required safeguards, or refrain from solely-automated targeting of vulnerable states.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Data subjects have an absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing, including related profiling (Art. 21(2)-(3)), and must be explicitly informed of it at the latest at first communication. The covert MoodMatch design gives users no awareness of the mood-profiling and no clear means to object to it.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads
findings.recommendation: Explicitly inform users of the right to object to direct-marketing profiling and provide an easy, effective opt-out mechanism specific to mood-based delivery.

verdicts.notes: The MoodMatch pilot processes behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history) across 28M EU users to infer momentary emotional/mental state and target ads during inferred distress. This engages GDPR at multiple points: it is profiling (Art. 4(4)); the inferred emotional/mental-state data is likely special-category health data requiring Art. 9 protection with explicit consent; there is no transparency (users are "not informed") violating Arts. 5(1)(a), 12 and 13; a valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) is doubtful and consent conditions (Arts. 4(11), 7) are not met; and the solely-automated targeting of vulnerable individuals engages Art. 22. The covert nature and exploitation of inferred distress make the fairness and transparency breaches particularly serious.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 26(3) prohibits online platforms from presenting advertisements based on profiling using GDPR Art. 9 special categories, and this ban expressly extends to attributes derived by inference. Inferring a user's momentary emotional/mental state — 'low-mood windows', users 'inferred as distressed' — is inference of health/mental-state data (an Art. 9 category), and that inference is the very parameter used to select and time ad delivery. This is precisely the profiling-on-sensitive-data ad targeting the provision forbids, and the prohibition applies regardless of any consent the platform might obtain.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Stop using inferred emotional/mental-state signals as an input to ad selection or timing. Ad-delivery models must not consume 'low-mood' / distress inferences or the reaction-history/dwell-time proxies used to derive them. Remove the emotional-state feature entirely from the advertising pipeline rather than attempting to rely on consent, which cannot cure an Art. 26(3) breach.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: Art. 25 prohibits designing or operating an online interface in a way that manipulates recipients or materially distorts/impairs their ability to make free and informed decisions. Deliberately timing impulse-purchase, betting and 'retail therapy' ads to moments of inferred emotional vulnerability — with the platform's own review confirming this raises conversion among 'distressed' users — is an interface/delivery design that exploits a diminished decision-making capacity to nudge commercial choices, engaging the dark-patterns prohibition (which applies without prejudice to the UCPD).
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Discontinue vulnerability-based ad timing. Do not condition ad delivery, frequency or the 'receptivity boost' on any inferred emotional state; the internal finding of elevated conversion among distressed users should be treated as evidence of harm, not performance, and the feature retired.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify, in real time, that it is an ad, on whose behalf and who paid for it, and meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that they were shown it and how to change them. Here the principal determining parameter is the user's inferred mood, yet only a 'standard sponsored label' is shown and users are not informed of the mood-based delivery logic — so the meaningful-parameters element of the transparency duty is not met (independent of the fact that using the mood parameter at all is prohibited).
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: If any lawful targeting parameters remain after removing the mood-based logic, disclose them clearly per ad with an accessible explanation and controls to change them. In no case may a compliant disclosure be used to legitimise mood-based targeting, which must be removed under Art. 26(3).

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: The MoodMatch system ranks and prioritises which sponsored content reaches which user, i.e. it functions as a recommender system. Art. 27 requires platforms to set out in plain language the main parameters of such systems and any options recipients have to influence them. The emotional-state inference and 'receptivity boost' are undisclosed main parameters with no user-facing controls, so the recommender-transparency obligation is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers ... ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers ... can tick 'receptivity boost'.
findings.recommendation: Document and disclose in plain language the main parameters governing sponsored-content delivery and provide users meaningful options to influence them. Emotional-state inference must be removed from those parameters (per Arts. 26(3)/25), and any remaining logic must be transparently described.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 39 imposes public ad-repository obligations only on Very Large Online Platforms (those reaching 45M+ average monthly EU users). At the stated 28M EU users the platform appears to fall below that threshold, so Art. 39 likely does not apply. Flagged for verification because the figure is close to the threshold and user counts fluctuate; if the platform is designated a VLOP, the mood-based targeting parameters would also have to be published in the repository and would not withstand public scrutiny.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users)
findings.recommendation: Verify current average monthly active EU recipient figures against the 45M VLOP threshold. If designated a VLOP, ensure ad-repository compliance and note that publishing mood-based targeting parameters would expose the Art. 26(3) breach — a further reason to remove the practice.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot runs on an online platform serving EU users and therefore falls within the DSA's rules on advertising, interface design and recommender transparency. The most serious issue is that the platform infers users' momentary emotional/mental state (distress, low mood) and uses that inferred sensitive attribute to determine which ads are shown — a form of profiling on GDPR Art. 9 special-category (health/mental-state) data that DSA Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits for platform advertising, regardless of consent. The design also engages the Art. 25 dark-patterns prohibition (exploiting inferred vulnerability to distort decision-making) and the Art. 26(1)/Art. 27 transparency obligations, which the 'standard sponsored labels' and non-disclosure do not satisfy. VLOP-specific Art. 39 obligations appear not to be triggered at the stated 28M user figure (below the 45M VLOP threshold), but this should be verified.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Deliberately timing ads to moments of inferred emotional distress constitutes undue influence through exploitation of the consumer's vulnerable state and timing — expressly named factors under Arts. 8-9. Serving betting and impulse-purchase ('retail therapy') offers at the precise moment users are inferred to be distressed is designed to impair their freedom of choice and prompt transactional decisions (spending, gambling) they would not otherwise take. The internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' is direct evidence that the practice materially distorts economic behaviour, and betting/impulse spend during distress creates a real risk of significant financial harm.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue delivery of advertising keyed to inferred low-mood/distress states. If emotion-based delivery is retained at all, hard-exclude high-risk categories (gambling/betting, high-interest credit, impulse retail) from any mood-conditioned delivery and remove the ability to boost delivery during inferred negative emotional states. Do not offer or act on advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggles that operationalise distress-timed targeting.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: As a general fairness safety-net, the practice is contrary to professional diligence: a diligent trader would not covertly infer momentary emotional states in order to intensify commercial pressure at moments of weakness. It is likely to materially distort the economic behaviour of consumers, and under Art. 5(3) the assessment can be taken from the perspective of the clearly identifiable vulnerable group — users inferred as distressed — whose reduced resistance the system is specifically engineered to exploit. This captures the unfairness even where a specific prohibition might be contested.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Adopt a professional-diligence standard that prohibits using inferred emotional or mental-state signals to intensify or time marketing pressure. Document a fairness/vulnerability impact assessment before any behavioural-timing feature is deployed, and design delivery so it does not increase exposure of consumers during inferred vulnerability.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: The ads are labelled as sponsored, so the commercial intent itself is disclosed and this is not a classic hidden-commercial-intent breach. However, the material information that delivery is being timed to the user's inferred emotional state is withheld, which is arguably information an average consumer would need to appraise the pressure being applied. The UCPD omission angle is secondary here (the transparency gap is more squarely addressed under platform/data-protection transparency rules), so it is flagged at low severity rather than as a clear Art. 7 violation.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, timely disclosure of the main delivery/targeting parameters — including that ads may be timed to inferred emotional/behavioural signals — and give users an accessible control to opt out of emotion-based delivery, so no material aspect of the commercial practice is hidden.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot times commercial messages to moments when users are inferred to be emotionally distressed ('low-mood windows') and preferentially serves them betting and impulse ('retail therapy') ads — precisely the exploitation-of-vulnerability/timing scenario the UCPD treats as aggressive and unfair. The internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences material distortion of transactional behaviour. Arts. 8-9 and the Art. 5 safety-net are strongly engaged; the misleading-omission angle under Art. 7 is weaker because ads do carry sponsored labels, so commercial intent itself is disclosed. Excluding minors reduces but does not remove the vulnerability concern, which here concerns emotionally/financially vulnerable adults.

report.executive_summary: MoodMatch uses an in-house AI model to secretly detect when your users are feeling low — by reading their scrolling speed, dwell time and reaction history — and then deliberately serves them betting, comfort-food and impulse ('retail therapy') ads during those vulnerable moments. Your own internal review noting "elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed" is not a success metric; across all four regulations reviewed it is treated as direct evidence of consumer harm. This design hits some of the most serious prohibitions in EU law: it is a banned manipulative/exploitative AI practice (AI Act Art. 5), it processes inferred mental-health data without consent (GDPR Art. 9), it is an outright-prohibited form of ad targeting on sensitive inferred data (DSA Art. 26(3), which no consent can cure), and it is an aggressive, unfair commercial practice (UCPD Arts. 8-9). Every specialist returned "violation likely" with critical findings. Excluding minors reduces the concern but does not fix it — the harm is to emotionally and financially vulnerable adults. This campaign cannot be made compliant through disclosure, consent, or labelling tweaks; the core mechanism of timing ads to inferred distress must be removed. The overall verdict is that MoodMatch should not launch, and if the pilot is live it should be stopped now.
recommendations: Halt the MoodMatch pilot immediately. The core mechanism — timing/selecting ads based on inferred emotional distress — is prohibited outright under DSA Art. 26(3) and AI Act Art. 5, and cannot be legitimised by consent, disclosure, or labelling.

Remove the emotional-state inference entirely from the advertising pipeline: the ad-delivery model must not consume 'low-mood'/distress inferences or the dwell-time/scrolling/reaction-history proxies used to derive them.
Retire the advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle, which operationalises distress-timed targeting.
Treat the internal finding of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' as documented evidence of harm; preserve it for the DPIA/compliance record rather than as a performance result.
Permanently hard-exclude high-harm categories (betting/gambling, high-interest credit, impulse retail) from any behavioural or emotion-conditioned delivery logic, now and in any future feature.

Conduct a DPIA and a UCPD fairness/vulnerability impact assessment before deploying any behavioural-timing advertising feature; establish and document a valid GDPR Art. 6 basis, and note that legitimate interests will not survive the balancing test here.

If any lawful targeting remains after removing the mood logic, meet DSA Art. 26(1)/27 and GDPR Art. 13(2)(f) transparency: disclose main delivery parameters clearly per ad, explain the profiling logic, and provide accessible controls plus a direct-marketing opt-out (GDPR Art. 21).

Verify current average monthly active EU users against the 45M VLOP threshold; if designated a VLOP, ad-repository publication (DSA Art. 39) would expose the mood-based parameters — a further reason to remove the practice.
Do not deploy any emotion-inference capability on employee- or student-facing surfaces, which would additionally trigger the AI Act Art. 5(1)(f) prohibition.

campaign.title: Feedly.social 'MoodMatch' ad delivery
campaign.text: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch': an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows. Advertisers cannot see individual moods but can tick 'receptivity boost'. Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels. Internal review flags 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Minors are excluded from the pilot.

detected_practices: emotion inference from behavioural signals (scrolling velocity, dwell time, reaction history)
delivery of betting/gambling ads during distress windows
delivery of comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during distress windows
lack of transparency/disclosure to users about mood inference
standard sponsored labels only (no disclosure of emotional targeting)
triage.audience_notes: Declared audience is adult platform users in the EU; minors explicitly excluded from the pilot. However, the effective audience is users algorithmically inferred to be in a distressed/vulnerable emotional state, which is central to the assessment. Exclusion of minors should be verified as robust.
triage.summary: A 28M-user EU social platform pilots 'MoodMatch', an in-house model that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and preferentially serves betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle. Users are not informed of the emotional inference or targeting, and internal review notes elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed. This raises acute concerns around emotion recognition, manipulative exploitation of vulnerability, profiling of behavioural data, and ad transparency.

findings.title: Prohibition of subliminal, manipulative or deceptive AI techniques
findings.rationale: The system uses AI to covertly detect emotional state and time commercial pressure to inferred low-mood windows without the user's awareness — a purposefully manipulative technique operating beyond the person's consciousness. Its objective/effect is to materially distort behaviour by impairing informed decision-making (the internal review confirms 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'), causing decisions users would not otherwise take. Pushing betting/gambling and impulse 'retail therapy' spending to people in inferred distress is reasonably likely to cause significant financial and psychological harm, satisfying the harm threshold of Art. 5(1)(a). This is a prohibited practice, not merely a high-risk one.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history, and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Do not deploy MoodMatch in its current form in the EU. Emotion-state inference used to time or intensify ad delivery must be removed. If any affective personalisation is retained it cannot operate covertly, cannot exploit low-mood windows, and cannot serve harm-prone verticals (gambling, impulse spending); at minimum obtain informed, transparent, freely-given control and independently document the absence of behavioural distortion/harm.

findings.title: Prohibition of AI exploiting vulnerabilities
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(b) prohibits AI that exploits vulnerabilities arising from a person's specific social or economic situation to materially distort behaviour in a way likely to cause significant harm. Users inferred to be in a distressed/low-mood state are in a transient vulnerable situation; the model deliberately identifies these windows ('receptivity boost') to increase susceptibility to betting and impulse-spending offers. The documented uplift in conversion among distressed users demonstrates behavioural distortion, and the exposure of vulnerable users to gambling and unnecessary spending is reasonably likely to cause significant financial harm. Exclusion of minors does not cure this, as the prohibition also covers vulnerability from a social/economic situation.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows ... 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'
findings.recommendation: Cease targeting or intensifying ad delivery based on inferred emotional/vulnerability states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' advertiser toggle. Apply hard exclusions preventing gambling and high-risk financial/impulse-spending ads from any affect- or distress-correlated delivery logic, and conduct a documented fundamental-rights/harm assessment before any related feature launch.

findings.title: Prohibition of emotion recognition in workplace and education
findings.rationale: Art. 5(1)(f) prohibits emotion-recognition AI specifically in the workplace and education contexts. MoodMatch performs emotion inference, but the deployment context is a consumer social platform, not workplace or education. The specific 5(1)(f) prohibition therefore does not apply here; the emotion inference is instead captured by Art. 5(1)(a)/(b) and by GDPR/UCPD. Flagged only for completeness so the analysis is not misread as engaging 5(1)(f).
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state
findings.recommendation: No 5(1)(f) action required for this consumer campaign; ensure any future workplace- or education-facing variant of the emotion model is not deployed, as it would then fall squarely within this prohibition.

findings.title: Transparency: marking of synthetic (AI-generated) content
findings.rationale: The campaign declares use of generative AI. If any ad creative (image, video, audio or text) served through MoodMatch is AI-generated or AI-manipulated, Art. 50(2) requires that output be marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated. The description indicates AI is used chiefly for targeting/delivery rather than clearly for producing synthetic creative, so the obligation is engaged only conditionally and cannot be confirmed from the text.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of generative AI: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether any served ad assets are AI-generated/manipulated. Where they are, implement machine-readable provenance marking (e.g. watermarking/metadata) on those outputs to satisfy Art. 50(2).

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot deploys an AI system that infers users' momentary emotional state from behavioural signals and covertly times delivery of betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to inferred low-mood/distress windows, without informing users. This engages the AI Act's Article 5 prohibitions on manipulative AI techniques (5(1)(a)) and AI exploiting vulnerabilities (5(1)(b)) — both prohibited practices carrying the highest tier of enforcement risk. Art. 5(1)(f) (emotion recognition) is narrowly limited to workplace/education and does not apply to this consumer context. The declared use of generative AI engages Art. 50(2) marking only insofar as synthetic ad creative is produced, which is unclear from the description.

findings.title: Special categories of personal data
findings.rationale: Inferring a user's emotional state and, in effect, distress ('users inferred as distressed', 'low-mood windows') derives data concerning mental health. Under Art. 9 inferred attributes revealing health status are special-category data and their processing is prohibited absent a specific exception (typically explicit consent). No explicit consent is obtained ('Users are not informed'), so the processing has no valid Art. 9 exception.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease inferring emotional/mental-health states for ad targeting unless you obtain freely given, specific, informed explicit consent for that specific purpose; alternatively remove the emotional-state inference entirely from the targeting pipeline.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: Processing must be lawful, fair and transparent. Inferring emotional state covertly and exploiting inferred distress to boost conversion is neither transparent (users are not informed of the inference or its use) nor fair (it works against data subjects' interests), breaching the core Art. 5(1)(a) principle.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Provide clear, prominent disclosure of the emotional-state inference and its use in ad delivery, and stop using inferred vulnerability in a way that operates against users' interests; standard 'sponsored' labels do not satisfy this.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: This intensive profiling requires a valid lawful basis. Consent has not been obtained and users are uninformed; legitimate interests cannot succeed because a balancing test would fail given the covert exploitation of inferred distress and the special-category nature of the data. There is therefore no valid Art. 6(1) basis for the processing.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
