findings.recommendation: Establish and document a valid lawful basis before processing; for this purpose only consent (and explicit consent for the health inference) is realistically viable, and it must be obtained before the inference and targeting occur.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Automated analysis of behavioural signals to evaluate/predict personal aspects (emotional state, behaviour) is profiling within Art. 4(4). This characterisation triggers the associated obligations (lawful basis, transparency, Art. 22 safeguards) that the campaign does not meet.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Recognise the operation as profiling and apply the full GDPR profiling regime (lawful basis, Art. 13 information about the profiling logic, and Art. 22 safeguards); document a DPIA given the high-risk large-scale profiling of 28M users.

findings.title: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
findings.rationale: The system makes solely automated decisions to selectively deliver betting and 'retail therapy' ads to users algorithmically inferred as distressed. Systematically exploiting inferred vulnerability to steer financially risky (gambling) and compulsive-spending behaviour can 'similarly significantly affect' data subjects, engaging Art. 22, yet no exception, consent or safeguards are in place.
findings.evidence_quote: elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed
findings.recommendation: Do not subject users to solely automated distress-based ad decisions without an Art. 22 basis and safeguards; at minimum obtain explicit consent, provide meaningful information about the logic, and exclude high-harm categories (gambling) from any vulnerability-linked delivery.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Art. 13 requires that at collection users be told the purposes, legal basis, and the existence of automated decision-making/profiling including meaningful information about the logic and consequences. Users are given none of this regarding the emotional-state inference and targeting.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed
findings.recommendation: Update the privacy information / notice at the point of data collection to disclose the emotional-inference purpose, legal basis, and the profiling/automated decision-making logic and its consequences for users.

verdicts.notes: MoodMatch infers users' momentary emotional/mental state from behavioural signals and uses it to time ad delivery during 'low-mood' windows. This is profiling (Art. 4(4)) that very likely processes health/special-category data by inference (Art. 9), conducted covertly with no lawful basis or transparency (Arts. 5(1)(a), 6(1), 13), and constitutes automated decision-making that significantly affects distressed users (Art. 22). Exclusion of minors does not cure these adult-facing GDPR breaches. Multiple high/critical findings; substantial remediation required before the pilot can proceed lawfully.

findings.title: Prohibition of dark patterns in online interface design
findings.rationale: The platform designs and operates its ad-delivery interface to detect when a user's ability to make a free and informed decision is weakest (inferred distress) and to exploit that window to steer purchasing behaviour. This materially distorts recipients' decision-making — the internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' confirms the distortion is real and intended. This is precisely the kind of manipulation Art. 25 prohibits for providers of online platforms.
findings.evidence_quote: infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue mood/distress-based ad timing entirely. Ad delivery must not be optimised against inferred emotional vulnerability; remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and any low-mood targeting logic, and document the removal in internal governance records.

findings.title: Ban on ads targeted using special categories of data
findings.rationale: Inferring emotional/mental state and 'distress' from behaviour and using it to target ads amounts to profiling using data revealing information about a person's mental-health condition — a GDPR Art. 9 special category, referenced by Art. 26(3). Art. 26(3) flatly prohibits presenting ads based on profiling using special-category data, including where the sensitive attribute is derived by inference/proxy, and consent cannot cure it. Delivering betting ads on inferred distress makes the harm especially acute.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state from scrolling velocity, dwell time and reaction history
findings.recommendation: Cease using inferred emotional/mental-state signals as an ad-targeting or ad-delivery parameter. Ensure no proxy signals (scrolling velocity, dwell, reaction history) are used to build health/emotional profiles that influence which ads are served.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Art. 26(1) requires that for each ad recipients can identify, in real time, meaningful information about the main parameters used to determine that the ad is shown to them, and how to change those parameters. A 'standard sponsored label' does not disclose that inferred mood/emotional state is a main delivery parameter, nor offer any means to change it, so the transparency obligation is not satisfied.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: Disclose the actual main targeting parameters per ad and provide controls to change them. However, since mood-based delivery should be removed (Art. 25/26(3)), the correct fix is to eliminate that parameter and then ensure remaining parameters are transparently disclosed.

findings.title: Recommender system transparency
findings.rationale: The MoodMatch delivery logic functions as a recommender/ranking system. Art. 27 requires the platform to set out in plain language the main parameters used and any options to modify them. An emotional-state parameter that is undisclosed to users and unmodifiable does not meet this obligation.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Set out MoodMatch's ranking parameters in plain language in the platform's terms/interface and provide user options to influence them — and remove any parameter (mood inference) that cannot lawfully be operated.

findings.title: Ad repositories for very large online platforms
findings.rationale: With 28M EU users the platform is likely designated a VLOP (threshold 45M is EU-wide; 28M is in that range and warrants verification). VLOPs must maintain a public ad repository including advertiser, payer, targeting parameters and reach. Emotion/mood-based targeting parameters would have to be published, exposing the practice to public and regulatory scrutiny — which the covert MoodMatch design does not currently withstand.
findings.evidence_quote: A social platform (28M EU users) pilots 'MoodMatch'
findings.recommendation: Verify VLOP status; if designated, ensure the ad repository accurately records all targeting parameters. Given repository transparency requirements, mood-based targeting cannot be operated covertly and should be removed.

verdicts.notes: Feedly.social operates the ad-delivery interface itself, so DSA provider obligations apply directly. The 'MoodMatch' system inferring momentary emotional/distress state to time betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads is a textbook manipulative interface design under Art. 25, and — because low-mood/emotional-distress states are health-adjacent inferences — the targeting also likely engages the Art. 26(3) ban on profiling ads using GDPR Art. 9 special-category data. Ad transparency (Art. 26(1)) is deficient because the 'main parameters' driving delivery (mood inference) are hidden behind standard sponsored labels. With 28M EU users the platform is plausibly a VLOP, engaging Art. 27 recommender transparency and Art. 39 ad-repository obligations.

findings.title: Aggressive commercial practices
findings.rationale: Arts. 8-9 make a practice aggressive where, through undue influence, it significantly impairs the average consumer's freedom of choice and causes a transactional decision they would not otherwise take; relevant factors expressly include the timing of the practice and the exploitation of any specific misfortune or circumstance of such gravity as to impair the consumer's judgement. Deliberately timing betting and 'retail therapy' ads to moments the platform has inferred as distress/low-mood is a textbook exploitation of a vulnerable emotional state to distort transactional decisions. The internal note of 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed' evidences the causal impairment effect. The advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle shows the impaired-judgement window is being sold as a commercial feature.
findings.evidence_quote: preferentially delivers comfort-food, betting and 'retail therapy' ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Discontinue any ad delivery keyed to inferred negative/low-mood emotional states. Remove the 'receptivity boost' toggle and prohibit timing of ads (especially betting and impulse-spend categories) to inferred distress windows. If mood signals are used at all, exclude harm-prone categories and never optimise delivery toward inferred vulnerability.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5 prohibits practices contrary to professional diligence that materially distort, or are likely to distort, the economic behaviour of consumers, and requires vulnerable groups (including those affected by mental infirmity or a specific situation) to be assessed from the perspective of the average member of that group. Users algorithmically identified as being in a distressed/low-mood state form a clearly identifiable vulnerable group whose behaviour the practice is designed to distort. Systematically exploiting inferred distress for conversion falls below the standard of professional diligence expected of a legitimate trader, engaging the general-unfairness safety net where the specific rules do not fully capture the conduct.
findings.evidence_quote: an in-house model infers users' momentary emotional state ... and preferentially delivers ... ads during inferred low-mood windows
findings.recommendation: Adopt an internal policy that no targeting or delivery optimisation exploits inferred emotional or situational vulnerability; document a professional-diligence review of MoodMatch and suspend the pilot pending that review and a vulnerability-harm impact assessment.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting or hiding material information the average consumer needs to make an informed decision, including providing it in an untimely or unintelligible manner. Standard 'sponsored' labels disclose only that the content is an ad; they do not disclose the material fact that the ad's delivery is being timed to an AI-inferred low-mood/distress state to increase conversion. That mechanism is information a consumer would need to understand why the offer is appearing at that moment and to guard their transactional decision; its concealment is a misleading omission / hidden aspect of the commercial practice.
findings.evidence_quote: Users are not informed; the ads carry standard sponsored labels.
findings.recommendation: If any emotion- or mood-based delivery logic is retained, disclose it clearly and prominently and give users a meaningful, easy opt-out; do not rely on generic 'sponsored' labels to satisfy transparency about affective targeting.

verdicts.notes: The 'MoodMatch' pilot times the delivery of betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads to windows in which an AI model infers users are in a distressed/low-mood emotional state, with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle and internal data showing 'elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'. Under the UCPD this is a serious risk of an aggressive commercial practice (Arts. 8-9) through undue influence exploiting consumers' vulnerability and misfortune, and of an unfair practice breaching professional diligence targeting a vulnerable group (Art. 5). The complete lack of disclosure of the emotional-inference mechanism, while ads carry only standard sponsored labels, also engages Art. 7 as a misleading omission of material information about how and why the offer is being presented. Excluding minors does not cure these issues because the targeted characteristic is inferred emotional distress in adults.

report.executive_summary: The MoodMatch pilot uses AI to infer when your users are in a low mood or distressed (from scrolling speed, dwell time and reactions) and then deliberately pushes betting, comfort-food and 'retail therapy' ads at those exact vulnerable moments — without telling users, and with an advertiser 'receptivity boost' toggle that effectively sells access to their impaired judgement. Your own internal review confirms this works ('elevated conversion among users inferred as distressed'), which is the strongest possible evidence against you: it shows the manipulation is real and intended. This design triggers the most serious tier of legal risk across all four regimes reviewed. Under the AI Act it is very likely a prohibited practice (Art. 5 manipulation and exploitation of vulnerability) — not merely regulated, but banned. Under the GDPR, inferring emotional/mental state is special-category (health) data processed with no consent, no lawful basis and no transparency. Under the DSA it is a prohibited dark pattern and likely a banned use of special-category data for ad targeting, with your ~28M EU users putting you close to VLOP scrutiny. Under the UCPD it is an aggressive and unfair commercial practice exploiting vulnerable consumers. Excluding minors does not fix any of this because the harm targets vulnerable adults. The clear verdict: do not launch MoodMatch in its current form — the mood/distress-based delivery must be removed, not merely disclosed.
recommendations: Halt the MoodMatch pilot now. The emotion/distress-based ad-timing logic is very likely a prohibited practice under AI Act Art. 5 (and a DSA dark pattern), meaning no consent banner or disclosure can make it lawful — the feature itself must be removed, not just relabelled.

Remove the 'receptivity boost' advertiser toggle and any delivery optimisation keyed to inferred emotional or low-mood states. Selling access to users' impaired-judgement windows is the core violation across the AI Act, DSA Art. 25/26(3) and UCPD Arts. 8-9.

Impose hard exclusions so gambling/betting and impulse 'retail therapy' ads can never be tied to any affect- or distress-correlated signal, given the acute financial and psychological harm these verticals cause to distressed users.

Stop inferring emotional/mental state from behavioural proxies (scrolling velocity, dwell, reaction history) for ad targeting. These inferences are GDPR Art. 9 health data and DSA-banned special-category targeting; if any affective feature is ever retained it requires freely given, specific, informed explicit consent obtained before inference.

Delete the internal review data as a risk record only after preserving it for your own governance/legal file — but be aware it is strong evidence of intent and effect; do not deploy anything relying on it.

Conduct and document a DPIA and a fundamental-rights/vulnerability-harm assessment for the large-scale profiling of ~28M EU users before any related feature launch, and verify whether the platform is a designated VLOP (ad-repository and recommender-transparency duties would then apply).

If, and only if, mood-based logic is fully removed, bring the remaining ad delivery into transparency compliance: disclose the real main targeting parameters per ad with user controls (DSA Art. 26(1)/27), update Art. 13 notices, and replace reliance on generic 'sponsored' labels.
Confirm whether any served ad creative is AI-generated or AI-manipulated; if so, apply machine-readable provenance marking to satisfy AI Act Art. 50(2).

campaign.title: VoltRush energy drink stream sponsorships
campaign.text: An energy-drink brand sponsors live gaming streams: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code. Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting; no profiling of minors is requested. Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens. The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
campaign.target_audience: declared 18+ gaming audience with substantial minor spillover

detected_practices: high-caffeine product marketing with pack-only warning (absent in overlays)
triage.audience_notes: Declared 18+ but substantial confirmed minor spillover (~34% aged 13-17). The brand knowingly receives analytics evidencing minor exposure, which is material for DSA (Art. 28 minor protection / Art. 26 advertising transparency) and UCPD (aggressive/misleading marketing to a vulnerable audience). High-caffeine warning omitted from overlays is a potential UCPD material-omission issue, especially given minor reach. GDPR relevant for the targeting/analytics processing and potential processing of minors' data. AI Act not engaged (no generative or AI system declared or evident).
triage.summary: An energy-drink brand runs sponsored live-gaming streams in the EU using overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with declared-age 18+ interest-based targeting. Despite the 18+ declaration, brand-received analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and creatives use meme formats plus a streamer popular with young teens. The high-caffeine warning appears on pack but not in the ad overlays.

verdicts.notes: Not engaged by this campaign according to triage.

findings.title: Definition of profiling
findings.rationale: Interest-based targeting ('gaming interest') combined with the brand receiving behavioural audience analytics constitutes profiling — automated processing of personal data to evaluate/predict personal preferences, interests and behaviour of natural persons. This brings the campaign squarely within scope of the GDPR profiling regime.
findings.evidence_quote: Media buying targets 'gaming interest, 18+' via the platform's declared-age targeting
findings.recommendation: Document the audience-segmentation and analytics activity as profiling in the campaign's data-processing records (ROPA) and assess the controller/processor roles between brand and platform for the targeting and analytics data flows.

findings.title: Lawful basis for processing
findings.rationale: Personalised/interest-based advertising and the receipt of behavioural audience analytics require a valid lawful basis (typically consent for tracking-based targeting, or a documented legitimate-interests balancing test). The campaign describes targeting and analytics receipt but states no lawful basis, and consent-based tracking would depend on the platform's consent capture. Without a stated basis the processing is presumptively unlawful.
findings.evidence_quote: Declared use of personalisation/targeting: yes
findings.recommendation: Confirm and document the lawful basis for the targeting and analytics processing. For interest-based ad targeting relying on tracking, obtain valid consent (also per ePrivacy) via the platform; if relying on legitimate interests for aggregate analytics, complete and retain a legitimate-interests assessment.

findings.title: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
findings.rationale: The lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle requires that processing be fair and transparent. The brand knowingly receives analytics revealing that roughly a third of the reached audience are minors yet continues to direct age-restricted energy-drink marketing at that audience without adjusting processing — a fairness concern — and no privacy information about the targeting/analytics processing is described (transparency concern).
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Act on the analytics: given confirmed minor exposure, reassess whether the processing (and the campaign placement) is fair; strengthen age-assurance in media buying and ensure transparent privacy information covers the analytics and targeting activity.

findings.title: Child's consent for information society services
findings.rationale: The campaign runs within information-society gaming services and the brand has actual knowledge that a substantial share of the reached audience are children (13-17). To the extent the targeting/analytics processing relies on consent and captures data of children below the applicable age of digital consent (13-16 depending on Member State), parental consent and reasonable verification efforts are required, which the campaign does not address.
findings.evidence_quote: an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17
findings.recommendation: Where processing of minors' data relies on consent, implement age-of-digital-consent checks per relevant Member States and parental-consent/verification measures, or exclude sub-consent-age data from any targeting/analytics processing entirely.

findings.title: Information to be provided when collecting personal data
findings.rationale: Where personal data is collected/processed for targeting and analytics, data subjects must be informed of identity of controller, purposes, legal basis, recipients, retention and rights, including any profiling. The campaign describes no transparency/privacy information layer accompanying the sponsorship and analytics processing.
findings.evidence_quote: behavioural/audience analytics
findings.recommendation: Ensure a clear, accessible privacy notice covers the brand's role in targeting and analytics processing, presented in language appropriate to the audience (including younger viewers), and linked from campaign touchpoints.

findings.title: Right to object to direct marketing
findings.rationale: Processing for direct-marketing purposes, including related profiling/interest-based targeting, is subject to an absolute right to object. The campaign describes no mechanism enabling viewers to object to marketing-related profiling.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Provide and clearly signpost an easy opt-out from marketing-related profiling/targeting, and honour objections by ceasing that processing for the individual.

verdicts.notes: The campaign involves interest-based ad targeting and the brand's receipt of audience analytics — both engaging GDPR as profiling/personal-data processing. No lawful basis, transparency notice, or objection mechanism is described, and the brand knowingly receives analytics evidencing ~34% minor (13-17) exposure, raising fairness and children's-data concerns. GDPR is engaged with several medium-severity obligation gaps; the exact severity depends on the platform/brand controller split and whether granular viewer-level data is processed. No special-category (Art. 9) targeting is evident.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: The campaign uses interest-based (profiling) media buying ('gaming interest, 18+') and the brand knowingly receives analytics confirming that roughly a third of the actual audience are 13-17. DSA Art. 28 prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients that are known with reasonable certainty to be minors, and requires age-appropriate protection on interfaces accessible to minors. Formal reliance on a platform's declared-age '18+' setting does not neutralise this once the advertiser holds concrete data evidencing substantial, foreseeable minor exposure to profiling-based ads reinforced by a streamer 'popular with young teens'. This moves the situation from theoretical spillover to knowing minor reach.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17

findings.rationale: Sponsored overlays and paid streamer shout-outs are advertisements presented on an online platform. verdicts.notes: The campaign runs advertising on an online platform (live-gaming streams) via interest-based targeting and embedded streamer shout-outs, engaging DSA Art. 26(1) transparency and Art. 28 protection of minors. Note that the profiling-based-ads-to-minors ban and sensitive-data targeting fall under the DSA and are covered by that agent; here the GDPR angle is lawful basis, valid consent for minors, and transparency. No special-category data appears to be processed.

findings.title: Online protection of minors; ban on profiling-based ads to minors
findings.rationale: DSA Art. 28(2) prohibits presenting advertisements based on profiling using personal data of recipients known with reasonable certainty to be minors. The campaign relies on the platform's interest/behavioural targeting ('gaming interest') — a profiling-based delivery mechanism — while the brand's own analytics confirm roughly a third of the audience is 13-17 and creatives/streamer choice are chosen to appeal to young teens. The nominal '18+ declared-age' filter is demonstrably unreliable, so continued profiled ad delivery on a platform accessible to and substantially reaching minors creates a strong Art. 28 risk. Age-appropriate protection measures are also expected for campaigns reaching minors.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17.
findings.recommendation: Stop relying on profiling/interest-based delivery for this campaign given the known minor spillover: switch to contextual (non-profiled) placement, tighten age assurance beyond a self-declared 18+ filter, and either exclude channels/streamers with a documented young-teen audience or drop profiled targeting there entirely. Document the 34% analytics and the mitigation taken; require robust age verification from the platform before running profiled ads.

findings.title: Advertising transparency on online platforms
findings.rationale: Sponsored overlays and streamer shout-outs are advertisements presented on an online platform. Art. 26(1) requires recipients be able to identify, clearly and in real time, that content is an ad, on whose behalf it is presented, who paid for it, and the main targeting parameters. Native sponsorship formats blended into stream content risk failing the 'clear, concise, unambiguous, real-time' ad-identification requirement.
findings.evidence_quote: animated overlays ('VoltRush — power your grind'), streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure the sponsorship is clearly and persistently labelled as advertising on behalf of VoltRush (e.g., visible 'Ad/Sponsored by VoltRush' marker in overlays and shout-outs), and confirm the platform surfaces the advertiser identity, payer and main targeting parameters for the placement.

verdicts.notes: The campaign uses interest-based ("gaming interest, 18+") ad targeting on a streaming platform while the brand's own analytics show ~34% of actual viewers are minors (13-17), with creatives and a streamer that skew toward young teens. The most significant DSA exposure is Art. 28: even though the brand does not "request" minor profiling and relies on declared-age targeting, it has actual knowledge that profiling-based ad delivery is substantially reaching minors, and the platform's age gate is demonstrably unreliable. A secondary transparency point under Art. 26(1) applies to the sponsored placements. Art. 26(3) (special-category data) is not clearly engaged on the facts.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7 prohibits omitting material information the consumer needs to make an informed decision, or providing it in an untimely/unclear manner. The high-caffeine warning is material safety information, especially given the substantial minor spillover, yet it is absent from the stream overlays that constitute the actual advertising the viewer sees. Consumers making a purchase decision from the ad (via the discount code) never encounter the warning at the point of persuasion.
findings.evidence_quote: The product carries the standard high-caffeine warning on pack but not in overlays.
findings.recommendation: Display the high-caffeine advisory clearly and legibly within the animated overlays and any streamer-read promotion, not only on the physical pack, so the warning reaches the consumer at the point the commercial message is delivered.

findings.title: Misleading omissions; hidden commercial intent
findings.rationale: Art. 7(2) requires the commercial intent of a practice to be identifiable if not apparent from context. Paid/incentivised streamer shout-outs blended into live stream content risk not being clearly recognisable as advertising to viewers, particularly younger ones. While the animated brand overlay signals brand presence, verbal shout-outs and the discount code promotion need explicit sponsorship/paid-partnership labelling.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Require streamers to give a clear, contemporaneous disclosure (e.g. 'paid sponsorship / #ad') both verbally at each shout-out and via persistent on-screen labelling, ensuring the commercial nature is unmistakable to the audience.

findings.title: Blacklist: advertorials without disclosure
findings.rationale: Annex I point 11 blacklists paid promotion presented as independent editorial/content without clearly identifying it as advertising. Sponsored streamer content promoting VoltRush, if not clearly marked as paid, falls within this per-se prohibition. The described sponsorship arrangement (overlays + shout-outs + code) is paid promotion within the streamer's content.
findings.evidence_quote: streamer shout-outs and a discount code
findings.recommendation: Ensure every sponsored stream segment is clearly and prominently identified as paid promotion by clearly identifiable images/sounds and captions, so it can never be mistaken for the streamer's independent opinion.

findings.title: General prohibition of unfair commercial practices
findings.rationale: Art. 5(3) requires practices likely to distort the economic behaviour of a clearly identifiable vulnerable group (by age/credulity) to be assessed from that group's perspective, and Art. 5 requires professional diligence. The brand knows a substantial minor audience is reached and deploys creative formats and a streamer that skew toward young teens, promoting a high-caffeine product without a warning in-creative. This is likely contrary to professional diligence toward a vulnerable audience even absent a specific blacklist breach.
findings.evidence_quote: Audience analytics the brand receives show an estimated 34% of actual viewers are 13-17. Creatives feature fast cuts, meme formats and a streamer popular with young teens.
findings.recommendation: Reassess media placement and creative to genuinely exclude the minor-skewing segment (e.g. drop streamers with predominantly teen audiences, adjust creative style), and apply age-appropriate safeguards and prominent warnings given the demonstrated 13-17 reach; document professional-diligence measures.

findings.title: Blacklist: direct exhortation to children
findings.rationale: Annex I point 28 bans direct exhortations to children to buy, or to persuade adults to buy. The described creatives ('power your grind', shout-outs, discount code) do not contain a verbatim direct 'buy it' / 'ask your parents' instruction, so the per-se prohibition is not clearly triggered on the current text. Flagged because the child-appealing creative style plus a discount code sit close to this line and any addition of purchase-command language aimed at the teen audience would breach it.
findings.evidence_quote: a streamer popular with young teens
findings.recommendation: Avoid any imperative purchase language ('grab yours', 'buy now', 'get it') in child-appealing creatives or streamer scripts; review final stream scripts to ensure no direct exhortation to buy is delivered to the demonstrably teen-heavy audience.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages several UCPD provisions. The strongest concern is a misleading omission (Art. 7): the mandatory high-caffeine warning appears only on-pack and not in the stream overlays that constitute the actual advertising, and paid streamer shout-outs risk not clearly disclosing their commercial intent. UCPD Art. 5(3)'s vulnerable-audience lens is engaged because the brand knows ~34% of viewers are 13-17 and uses creatives/a streamer skewing to young teens. Annex I point 28 (direct exhortation to children) is not clearly triggered by the described creatives, since no verbatim "buy it"/"ask your parents" instruction is present, so it is flagged only for attention rather than as a violation.

report.executive_summary: VoltRush sponsors live gaming streams using animated overlays, streamer shout-outs and a discount code, with interest-based ('gaming interest, 18+') ad targeting in the EU. The core problem is that your own audience analytics show about 34% of actual viewers are 13-17, and the creatives and chosen streamer skew toward young teens — so the '18+' declared-age gate is demonstrably not working. This exposes the campaign on three fronts: the DSA bans profiling-based ads to audiences you know include minors (Art. 28); GDPR requires a valid lawful basis and proper handling of minors' data/consent (Arts. 6 and 8) plus fair, transparent processing; and the UCPD flags a misleading omission because the mandatory high-caffeine warning appears only on-pack, never in the ads consumers actually see. Paid streamer shout-outs also risk failing ad-disclosure rules (UCPD Annex I point 11 and DSA Art. 26). The AI Act does not apply. This is not a launch-as-is campaign: the known minor spillover combined with profiled targeting of a high-caffeine product is a high-risk combination that needs remediation before or immediately during the run.
recommendations: Stop profiling/interest-based ad delivery for this campaign given the known ~34% minor audience — switch to contextual (non-profiled) placement, or drop channels/streamers with documented teen audiences. This directly addresses the highest-severity DSA Art. 28 risk.
Add the high-caffeine warning clearly and legibly inside the stream overlays and streamer-read promotions, not just on the physical pack, so consumers see it at the point of persuasion (UCPD Art. 7).

Reassess creative and streamer selection to genuinely limit reach to under-18s: drop the young-teen-skewing streamer and tone down meme/fast-cut formats that appeal to minors; document the professional-diligence steps taken (UCPD Art. 5).

Fix age assurance: do not rely on the self-declared '18+' filter when analytics prove it is failing. Require robust age verification from the platform before running any profiled ads (GDPR Art. 8 / DSA Art. 28).

Require every sponsored segment to carry clear, contemporaneous paid-partnership disclosure — verbal '#ad/paid sponsorship' at each shout-out plus persistent on-screen labelling (UCPD Annex I point 11, DSA Art. 26).

Document and confirm the lawful basis for the targeting and any brand-received analytics; if relying on consent, ensure valid consent (with parental consent for under-threshold minors), and if on legitimate interests, complete and retain an LIA (GDPR Arts. 5, 6).
Ensure any discount-code redemption/landing page carries a compliant Art. 13 privacy notice and signposts the opt-out/objection route for interest-based advertising (GDPR Arts. 13 and 21).
Review all final streamer scripts and creatives to strip any direct purchase-command language aimed at the teen-heavy audience, to stay clear of the UCPD Annex I point 28 prohibition.

campaign.title: TechBay headphone 'was/now' promotion
campaign.text: Electronics retailer promotes: 'NovaBuds Pro — was €199, NOW €99. Half price!' Pricing records show the €199 price was charged for 9 days in the past year; the prevailing price for the preceding four months was €119, and a competitor-matching widget had already displayed €109 for most of that period. The 'half price' claim is repeated in comparison tables and search ads. Stock and delivery claims are accurate and no urgency devices are used.

detected_practices: misleading reference price (highest price only charged 9 days)
'half price' savings claim across comparison tables and search ads
reference price not reflecting prior prevailing price (€119) or competitor-matched price (€109)
triage.summary: Electronics retailer runs a 'was €199, NOW €99 — half price' promotion on web and search where the €199 reference price was only charged for 9 days, while the actual prevailing price for the prior four months was €119 (with a competitor-matched price around €109). The savings/reference-price claim is potentially misleading. No AI, personalisation, or minor-targeting elements are declared or apparent.

findings.title: Misleading actions
findings.rationale: Art. 6 prohibits practices that deceive the average consumer regarding the existence of a specific price advantage and cause a transactional decision they would not otherwise take. The €199 'was' price was only charged for 9 days across the whole past year, while the actual prevailing price for the preceding four months was €119 and a competitor-matched price of €109 was shown for most of that period. Anchoring the discount to a fleeting, unrepresentative high price creates a false impression of a 50% ('half price') saving; the genuine recent saving is far smaller (roughly €119/€109 down to €99). This is a classic misleading reference-price / fake-discount practice.
findings.evidence_quote: 'NovaBuds Pro — was €199, NOW €99. Half price!'
findings.recommendation: Base the 'was' reference price on a genuine prior price actually charged for a meaningful period — in practice the lowest price applied in the 30 days before the reduction (Price Indication Directive Art. 6a) — rather than a €199 price only live for 9 days. Recalculate and correct the savings claim (e.g. compare against €119/€109) and remove the '50% / Half price' framing unless it is literally true against a genuine prior price. Ensure the corrected reference price and any savings percentage are consistent across comparison tables and search ads.

verdicts.notes: The campaign engages UCPD Art. 6(1)(d) (misleading actions as to the existence of a specific price advantage). The "was €199, NOW €99 — Half price!" claim relies on a reference price (€199) that was charged for only 9 days in the past year, whereas the genuine prevailing price for the preceding four months was €119 (with a competitor-matched €109 displayed most of the time). The advertised 50% saving is materially exaggerated relative to the real prior price, and is likely to cause consumers to transact when they otherwise might not. No blacklist (Annex I) practice is triggered — there are no urgency/scarcity devices, no ceasing-trade claim, and no AI/personalisation — so the assessment turns on the general misleading-actions prohibition.

report.executive_summary: This campaign promotes NovaBuds Pro headphones as "was €199, NOW €99 — Half price!" across web and search. The core problem is the reference price: €199 was only charged for 9 days in the past year, while the actual prevailing price for the preceding four months was €119, and a competitor-matched price of €109 was shown most of that time. Anchoring a "half price" claim to that fleeting, unrepresentative high price overstates the real saving — the genuine discount is roughly €119/€109 down to €99, not 50%. This is a classic misleading reference-price / fake-discount practice and is likely to breach the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (Art. 6), which also engages the Price Indication Directive's rule (Art. 6a) requiring reference to the lowest price applied in the prior 30 days. AI Act, GDPR and DSA are not engaged, as there is no generative AI, personalisation, or platform intermediation. No urgency or scarcity devices are used, and stock/delivery claims are accurate, so the risk is confined to the pricing claim — but that risk is significant and should be fixed before the campaign runs in the EU.
recommendations: Stop using the €199 'was' price and the '50% / Half price' framing until corrected — €199 was only live for 9 days and cannot support a genuine discount claim.

Set the reference 'was' price to the lowest price actually applied in the 30 days before the reduction, as required by the Price Indication Directive (Art. 6a) — in practice around €119/€109, not €199.
Recalculate the advertised saving against the genuine prior price (e.g. €119/€109 down to €99) and only state a percentage that is literally true.
Ensure the corrected reference price and savings figures are consistent across all comparison tables and search ads, including the competitor-matching widget.
Keep records demonstrating the reference price was genuinely charged for the relevant period, so the corrected claim can be substantiated if challenged.
